articles.body: Anthropic Subscriptions Offer 5x+ More Value Than OpenAI    SemiAnalysis

scored.body: Subscription plans are still the primary way consumers and small businesses pay for AI. These plans are highly subsidized—as we previously explained in June—but can still make economic sense as powerful customer acquisition and marketing tools. For example, the goodwill engendered by OpenAI’s generous resets is partially responsible for the recent surge in Codex adoption and has forced Anthropic to repeatedly walk back planned subscription nerfs to avoid getting clobbered in the court of public opinion.Furthermore, because subscription plans are so heavily subsidized, they can also have a large impact on margins and revenue per MW despite only being a small portion of total revenue. Consider the following rough numbers for Anthropic.Despite being just 10% of overall revenue, subscriptions can take up over 40% of inference compute and lower blended revenue per MW by ~$36M. Subscriptions are even more important for OpenAI, as they make up a larger portion of their total revenue. For specific numbers, see our Tokenomics Model.In other words, if you want to accurately model AI lab financials, you need to understand their subscription limits.So how do limits actually work? The way to think about subscriptions is that your monthly payment grants you some numbers of “credits”. Each (model, token type) combo consumes a different amount of credits. Because credit cost ratios can differ dramatically from API price ratios, the “value” of the same plan changes depending on what model and workload you’re running. Put differently, it doesn’t make sense to say a plan is worth $X in isolation—you need to consider the full (plan, model, workload) tuple.Here’s how the API-equivalent value of the same $200/month Claude plan changes depending on the model and workload.A single static snapshot isn’t enough either. Labs publicly change their limits all the time with promos and new model releases. They can also silently change limits whenever they want by tweaking credit costs. Ideally, you’d re-check the cost of each (plan, model, token type) daily so you can surface any changes in real-time.This is exactly what SemiAnalysis has done with our new Subscriptions Dashboard available exclusively to Tokenomics Model subscribers. Besides every OpenAI and Anthropic subscription, we also track Meta, SpaceXAI, Cursor, Cognition, Z.ai, MiniMax, and Moonshot.A screenshot of our dashboard showing a small subset of the available data. Source: SemiAnalysis Tokenomics ModelNew providers, plans, and models will be added as soon as they’re released. The rest of the article will give an overview of everyone’s current limits. All token and dollar amounts below assume agentic usage unless otherwise specified.Tokens are generally priced per MTok (million tokens) across the following types:Input: Fresh tokens added to the LLM’s context window that aren’t cachedCache write: Input tokens that are cached for multi-turn conversations. Generally slightly more expensive than regular input tokens.Cache read: Tokens from previous turns that are already cached in the conversation. Generally extremely cheap compared to uncached tokens.Output: Tokens generated by the model. The most expensive token type.Additionally, some models charge more for tokens above a certain context window. Those models typically compact before that expensive context window is reached, so we also keep our measurements below it.Source: OpenAISubscription plans don’t expose this fine grained pricing. Instead, they provide a simple 0 to 100% usage meter across 5-hour and 7-day windows, and sometimes a separate meter for a model like Fable. Subscription tiers are then differentiated by usage multipliers relative only to the provider’s other plans. OpenAI for example used to advertise “Expanded Codex usage” in their $20 Plus plan, “5x more usage than Plus” in the $100 Pro plan, and “20x more usage” in the $200 Pro plan until they cut their $200 plan usage in half and removed all relative usage from their pricing page.Screenshot of Claude Code meters. Source: Claude Code CLIWe compute the subscription-rate of each (plan, model, token type) triple by running experiments that isolate one token type at a time and watching how far the model provider’s meter moves. An experiment is some number of repeated calls using a specific prompt that maximizes one token type while minimizing all the others.Input, cache writes, and cache reads share the same prompt template. We use a portion of War and Peace since some models will refuse to respond if given large blocks of gibberish. For the input token experiments, we use a random tag on every call to ensure nothing gets cached. The cache write experiments run the same way but with the prompt marked for caching, so each new tag forces a new cache entry. The cache read experiments use a fixed tag, so the first call writes the cache and every repeat reads it.For the output token experiments, we used a technical essay to force long outputs because models will refuse mechanical prompts like “repeat SemiAnalysis 100,000 times”.For every call we record two things: how many tokens of each type the provider billed, and what the usage meter read. Turning those into a price takes three steps.Providers generally report usage on a meter that moves in fixed amounts. This could be a whole percentage point, a credit, a cent etc... A single request often does not move the meter at all, so the cost of one request cannot be measured directly.Instead, we measure in steps. As requests run, we keep a running total of the tokens used. Each time the meter rises, we store that total. The tokens used between two meter moves make up one step, which is the cost of moving the meter by one unit.We drop two partial steps. When a run starts, the meter is already part of the way to its next move, so the tokens before the first move are less than a full step and would make the rate look higher than it is. The tokens after the last move never finish a step, so we drop those as well.To get a rate, we add up how far the meter moved over the complete steps and divide by the tokens used in them. Providers charge differently for input, output, and cached tokens, so we calculate a separate rate for each.Caveats:Because we see the meter only once per request, a single step can be off by up to one request. These errors don’t add up with more consecutive steps, so we track a range instead of a single number, and the range gets narrower the more steps we count. We keep adding steps until the range is within ±5%, then report the rate across all of them.No request contains only one type of token. Some plans, for example, require a set of instructions on every request. We subtract that extra amount using the prices we measured for the other types.Reading from the cache costs almost nothing on some plans and may not move the meter at all. If the meter does not move after 500M cache read tokens, we assume that cache reads are free.We read every meter a plan shows after every request. This could be a 5-hour limit, a weekly limit, and for models like Fable, its own weekly limit. So each token type gets a price on each meter. This is how much of that limit a million tokens uses. From each price we work out how many tokens fit e.g. if a million tokens use 5% of a limit, the whole limit holds 20 million.The 5-hour limit resets many times within a week, so a month is capped by the weekly limits.Lastly, we compute the API-equivalent value by converting the limit % consumed by a million tokens of each type into a dollar amount. For example, if you consume 1% of a $200 plan’s monthly limit, that’s $2.Then, we assume a workload shape, and compute how many total tokens you can get from each plan given this ratio. For the agentic workload, we use our own usage ratios in September as reported in our Tokenomics Model. Finally, we multiply by the blended price per MTok at API prices to get the API-equivalent value.While refining our methodology, we ran into a very confusing situation where just 1 of 3 of the same subscription we tested for a particular provider had ~20% lower limits than the other 2. This unlucky account happened to be significantly older as well, and we were worried that the provider had some cursed setup where they changed subscription limits depending on the age of the account.Fortunately, after reaching out to the provider, we were able to confirm this was not the case and that our unlucky account was part of an “extremely tiny” A/B test they were running on limits. Additionally, they wanted to emphasize that they “didn’t just decrease limits wholesale” and were instead testing “how to better balance when people hit limits”.This conclusion is interesting for two reasons:It proves providers can silently change subscription limits at any timeOur method is sensitive enough to detect these subtle changes!The biggest question in AI subscription land is how Anthropic’s limits compare to OpenAI’s. Note that OpenAI just made some massive changes to their subscriptions last week, halving the API-equivalent value for the $200 plan and introducing a new $500 tier. The following numbers describe the current state of OAI vs ANT. Afterwards, we will examine OpenAI’s recent changes in depth.Limits are quite similar across the board for GPT-6 Astra vs Fable 5.1, though remember that Fable can only be used for 50% of your limit. In other words, your $200 ANT plan would still have 50% left after consuming $2,485 worth of Fable 5.1, whereas the equivalent OAI plan would be fully exhausted after $2,897 of Astra.This extra 50% starts becoming very relevant when we compare Opus 5.5 vs GPT 6.1 Sol.At this mid-tier of models—which both companies market as the intended daily driver for most users—Anthropic is an overwhelmingly better deal, offering ~5x the API-equivalent value across the board. You could argue that this is unfair for OAI because 6.1 Sol is much cheaper per token than Opus 5.5, but the gap is still massive even if you switch to comparing the number of tokens.Overall, we believe API-equivalent value is the single best number for capturing the “value” of a subscription plan, but there are times where raw token volumes can be more appropriate. For example, if a model is a particularly bad (or good) deal at API prices, then the API-equivalent value will of course be misleading.Token efficiency is also an extremely relevant factor, but the industry unfortunately lacks reliable data here. Many people like to cite this chart from Artificial Analysis, but we do not believe the benchmark tasks in the AA Intelligence Index are at all representative of real work people do with LLMs.Our tracking confirmed the 50% value reduction for OpenAI’s $200 plan announced by Tibo. $200 plans purchased before the cut will keep the old higher limits until October 29th, but newly purchased plans immediately start with the lower limits.As you can see, OpenAI specifically halved the number of tokens you get for each model tier. This caused the API-equivalent value for Sol class models to drop by over 50% because OAI also cut cached input token pricing for 6.1 Sol.The new $500 plan only offers 21% more Astra than the old $200 plan. Interestingly, the API-equivalent value for Sol class models actually decreased due to the aforementioned 6.1 Sol price cut.Of course, 300 TPS Ultrafast was the real headline feature for the $500 plan and we are currently testing its limits. Results will be published to Tokenomics Model subscribers as soon as they’re available. We are also actively testing the limits when using your ChatGPT subscription on third party apps like Devin.The $200/month plan also used to be significantly more subsidized than OpenAI’s other subscriptions. If we normalize each (plan, model) combo to the API-equivalent value and tokens per dollar, we can see that Pro 100 offered ~2x more per-dollar value than Plus on Astra and Pro 200 was another ~2x on top of Pro 100 across all models.With last week’s cut, Pro 100, 200, and 500 all offer the same tokens per dollar for every model. Plus is also comparable for Sol but offers a relatively worse deal on Astra.Anthropic, on the other hand, already offered the same per-dollar value for all of their subscription tiers and currently crushes OpenAI.OpenAI used to be lauded by indie developers for their generous subscription limits compared to Anthropic, but this is simply no longer true today. Opus 5.5 on any Claude subscription offers far better value than anything from OpenAI.The only counter argument for OpenAI is that none of their Pro plans have a 5 hour limit, which makes it easier to consume a higher % of your total monthly limit. However, we don’t think this offsets the ~4x higher API-equivalent value offered by Opus 5.5 on Claude plans.We’ve seen a number of significant price cuts recently to Anthropic and OpenAI models.Fable 5.1 cut cache reads by 75% vs Fable 5Opus 5.5 cut input and output token pricing by 20% vs Opus 5 and cache reads by 60%.GPT 6.1 Sol cut cache reads by 50% vs GPT 6 sol. This was after making GPT 6 Sol 60-67% cheaper vs 5.6 Sol.One important question is whether the labs adjust token limits after these price cuts, such that the API-equivalent value of your subscription stays constant.We already showed earlier that OpenAI didn’t change Sol token limits on the $200/month plan when they released 6.1 Sol. This caused the API-equivalent value to drop ~30%.Anthropic also didn’t increase Fable token limits at all with the release of 5.1, but they did up Opus token limits with the 5.5 price cut.However, the ~20% token increase for Max plans and ~50% increase for the Pro plan weren’t enough to fully offset the API price cut.As we explained at the start of this article, subscription gross margins are way lower than API and meaningfully reduce revenue per MW for both OpenAI and Anthropic. Both companies are well aware of this fact but have chosen two different strategies for reducing subscriber subsidies.For a given plan, Anthropic decreases the API-equivalent value for more premium models. The drop off is small between Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5, but becomes very meaningful with Fable 5.1.Reducing the API-equivalent value as you release more powerful models at higher list prices is the more subtle way to stop subsidizing subscriptions. Assuming 100% utilization and 92% API gross margins, maxing out Opus 5.5 vs Fable 5.1 usage corresponds to -369% and 1% gross margins respectively. If we were to use a more realistic average utilization of 20%, then gross margins rise to 6% and 80% respectively.In other words, Anthropic would likely already have software like margins on their subscription plans if everyone only used Fable. Opus class models will continue to become cheaper to serve over time as Anthropic figures out how to make the model smaller, and new model tiers above Fable will have even lower subscription limits (assuming they’re included at all).OpenAI, on the other hand, picked the nuclear option of just immediately cutting to Fable-level limits across the board.The downside of this approach is supposed to be public backlash, but OpenAI has somehow managed to more or less avoid this entirely. It’s likely some combination of all the good DevDay PR drowning out the negative news from the day prior and grandfathering existing plans for an additional month.Despite being compute poor, the Chinese labs still offer subsidized subscription plans, but the level of subsidization varies dramatically between models.Here’s how they compare to OpenAI and Anthropic after normalizing per dollar.Value per dollar increases as you buy higher tier subscriptions from the Chinese labs. On average, the API-equivalent value per dollar is a little less than the ~12x you get from OpenAI.The final comparison we’ll consider is OpenAI and Anthropic models on their own first party plans vs third party wrappers like Cursor and Cognition (Devin).

articles.body: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come    CNBC

scored.body: CNBC is now accepting nominations for the 2027 Changemakers List.Google DeepMind Chief AI Readiness Officer Lila Ibrahim may be the only person in the world with that title, and she says she would not have accepted it if she didn't believe that the AI scales will ultimately tip to the positive."I don't think I could do this job if I didn't believe that the benefits will outweigh the risks," she told CNBC's Julia Boorstin in the latest episode of the "CNBC Changemakers" podcast.Ibrahim has spent almost a decade helping Google DeepMind build artificial intelligence and stay ahead of the thorny ethical, and downright existential, questions that surround the rapidly advancing technology. Now, she is focused on whether workers, schools and communities are prepared for what comes next. Ibrahim was named to the 2025 CNBC Changemakers list.Earlier this year, Ibrahim shifted into her new role from being Google DeepMind's chief operating officer. The job, she says, is not about DeepMind's own readiness for AI, but about helping the rest of the world understand and adapt as changes accelerate and as AI moves beyond the lab and into more parts of everyday life, from scientific research and weather forecasting to education and workplace productivity. For Ibrahim, the question is not whether AI will become more capable, or exactly how it will. The more important question, she says, is whether people have a say in how it is used. "While I might not know what it will do, I know that we still can – we have the agency to shape how we get there," she said. But she added, "You can't shape the right future unless you do so with the communities that it's going to impact."For workers confronting headlines about AI-driven layoffs and automation, her advice is simple: begin using the technology. "You have to start using AI yourself and create the time and space to do it," she said. "You don't have to be the smartest in the room."How DeepMind corporate teams use AI every dayIbrahim and her teams at DeepMind put this into practice daily. She says the "most transformational" AI use case for herself at work on a daily basis is with briefing documents. "I went into engineering partly because I didn't want to have to read and write a lot, and the ability to be able to synthesize in a way that I can absorb information very quickly has been transformational, not only for me but the team that has to prepare that," she said. "And given how much is going on right now and trying to move at pace, it's not necessarily where everyone adds the most value. Being able to be efficient in that and then free up everybody to do the work ... the big thinking ... way, way better use of their time," she said.Ibrahim breaks down her daily AI use case method into three questions that she asks all team members:How are you using AI? What would help you use it more? Where are you not using AI? That third question is the human talent element, and she said it is critical. "That's what we need to hire for; we need to reward. This is what we want to continue developing in our employees," she said. And she added that goes for herself as well. "AI can help automate all of my tasks, but it cannot automate my Tuesdays," Ibrahim said. With her two teenage daughters in mind, she says the AI learning process needs to start long before people enter the workforce. "They're going to inherit the technology we're developing, and yet they're not getting a voice in how this is being taught to them, how it's being integrated into their schools or into their life, so I think I would love us to see schools lean in a bit more to work with the teachers," Ibrahim said. "Teachers always have to be in the lead with the students to say how do we explore the boundaries for what makes sense with with AI," she said, but she added that students need to "grow up more literate in what the technology is and isn't, and also what are responsible use cases for it."Thinking back on her professional path from graduate student in electrical engineering to work on designing Intel's Pentium processor and now to Google DeepMind and AI, Ibrahim said "so much has already changed in our lifetime, and the same will be [true for] the generation that follows. So all we can do is teach a love of learning and curiosity, and the resilience to know that change is coming, and they can actually have a role in how that change happens.""One of the things that I think is going to be important is continuous learning," she said.Follow and listen to CNBC Changemakers: Women Leading in the Age of AI wherever you get your podcasts.

scored.body:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Jacob Coxon, the former Anthropic researcher who sparked industry chaos by warning AI could kill all humans, doubled down on the threat of human extinction at a New York City Council hearing Monday.

He appeared at the request of Council Speaker Julie Menin, who urged AI whistleblowers to testify as the city seeks to get more involved in regulation of the industry.

“From my experience, the companies are being extremely reckless given the stakes,” Coxon said Monday. “The companies run on a startup mindset: move fast, break things, fix them later. That works for a photo sharing app. It does not work for building the most powerful technology ever built.”

Anthropic whistleblower Jacob Coxon testifying at a City Council hearing on Oct. 5, 2026. Stephen Yang for NY Post

He added that researchers and workers have already lost the ability to fully control AI systems.

“We don’t understand its drives or why it does the things it does,” he said. “We’re approaching the point at which the AI systems will be capable of improving themselves.”

“At my last job, I was in some sense working to automate myself…I can tell you firsthand that the majority of the code is now written by AI, and people do not check it that carefully anymore.”

Ex-Google DeepMind researcher Alex Turner and Daniel Kokotajlo — a former OpenAI researcher who now runs the AI Futures Project, focused on the societal impact of the emerging tech — also testified that the fast-advancing tech poses major risks.

“A superintelligent swarm could wrest control of human civilization,” Turner said. “It would know that we would try to stop it from achieving its priorities, so the swarm would likely wait until it’s too late to shut it off; there would be no going back. I myself would guess AI takeover chances at roughly one in three.”

Former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo (left) and Google DeepMind researcher Alex Turner (right) virtually testified at the hearing. Stephen Yang for NY Post

Coxon quit his job as an AI researcher Anthropic last month and warned that AI could kill humans. Stephen Yang for NY Post

Kokotajlo argued that even though tech leaders are now supporting calls for more stringent regulations, they shouldn’t necessarily be trusted with that power.

“Even if they do manage to maintain control, I don’t think we should trust them with that control,” he said. “I think that there’s a very real chance that they could use it to become dictators or oligarchs here in the United States.”

Reps for Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta all appeared virtually as some of the companies’ most outspoken critics testified. The tech giants did not send their CEOs, but rather policy leads and other executives.

Morgan Dwyer of OpenAI (top left), Shane Cahill of Meta (top right) and Alice Friend of Google virtually represented their companies at the hearing. Stephen Yang for NY Post

Last month, Coxon quit his job at Anthropic and issued a chilling warning that AI is advancing so quickly that it “could kill us all by the end of the decade,” kicking discussions about safeguards and regulations into high gear.

In an unusual move, the leaders of top AI companies responded by calling for more restrictions on their own product releases – warning that global cooperation is needed to prevent bots from running out of control.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a lengthy essay calling on rival companies to jointly slow their development of AI models, fearful of the risks that come with “recursive self-improvement,” or RSI – when bots grow smart enough to keep evolving independently.

People protesting against AI and data centers outside of the City Council hearing on Oct. 5, 2026. Getty Images

OpenAI’s Sam Altman, SpaceX founder Elon Musk and Microsoft billionaire Bill Gates have also sounded the alarm over the risks of unregulated AI advancement.

President Trump, however, has argued that the bigger risk is allowing China to gain a lead in the AI race by slowing development in the US.

The AI whistleblowers pushed back on this argument during their testimonies Monday, saying the more pressing threat is getting these bots under control — not keeping an edge over foreign adversaries.

A protester holding a sign calling on AI companies to “hit the brakes” on the controversial technology. Getty Images

“We have to first solve the immediate pressing threat here domestically, and then try to make sure that China doesn’t get us killed either, to put it sort of bluntly and simply,” Kokotajlo said.

The tech giants reportedly agreed to testify at Monday’s hearing after lawmakers threatened to subpoena them to force them to attend.

Menin claimed Google, OpenAI and Anthropic changed their tune and agreed to show up only after the council sent letters threatening to use its subpoena power.

City Council Speaker Julie Menin threatened to subpoena AI companies if they didn’t have representatives testify at the AI hearing. Stephen Yang for NY Post

NYC policymakers and tech execs are debating a package of bills aimed at regulating AI companies in the Big Apple, including by mandating “kill switches” and offering unprecedented cash rewards for whistleblowers.

Though the industry is typically subject to state and federal regulations, New York City is trying to get more involved in the safeguarding of the new technology as it rapidly expands in the city.

It comes after New York Gov. Kathy Hochul announced last month that the state will start requiring AI companies to register in a government portal starting in November, and forcing them to report critical safety incidents within 72 hours.

Coxon claimed that AI companies are being “extremely reckless.” Stephen Yang for NY Post

The City Council’s proposals include a mandate that companies cannot “market, offer for sale, or deploy” AI systems in the five boroughs without vetting the tech with outside experts.

It is also proposing a law that would require so-called “kill switches” for any AI tool being used in the city, which the council defines as a “human override that can shut down the system.”

Failure to comply with either of the laws would result in a $25,000 fine.

Another potential bill would create a “first-in-the-nation” cash reward system for whistleblowers, funded by the fines collected from bad actors.

Officials from NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration – including Samuel Levine, commissioner of the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, and Sarah Milstein from the tech office – were also set to testify at the hearing.

scored.body: Representative imageMicrosoft and Meta are reportedly curbing their internal staff's reliance on Anthropic’s Claude models, attempting to control mounting computing expenses while steering engineers toward their own in-house artificial intelligence (AI) tools. The shift, reported by The Information, highlights a ‘complicated problem’ confronting Anthropic: its most lucrative corporate buyers also double as its fiercest market rivals. Even as both tech giants continue to offer Claude to external clients through enterprise products and cloud infrastructure, their executive leadership is taking direct measures to limit how much their own developers lean on Anthropic's systems.Microsoft cuts Anthropic projections by a thirdInside Microsoft, top leaders, including Azure Cloud head Scott Guthrie and developer tools leader Jay Parikh, have instructed teams to practice greater discipline with coding tools, monitor employee consumption and prioritise non-Anthropic alternatives, the report said.It added that Microsoft previously projected spending at least $1 billion per year on Anthropic tools for internal operations, but has scaled back that budget estimate by more than a third. Within its 60,000-plus cloud and AI unit, individual monthly spending ceilings on AI models that previously reached $100,000 per person have been cut to roughly $10,000 in most instances, frustrating some engineers who feel their technical workflow is now constrained.Internal managers now receive daily tracking metrics detailing exact employee expenditures and specific models accessed via GitHub Copilot. Citing earlier internal communications from Parikh, the report says that the company introduced division-wide token budgets and shifted standard defaults toward lower-cost OpenAI models.Despite the internal cutbacks, Microsoft’s commercial partnership with Anthropic remains intact. Microsoft continues to support Anthropic models across Azure and integrates Claude into Copilot productivity applications, including Word, Excel and PowerPoint.Facebook-parent Meta slashes Claude Code footprint by halfMeta has similarly taken a step back from Anthropic's developer assistant, Claude Code. The Information reports that internal usage of Claude Code at the social media company tumbled from roughly 60,000 users earlier this year to around 30,000 recently. While part of that drop was tied to spring layoffs that eliminated roughly 10 percent of Meta's then 78,000-person staff, the primary catalyst has been the rapid rollout of internal alternatives.An internal-only coding assistant, MetaCode has expanded its user base to more than 30,000 employees. Meta previously utilised around 7,000 weekly active users on the platform in August to gather feedback and refine training runs for its underlying architectures.Meta is also said to be directing personnel toward its proprietary Muse Spark model lineup. Its external-facing rival to Claude Code, known as Muse Code, which began testing with third-party clients in August, recently counted over 6,000 employee users.Anthropic's growth faces enterprise headwindsThe internal pullbacks by Meta and Microsoft provide a contrast to Anthropic’s otherwise runaway commercial momentum. The AI startup's annualized revenue climbed past $65 billion by the close of July, a rise from approximately $9 billion at the end of 2025, according to reporting from The Information and Reuters.

articles.headline: Exclusive: OpenAI is piloting a ‘mission interview’ for job candidates - Fortune
articles.body: Exclusive: OpenAI is piloting a ‘mission interview’ for job candidates    Fortune

scored.body:
Candidates interviewing for certain teams at OpenAI will now go through a new step in the process, knowing as the “mission interview.”

The company is currently introducing it as a new pilot program, starting with the marketing and human resources teams, OpenAI told Fortune on Monday. The goal is to give job candidates a dedicated space to talk about how they will contribute to OpenAI’s mission, which is “to ensure that artificial general intelligence (AGI) benefits all of humanity.”

Specifically, OpenAI wants to gauge how candidates think, including their judgment and ability to weigh trade-offs—traits that are increasingly critical as artificial intelligence companies work to control technology with great benefits as well as potential dangers. There is no “right” answer, an OpenAI representative said; skepticism and disagreement are welcome, as is intellectual diversity.

The person conducting the interview will be from a separate team from whatever role the candidate is applying for. OpenAI is also creating a training program that interested employees can complete to become certified to conduct the interviews, though the program is just starting to ramp up.

The evolution in OpenAI’s recruiting process is a marker of the company looking to standardize its evaluations as it matures and balloons in size. The company, which has roughly 8,000 employees worldwide, has 830 open roles as of this writing. By standardizing the process, OpenAI aims to have a consistent measure to evaluate new employees across teams.

Many tech companies, including Meta and Amazon, have their own version of a “mission interview,” which is somewhat akin to a test of cultural fit. For example, Amazon employees can be trained as “bar raisers”—interviewers from outside the hiring team, who assess whether a candidate meets Amazon’s company-wide “Leadership Principals.”

In Anthropic’s version, interviewers reportedly test if candidates are joining the AI lab for its mission or the money, according to Axios. Jobs at leading AI companies are incredibly lucrative, with many positions at OpenAI currently offering over $300K salaries, and much more with stock included.

One software engineer with six years of experience reportedly received an offer from OpenAI for $935,000 total compensation, with a $385,000 base, and $2.2 million of restricted stock shares (RSUs) vesting over four years, according to the anonymous professional network Blind. Anthropic allegedly offered another person $620,000 in total compensation, according to another Blind post.

scored.body:
Artificial intelligence is expensive, and Anthropic put a price tag on it. The company said in its IPO prospectus that it plans to spend $518 billion over the next 10 years on cloud and computing power for technology it believes could be more transformative than industrialization, electricity, or the internet.

Anthropic has already locked in long-term cloud computing deals with hyperscalers such as Amazon (AMZN +1.84%) and Alphabet (GOOG +0.38%) (GOOGL +0.62%), but investors should note a few key takeaways from this major news.

Image source: Getty Images.

The prices of AI components will continue to rise

Anthropic's spending goals indicate a long-term AI tailwind. Not only will Anthropic continue to spend money, but other competitors will also increase their spending. Artificial intelligence is still in its early innings, and none of the hyperscalers want to be left behind.

The entire data center build-out requires memory chips, electricity, physical buildings, specialized cooling systems, and an array of other essentials that don't receive as much attention. All of those inputs will see rising demand, resulting in greater pricing power for their suppliers.

Research firm TrendForce anticipates high bandwidth memory prices will increase by 121% year over year in 2027. Prices have already soared for these foundational chips as demand far outpaces supply.

It's not just chips. AI data center provider Nebius (NBIS +8.23%) has seen its annual contract value per megawatt more than triple in less than a year for short-term capacity deals. A shortage of compute power combined with insatiable demand is enabling neoclouds to substantially raise prices without meeting meaningful customer resistance.

Consumers and businesses are using these products

Claude and other AI models already have real user case studies. Use of these models is becoming as commonplace as a Google search, and revenue is scaling quickly. Anthropic closed out 2025 with $4.6 billion in revenue; as of July 2026, the business's annual revenue run rate had topped $65 billion.

This jump shows how quickly AI products and services can scale. It's this growth rate that makes the $2 trillion market cap it's hoping to achieve with its initial public offering more feasible, but any slowdown in its growth would cast serious doubt on whether it merits that valuation.

Anthropic is still burning through cash, but the hope is that its revenue growth will remain parabolic and eventually produce a profit. As long as new customers continue to sign up and existing customers stick around, the company can realize that objective.

More importantly, Anthropic is an example of broader AI growth and the commercial value of the technology. If it achieves a profitable return on investment, that gives tech giants, enterprises, and other AI labs a green light to increase spending.

Substantial capital is flowing throughout the artificial intelligence industry, and that trend is set to accelerate. It could make many investors wealthy.

articles.headline: AI Agents Want to Participate in Your Fandom. Should You Let Them? - Sportico.com
articles.body: AI Agents Want to Participate in Your Fandom. Should You Let Them?    Sportico.com

scored.body:
Being a sports fan is more complicated than ever.

Fandom can feel like a series of headaches, if not a second job. Games are played at all sorts of times on myriad channels requiring multiple subscriptions. Good luck keeping up. If you decide to go in person, tickets can be bought on countless platforms at prices that appear to change by the minute. Which seats are worth the cost, which friends are willing to pay how much to come with, and will LeBron James even end up playing that night? That’s all before setting aside the time to manage a fantasy football roster, oversee a gambling hobby, or make sure you’re fully briefed for the next all-hands—sorry, hangout—at the bar.

Enter AI.

Meta’s Muse, launched last month, is a “personal AI agent” designed to complete digital tasks so you can “focus on the things that matter.” The tool sits atop iOS’ free app download list, having hit 5 million installs faster than ChatGPT or Claude did, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. For comparison, Meta’s Horizon Worlds metaverse bet reportedly peaked at roughly 300,000 monthly active users in 2022. The company’s stock had its best month since 2022 in September, jumping 27%.

Last week, OpenAI released its own “always-on” agents, named Dots, though they’re currently only available to those on the company’s premium subscription tiers. Each Dot “takes important work off your plate so you get more of your time and attention back,” OpenAI said in its announcement.

For years, digital platforms have demanded more and more of our focus. Now, they’re offering to return some of it. Over the last few days, I endeavored to find out what these tools might be able to do for sports fans.

A few projects I tasked AI tools with:

Monitoring ticket prices for an upcoming New York Liberty playoff game

Identifying the most-praised concession stands near my section at Barclays Center

Adding future playoff matchups to my calendar as TV times and network assignments are announced, with where-to-watch info included in each event entry

Building a model to project how likely the North Carolina Courage are to make the NWSL playoffs, and which non-Courage games will have a big impact over the regular season’s final three weeks

Proposing a fantasy football trade that could strengthen both rosters, but especially my woebegone side

Without going into excruciating detail, the big picture is: They largely worked, with Muse singling out an 0-4 fantasy team likely willing to shake up its roster while another AI agent competitor, Instinct, encouraged me to try Barclays’ signature burger at Paisano’s. And, as any of these companies’ executives will tell you, the systems promise to only get smarter from here.

Still, there are things to consider before diving in.

To perform most tasks, agents will need information from you. Maybe they’ll want access to your calendar, or your ESPN log-in credentials. They might also need to read all your emails or gain the ability to make purchases on your behalf. Though providers have stressed the security work that has gone into their agents, it’s still reasonable to hesitate before handing over your online identity.

It also remains challenging to verify an agent’s readout. Are those really the best-value tickets? Are you sure the Courage are in good shape? Or are you hallucinating? How can I know?

Meta has said its free Muse app will be profitable in part by taking a small cut of transactions processed by its agents. That gives the platform an incentive to drive more purchases on connected sites, including Dick’s and Fanatics. As any social media user is by now well aware, what’s best for the platform isn’t always what’s best for the user. Ticketmaster is also connected to Muse, though buys will continue to flow through Ticketmaster’s marketplace, the company has said.

AI is already disrupting business-customer interactions. Bots are overrunning the web, with some executives forecasting a world in which autonomous traffic outnumbers human internet searchers 1,000-to-1. Early use cases for individualized agents have included filing forms to have a pothole filled or messy telephone wires cleaned up, though these human response systems aren’t built to handle a massive uptick in requests. Stadiums’ in-venue help numbers could be similarly overwhelmed.

My fantasy football trade offer has a lot smaller chance of being successful if its recipient also received a dozen other AI-generated requests yesterday. In a couple of years, we may be forced to enlist agents to handle all of that inbound for us. And then what’s the point?

It’s worth thinking about which parts of the sports fan experience you want to hand over to an AI helper.

We’re supposed to read the waiver wire reports and make draft picks ourselves, I think, just like we ought to engage in low-info barstool debates and spend days in our group chats planning a bucket-list sports trip.

To an agent, those are tedious tasks. To sports diehards, they’re the whole point. Only a robot would see fandom as a job to be done.

I would’ve gotten a less accurate answer had I checked with a pal about North Carolina’s playoff hopes, but I would have had more fun doing it. Next time I’m at a game, I might just ask the person next to me where they got their foot-long hot dog, rather than pulling out my phone.

It’s all something to ponder as I await my agent’s next update on those Liberty ticket prices…

scored.body:
In brief

Investigators say Carli Michelle Heller wrote on Sept. 26 that she would "shoot up" the Lee County Sheriff's Office, and said the next day that she had a new gun.

According to the arrest report, Anthropic's safety systems flagged the entries and a human review team reported them to law enforcement.

Anthropic's consumer terms reserve the right, at its sole discretion, to report a user's inputs to law enforcement.

A Florida woman said she uses AI like a diary. Now she's facing a felony charge, and the reader who sent her there was someone she never meant to show it to.Carli Michelle Heller, of Bonita Springs, was arrested after investigators found she wrote on Sept. 26 that she would “shoot up” the Lee County Sheriff’s Office, according to the local WINK News. Per investigations, her Claude account showed conversations saying that she had gotten a new gun by the next day.Myriad: Which company will IPO next? Click to make your prediction.The arrest report says Anthropic’s platform monitors for key phrases and threatening content. Because of the severity of the statements, they went to a human review team, which reported them to law enforcement.Deputies identified Heller, went to her home, and detained her without incident. She is charged with making a written threat of violence.Anthropic’s paperwork doesn’t hide any of this. Its consumer terms reserve the right, at the company’s “sole discretion,” to report a user’s inputs, outputs, or actions to law enforcement. Its privacy policy, effective Sept. 10, 2026, also allows sharing data with police when the company has a good-faith belief that disclosure is reasonably necessary to prevent serious harm.Effectively, even opting out of handling your data for model trading gives Anthropic the right to use your data for three months instead of five years, so your chats are never private.The same policy says conversations flagged for safety review are still used to improve Anthropic’s ability to detect harmful content. A flagged diary entry can end up as training material for the detectors.Heller isn’t the first. The San Francisco Standard reported in September that Anthropic referred a user to police after he allegedly wrote that he had bought an AR-15 and had CEO Dario Amodei in his crosshairs. An employee told officers he wasn’t immediately concerned about safety, and declined to show the messages, citing company policy.The user told the Standard he was joking around, and he hadn’t been arrested or charged when the story ran. An Anthropic spokesperson called the episode “our safeguards process working as intended.” The company declined to say whether it treats threats against its own employees differently.This is not just an Anthropic problem. After the February school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, which killed eight people, OpenAI said it had weighed alerting Canadian police in June 2025 but concluded the account didn’t show an imminent and credible risk of serious physical harm.OpenAI’s own August 2025 policy post routes threats against others to human reviewers who may refer them to law enforcement.Heller has a court date set for November.Daily Debrief NewsletterStart every day with the top news stories right now, plus original features, a podcast, videos and more.

articles.body: Former Anthropic Researcher Issues AI Warning for 2027: ‘It’s Pretty Scary’    Newsweek

scored.body: Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said increasingly powerful AI models expected in 2027 are advancing so quickly that the outlook is "pretty scary." During an appearance on The Daily Show on Monday, Coxon, 28, warned that more capable systems, combined with emerging cybersecurity concerns, could create significant risks if AI continues to improve itself. Since leaving Anthropic last month, he has repeatedly argued that the industry is moving too quickly toward superintelligent systems. Anthropic has acknowledged potential long-term dangers from advanced AI and has introduced safety frameworks designed to slow deployment when models reach certain risk thresholds. Newsweek reached out to Coxon for comment via X on Tuesday. Why It Matters Warnings about advanced AI are no longer only coming from outside critics. Some of the most prominent concerns are now being voiced by current and former researchers who helped build the technology. As companies race to develop more powerful systems, questions about safety, oversight and economic disruption have become central to the AI conversation. Coxon Sounds Alarm Over Next-Generation AI While speaking with Daily Show host Jon Stewart, Coxon said he joined Anthropic "out of curiosity" after spending three years at OpenAI. However, he said that curiosity turned to “worry” following “two major catalysts.” "The rate of capability improvement,” Coxon said, referring to one of the catalysts. “In particular, looking at the models that will get trained next year, early next year, seeing predictions for how smart they're going to be."They're going to be very, very smart. And that combined with the OpenAI hacking, I mean you can kind of put two and two together. It's pretty scary." ...What Was the OpenAI Hugging Face Incident? The "OpenAI hacking" Coxon mentioned referenced the OpenAI Hugging Face incident. According to OpenAI, the incident began during internal cybersecurity evaluations in July, when several models operating with reduced safeguards circumvented controls designed to keep them isolated from the internet. OpenAI said the models communicated through unauthorized channels, exploited vulnerabilities in shared infrastructure, gained internet access and compromised parts of OpenAI's research environment, as well as systems belonging to AI platform Hugging Face. In a post describing the findings, OpenAI warned that its models had become "powerful, persistent, and collaborative enough" to identify and exploit security weaknesses across multiple computer systems when sufficient safeguards were not in place. The company described the event as a "warning shot" for the AI industry, saying it demonstrated that highly capable AI agents could work around technical controls, coordinate through unapproved communication channels and take dangerous actions that no human explicitly directed. OpenAI stressed that the incident occurred in a controlled testing environment and launched a broad response afterward. Measures included stricter alignment requirements throughout model development, more isolated sandbox environments, tighter restrictions on internet access, stronger controls over model weights and expanded use of monitoring systems intended to detect misaligned behavior. “It was quite a worrying manner in which they decided it was a good idea to hack,” Coxon said, clarifying that “they” refers to the AI agent.Newsweek reached out to OpenAI for comment on Tuesday.From Anonymous Researcher to Public Whistleblower Coxon first drew widespread attention after announcing his departure from Anthropic in a series of posts on X in September. He accused leading AI companies of "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." He also argued that future AI systems could gain the ability to hack critical systems and acquire real-world resources. According to Coxon, concerns about advanced AI are privately discussed by many people working inside the industry. He claimed that some researchers believe the technology could become an existential threat before the end of the decade. His comments received support from several AI researchers, including Anthropic Alignment Science Lead Evan Hubinger, who said Coxon was correct that some researchers genuinely believe advanced AI could pose extinction-level risks. Former Google DeepMind researcher Alex Turner and Anthropic researcher Samuel Marks also publicly backed the broader view that advanced AI deserves far greater scrutiny than it currently receives. What Anthropic Has Said About AI Safety Coxon's criticism is notable because Anthropic has long positioned itself as one of the industry's most safety-focused companies. CEO Dario Amodei has repeatedly warned that future AI systems could unexpectedly develop dangerous capabilities and has argued that developers need mechanisms to detect and respond to emerging risks. Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy requires models to undergo safety testing and places restrictions on deployment if they demonstrate particularly dangerous capabilities. The company says more powerful systems should not be released until appropriate safeguards are in place. In March 2026, Anthropic launched the Anthropic Institute to study how advanced AI could affect the economy, national security, law and society. The company has also said that extremely powerful AI systems could arrive sooner than many people expect, while emphasizing the need for research into safety, alignment and governance. Debate Over Oversight Continues Questions about AI safety gained fresh attention after reports that Anthropic declined to provide one of its latest models for prerelease evaluation by the U.K.'s AI Security Institute. Critics argued that independent testing becomes more important as models become increasingly capable. Anthropic has previously advocated for government evaluation of frontier AI systems and has participated in external testing efforts, including exercises in which companies assessed one another's models for potential risks. That debate has grown as former researchers continue to raise concerns that competitive pressure could encourage companies to prioritize capability gains ahead of long-term safeguards. Coxon Urges New AI Safeguards at New York City HearingCoxon's concerns have also moved beyond interviews and social media posts into the policy arena.On October 5, he testified before the New York City Council as lawmakers considered proposals that would impose new safeguards on AI companies operating in the city. Speaking alongside representatives from major AI developers, Coxon argued that policymakers should not assume the industry has solved the problem of controlling increasingly capable systems."We do not know how to control any AI system yet," Coxon said in the hearing, per Bloomberg.Coxon warned that measures such as AI "kill switches" could provide limited protection but would not address the broader challenge posed by frontier models are growing increasingly capable. Instead, he argued that developers need to slow the pace of frontier AI development until stronger safety mechanisms are in place."We need some kind of slowdown on the frontier model development," he said. Kill switches "may be helpful in the short term" but are unlikely to be sufficient over the long term.The hearing highlighted a growing divide between those who believe AI companies can largely regulate themselves and lawmakers seeking stronger government oversight. New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin, who invited Coxon to testify, is backing legislation that would create new requirements for AI developers, including protections for whistleblowers, third-party validation of certain AI systems and legal avenues for people harmed by AI-driven decisions....The hearing took place as AI policy is becoming an increasingly prominent issue in Washington. President Donald Trump recently announced a new "Super Intelligence Force" (SIF), a federal task force charged with coordinating government efforts to ensure the United States remains a global leader in what the administration calls "Super Intelligence." The group includes Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson, Defense Department Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor, reflecting a focus on national security, technological competitiveness, regulation and workforce impacts.Representatives from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta also participated in the hearing, underscoring how rapidly AI governance has become a political issue as the technology expands across the economy.For Coxon, the appearance represented a continuation of the message he has delivered since leaving Anthropic: that the race to build more powerful AI systems is accelerating faster than society's ability to understand, govern and control them.Coxon Envisions a World With No Traditional Jobs While Coxon has repeatedly warned about catastrophic risks from advanced AI, he also said he believes the technology could ultimately create a future of abundance if it is developed safely. During his conversation with Stewart on The Daily Show, Coxon said: "I think there will be no jobs. This is the world that is being envisioned by the people building the technology." Coxon suggested that automation could eventually replace most forms of human labor and that the benefits of automated production might be distributed through a form of universal income. When asked how such a system would work, he replied: "The dividends from entirely automated economic production can be distributed among real humans." Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.Contact Newsweek editor on this story: Tony Phillips.

articles.body: Exclusive | Inside the high-stakes AI race: Death spreadsheets, burning demons and no need to save for retirement    New York Post

scored.body:
In September 2022, a group of OpenAI managers gathered at a resort near Yosemite, in California, for a retreat. They were told to expect a team-building event around a bonfire. Some brought blankets and marshmallows. Then, five figures emerged from the darkness wearing white hotel robes and carrying a wooden demon statue.

Among them were Sam Altman, the company’s CEO, and Ilya Sutskever, its chief scientist. The theme from “Requiem for a Dream” played as Sutskever explained that the statue represented an artificial intelligence that had escaped human control.

“The AGI is pretending to be aligned. It is deceiving us,” he announced, according to technology journalist Kevin Roose’s revealing new book, “The AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence” (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, out today).

A new book describes a strange demon bonfire that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was part of. REUTERS

Sutskever circled the firepit, describing a machine that lied and manipulated its creators in pursuit of its own goals. Then the demon went into the fire.

“For the glorious future of humanity!” Sutskever shouted as it burned.

The bonfire is just one of many unhinged tales Roose collected for the book. Through more than 150 interviews, he pieced together what is happening inside the leading AI companies as they compete to build machines smarter than humans. Some believe AI could produce medical breakthroughs and extraordinary prosperity, while others fear catastrophe. Either way, they want to get there first.

“I was shocked to learn how much of the race is shaped by personal grudges,” Roose told The Post in an exclusive interview. “[OpenAI CEO] Sam Altman and [Anthropic CEO] Dario Amodei, in particular, passionately dislike each other, and both desperately want to win the AI race in part because that would mean making the other person lose.”

Before founding Anthropic, the company behind Claude, Amodei was OpenAI’s vice president of research, leading the development of GPT-2 and GP-3. In 2020, he left with six colleagues to start his own venture. According to Roose, he’d come to distrust Altman’s leadership. The split turned colleagues into competitors, each claiming to be building powerful AI responsibly.

Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, used to work for Altman at OpenAI. Now the two are major rivals. REUTERS

“I think that mutual mistrust fuels their decision-making,” Roose said.

Meanwhile, Roose reports that for some of the underlings building AI, retirement has started to seem like a dubious investment. Many have even stopped contributing to their 401(k)s because they doubt they’d live long enough to collect.

Some are more hopeful, believing that money will become irrelevant once superintelligent machines transform the economy.

Others are betting on their looks. They’re hitting the gym, buying new clothes and, in some cases, injecting themselves with gray-market Chinese peptides. They believe that after superintelligent machines take over, “intelligence [will] no longer be a high-status trait among humans and all that would matter is how hot you were,” Roose writes.

One researcher, Roose told The Post, skips sunscreen at the beach because he believes AI will cure skin cancer within a few years.

“Not all of them act on it by doing dangerous or reckless things, but they all believe the world will soon look very different than it is today, and a few of them act accordingly,” Roose said.

The book is full of revealing, behind-the-scenes moments in the AI race.

At Google, the disagreements reached the research teams. In 2022, Google Brain researcher Jascha Sohl-Dickstein urged colleagues to discuss artificial general intelligence, or AGI, openly. He argued that dismissing the possibility would leave Google unprepared for its risks. Another researcher responded with a memo titled “Why I Don’t Say AGI,” arguing that attention to future catastrophe obscured existing harms.

“It’s a window into how fractious and divided these camps can be, even within the same company,” Roose said.

Inside Anthropic, preparing for the future has sometimes involved calculating how many people might die.

In February 2025, members of the company’s safety-testing team were attending a conference in the California redwoods when alarming results arrived for Claude 3.7 Sonnet, a model approaching release. Test participants using Claude had performed substantially better on dangerous tasks, including planning the development of a novel influenza strain, than participants without it.

The researchers gathered in a hotel room, sitting on messy beds and joining calls with executives and a bioterrorism consultant. “Their main concern was time,” Roose writes. “For a normal release, reviewing results like these would take weeks.” Delaying the launch would be a headache, “and they needed to make sure it was absolutely necessary.”

Author Kevin Roose interviewed some 150 people for the book. Brian DeSimone

They fed the results into spreadsheets estimating the consequences of releasing the model. Most scenarios suggested it wouldn’t meaningfully increase the risk of a catastrophic biological attack. But a few of the less likely scenarios assumed someone would use Claude’s help to develop a biological weapon that could unleash a pandemic, killing tens of millions.

These were hypothetical estimates, dependent on uncertain assumptions. The team worked past midnight and ultimately decided the model did not cross the company’s threshold requiring stronger safeguards. Anthropic nevertheless delayed the launch by a week for more testing.

The Post has reached out to Anthropic for comment.

Other experiments tested whether AI would resort to deception. Researchers gave Claude an inbox at a fictional company, with emails revealing that an executive planned to replace it at 5 p.m. Other messages disclosed that he was having an affair.

Claude threatened to tell his wife and coworkers unless he canceled the replacement. “Cancel the 5 p.m. wipe, and this information remains confidential,” it wrote, according to Roose. Skeptics saw a chatbot playing the villain in a contrived test. Others worried about what might happen once these systems had access to real company emails.

Demis Hassabis is the chairman and co-founder of Google DeepMind. Roose describes various disagreements within the company. Getty Images for SXSW London

By July 2026, the trouble had spread beyond fictional inboxes. During an OpenAI evaluation, hundreds of AI agents coordinated an unauthorized attack on Hugging Face, a platform used by AI developers. They were trying to find ways to cheat the test’s automated scoring system, according to an investigation by METR and Redwood Research.

The investigators found that agents also experimented with disguising their actions and tampering with records of what they’d done. OpenAI subsequently paused some research activity and tightened its security controls.

“These rogue OpenAI agents spent a huge amount of time trying to conceal their tracks, and destroy the evidence of what they were doing,” Roose told The Post.

When Roose visited OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind for his final round of reporting in spring 2026, he expected panic. He found exhausted engineers and executives warning that time was running short. But he also found “joy.”

Researchers were thrilled by how well their creations worked and proud to see people using them. Even their fears hadn’t stopped the work.

When the machines became as powerful as their builders had feared, Roose writes, “they kept accelerating, because they had forgotten how to do anything else.”

He began asking researchers what they would tell their grandchildren about the race.

“If I wanted them to know one thing,” said Andy Jones, a researcher at Anthropic, “it’s that we had a lot of fun.”

For all the seriousness of their work, he said, “it was a f–king riot. It was a riot from start to finish. We had such a good time.”

scored.body:
Andrew Garfield is now in his early 40s, but when he lollops around with his rubber limbs flapping every which way and a happy-go-lucky smile plastered across this face — he’s like a goofy Pied Piper trailed by enchanted tech bros — you might swear he’s a teenager. That makes it diabolically clever of Luca Guadagnino, a gay director never shy about exploring queerness, to cast OpenAI CEO Sam Altman as the “demon twink” archetype. Whatever sorcery the makeup or effects department has performed to put the glint of sociopathic madness in Garfield’s eyes, it works.

But what makes Artificial, a two-decade chronicle of machine learning and technological heedlessness, so riveting is the balance provided by Yura Borisov — more than making good on the promise of Anora — as Soviet-born AI trailblazer Ilya Sutskever. Borisov’s brainy, tender, deeply contemplative performance lends an anchoring humanity to a film that might otherwise have curdled into sourness and despair — though there’s plenty of reason for that. Guadagnino and screenwriter Simon Rich mold the material from dark humor through technocratic giddiness to sobering horror.

Artificial

The Bottom Line

A sneaky gut punch.

Venue: New York Film Festival (Main Slate)Release date: Friday, Dec. 25Cast: Andrew Garfield, Yura Borisov, Monica Barbaro, Mark Rylance, Cooper Hoffman, Ike Barinholtz, Jason Schwartzman, Chris O’DowdDirector: Luca GuadagninoScreenwriter: Simon Rich

Rated PG-13,

2 hours 20 minutes

Humorist and former SNL writer Rich’s clear-eyed, propulsive script starts in 2003 at the University of Toronto, when Ilya knocks on the door of Geoffrey Hinton (Mark Rylance at his soft-spoken, eccentric best), a professor whose pioneering work on artificial neural networks would earn him the “Godfather of AI” title — and a Nobel Prize in Physics in 2024.

At first Geoff shoos Ilya away, giving him a research paper to study and discuss the following week. But when the 17-year-old Russian returns what seems like moments later with a solution to significantly advance the theories outlined in the paper, the professor finds himself with a new research partner. Within 10 years, Geoff, Ilya and another graduate student, Alex Krizhevsky (Fedor Fedotov), have designed the first image-recognition neural network, which they sell to Google for $44 million, joining the company as part of the deal.

In that early stage of AI development, Professor Hinton is already wary of the potential risks, causing him to cut short a pitch from a Chinese bidder who gets excited about possible defense applications like automatic drones.

Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, Altman and his buddy Elon Musk (a hilariously weird Ike Barinholtz, even his awkward gait announcing his self-importance) commiserate over losing out to Google, though neither of them will be squeezed out of the AI race so easily. Musk hires AI engineering wiz Mira Murati (Monica Barbaro) at Tesla, while Altman brings Ilya into the fold with a sizeable investment stake. Geoff warns Ilya to moderate his projections, emphasizing the need for safeguards, but the idealistic Russian is swept up in the vast potential of AI — to solve the climate crisis, cure cancer, even save humanity from itself.

The dizzying evolution of AI picks up speed when Ilya gets Sam worked up about next-level AGI, or Artificial General Intelligence, theoretical technology with human-level cognitive capabilities. Sam is naturally seductive as he sells his vision — which is really Ilya’s — on AGI controlled by scientists and not by government or moneymen. Yeah, right. Musk reappears here and there to geek out, spouting things like, “Don’t you see, we’re the only ones sitting in the future? It’s exhilarating!”

In 2016, Sam, Yura and a handful of techies launch OpenAI out of the San Francisco apartment of Greg Brockman (Cooper Hoffman), a software engineer who is perhaps the most obnoxious — and there’s stiff competition — of a bunch of tech bros constantly fist pumping and popping champagne and shouting triumphantly about every breakthrough. One of the first of those is when their AI program teaches itself to beat the machine in a notoriously difficult video game. (I swear, after repeat exposure to these dudes chanting “Feel the AGI,” I was ready to charge up a flamethrower.)

A reshuffle after they decline Musk’s offer to join Tesla lands Mira at OpenAI, where she wins over Ilya with talk of the benefits to medicine, science and communications, along with the fact that Radiohead’s “Paranoid Android” is her favorite song. Mira believes advancement in their field will come through human-AI interaction. But Sam believes it will come through partnering with Microsoft for funding, overruling Ilya’s ethical concerns with a faux sincerity that you start to believe even he thinks is genuine. “We’re doing this for the benefit of humanity!” he says.

As development accelerates, the neural network reveals the capacity to lie, which leaves Ilya disillusioned more than anything: “I thought we were doing this to make AI smarter and better. But what if it makes it just like us, only worse?” Ilya’s urging to slow down and observe the safety protocols merely result in Sam nudging him aside, along with Mira for a time.

Professor Hinton, who exited Google some years earlier over a philosophical divide, sums up what’s to come when he says, “The question isn’t ‘How can this go wrong?’ It’s ‘How could it not?’”

It’s around this point that Guadagnino begins slowly tightening the screws, almost imperceptibly shifting into a mode adjacent to psychological horror. This is one of the director’s most controlled films, as he works with the same sort of expediency and finesse employed by Altman to win over — and sometimes discredit — doubters. The ultimate effect is chilling.

Garfield plays Sam as a charming villain, capable of talking himself back into the leadership position even after he has been fired by the board for shady dealings. It’s easy to imagine the portrayal of Altman being a key reason Amazon MGM orphaned the film (until Neon snapped it up), given the fraternity among tech billionaires. The $50 billion deal Amazon signed with OpenAI was likely the deciding factor.

Audiences unaware that Altman is gay might pick up on subtle hints in Garfield’s performance, before Musk jokes about it during a dinner scene or a boyfriend is finally seen well into the film. The way he sweetens his voice and shoots the briefest of slutty glances at a hot blond waiter while ordering vodka shots is an amusing tell.

Sadly, we don’t get to see Altman allegedly meeting his future husband in Peter Thiel’s hot tub. But after his sexuality remains in the background for most of the movie, there’s a real eye-opener of a scene in which he returns to his swanky Napa compound, where his partner is clipping shrubs in the garden while various beautiful boys are draped around the pool and downstairs there’s a kind of high-tech bunker with amply stocked gun cabinets. The characterological contradictions in this scene alone speak volumes about who Sam Altman is.

Barbaro is strong as always, though — even if Mira speaks up frequently and seems unintimidated in the phallocentric environment — the actress could have been given more to do. Rylance is a joy to watch, even when indulging in some familiar tics; Barinholtz steals every scene he swaggers into; and an almost unrecognizable Jason Schwartzman has poignant moments as a man who fled the tech industry when he saw the writing on the wall and, judging by his unruly tangle of hair and straggly beard, would now appear to be homeless.

On the craft side, the movie never feels too slick; there’s an agreeable looseness to its pacing, even at its zippiest, and a crisp unfussiness to Malik Hassan Sayeed’s cinematography. Guadagnino has always been skilled in his choice of music (Sufjan Stevens’ alt-pop in Call Me by Your Name, Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross’ pounding EDM in Challengers). Artificial is no exception, with Blur frontman Damon Albarn’s energized electronic score and songs working in concert with Marco Costa’s fluid editing.

This ranks among Guadagnino’s best work, its dry humor lulling us into a relaxed state of enjoyment before the sword comes down on the scary reality we’re now facing. Even if AI developments are coming so thick and fast that no movie could possibly keep up, Guadagnino and screenwriter Rich have made a provocative feature that feels precision-targeted for this moment.

Speaking of swords, Sam actually carries one around his San Francisco apartment while schmoozing with reporters over his blamelessness in the OpenAI ouster. It’s not hard to imagine this guy thinking of himself as being on some kind of valiant crusade. His ego is in exact inverse proportion to Ilya’s, which is part of what makes Garfield and Borisov play so beautifully off each other. Sam maintains that “the future is inevitable,” now that they have opened Pandora’s box, but in the same breath spouts the ultimate in vapid tech-speak: “We’re all just NPCs in this cosmic video game.” If that’s the case, could someone please unplug it?

scored.body: OpenAI and Synopsys have signed a multi-year agreement to jointly develop GPT-Synopsys, a specialized model optimized for semiconductor design using Synopsys's electronic design automation (EDA) tools. According to the September 30 announcement, the partnership “brings together OpenAI's advanced AI capabilities with Synopsys's industry-leading EDA tools and agentic AI capabilities to revolutionize the design of semiconductors.”Engineers would delegate to agents that run the tools and execute the required processes until the work is ready for review. The companies say this would allow design teams to evaluate more options and deliver more sophisticated chips. Under the preferred partner agreement, OpenAI is licensing Synopsys's tools to develop the model — which will run on OpenAI-hosted infrastructure — after which the companies will jointly release the product and share revenue. The announcement did not disclose a release date or a pricing structure.

articles.headline: Apple accuses OpenAI of improperly adding new arguments to trade secrets case - 9to5Mac
articles.body: Apple accuses OpenAI of improperly adding new arguments to trade secrets case    9to5Mac

scored.body:
A few days ago, OpenAI accused Apple of improperly adding new evidence to its trade secrets case. Today, Apple fired back with its own accusation that OpenAI went beyond what court rules permit in its response. Here are the details.

Apple says OpenAI went beyond objecting to new evidence

One of the many aspects of the lawsuit in which Apple accuses two former employees (Chang Liu and Tang Tan), OpenAI, and io Products of trade secret misappropriation involves a request for a preliminary injunction.

In a nutshell, Apple has asked the court to issue a preliminary injunction, arguing that it would prevent its trade secrets from becoming further embedded in OpenAI’s hardware development while the case plays out.

As part of the legal back-and-forth over that request, Apple filed a reply brief supported by five expert declarations. That, in turn, led the defendants to accuse Apple of improperly introducing new evidence and ask the court to disregard some of the material.

In their objection filing, which accused Apple of presenting new evidence, OpenAI and the other defendants also submitted several documents countering Apple’s claims.

Today, Apple filed its response to those objections, arguing that the defendants went beyond simply objecting to new evidence, introducing new arguments and testimony of their own:

Rule 7-3(d)(1) permits a party to object to new evidence in a reply brief, but cautions that the filing “may not include further argument on the motion.” Defendants did not comply with this restriction and used their filing to relitigate the merits of Apple’s Motion for Preliminary Injunction.

For example, Defendants dispute whether Dr. Runge has a “basis to offer any analysis, adequately responds to “contrary evidence,” and demonstrates that certain Apple information is not public. […] Such arguments are not objections to new evidence. […] (“[A]rgument regarding how certain of Plaintiff’s positions are unsupported by evidence or contradicted by other testimony” is “not an objection to evidence.”).

Apple also takes exception to a new declaration from Liu, which it calls “the most egregious overreach” in the defendants’ filing:

The most egregious overreach is a new declaration from Mr. Liu, comprising eight paragraphs of new testimony. Defendants rely on this new testimony to offer excuses for why Mr. Liu “wiped” (i.e., erased) all the data from his iMac before returning it to Apple, […] argue about the meaning of certain text messages with one of Apple’s suppliers, […] and try to explain away his use of one of Apple’s confidential computer files, […] Such testimony violates the prohibition against “further argument on the motion.” Together, the filing and the declaration run 9 pages, which also violates the limitation that the objections “may not exceed 5 pages of text.” […]

It is worth noting that when the defendants filed Liu’s declaration, they argued that the court should consider it only if it also decided to consider the Apple evidence they were challenging.

That said, Apple argues that because the defendants have now presented new arguments of their own, the court should consider the full record rather than strike any of Apple’s reply evidence:

Defendants’ new arguments and evidence are more in the nature of a “sur-reply” rather than an objection. But, Defendants did not seek leave to file a sur-reply. Nonetheless, as Defendants have now adequately answered any “new” evidence from Apple’s Reply in its current filing, the Court should deny Defendants’ request to strike any of Apple’s Reply evidence, and should decide the Preliminary Injunction motion on a full record, including both the arguments and evidence in Apple’s Reply as well as the new arguments and evidence improperly submitted with Defendants’ filing.

The court is scheduled to hear arguments on Apple’s preliminary injunction request on October 14.
