OpenAI on Monday announced a visual ad format for

ChatGPT that will display these ads alongside results while users generate images.The ad unit expands its measurement tools and partnerships, as it works with brands to understand

suitability.The new visual ad format shows how people can discover a new brand, understand what makes an

offering distinctive, and decide what to buy.For advertisers, this creates new opportunities to tell their story through images, the company said in a blog post.Testing will begin in

the U.S. later this month with an initial group of advertisers.Initially, OpenAI will test the new ad format during image generation in ChatGPT, with ads clearly labeled. They will remain

separate from the image being created by the chatbot.advertisementadvertisementLike its other ad formats, advertising will not influence the answers that ChatGPT provides.Since February when ChatGPT launched

the first ads, brands have had a difficult time measuring return on investments. OpenAI changed that today with its latest round of updates, as it attempts to help brands monetize clicks and

requests from 1.2 billion weekly users.The company is piloting brand-suitability evaluations with DoubleVerify (DV) and Integral Ad Science (IAS) to give advertisers greater insight into the

ad environment. These independent partners will review how ChatGPT applies its brand-safety standards in a controlled test setting, without access to private user conversations.As OpenAI

continues to build out essential required metrics with tools and partners that businesses need to track whether their ChatGPT Ads generate sales and return on investments (ROI), it has partnered with

Tealium, LiveRamp, and Hightouch to act as secure data pipelines for conversion data.This integration allows the website or database owner to automatically tell ChatGPT Ads: "Hey, someone

just purchased a coat, and they clicked a ChatGPT ad earlier in the day."Attribution partners have been added, including AppsFlyer, Triple Whale, Adjust, DV Rockerbox, Northbeam, Branch,

Singular, Kochava, Airbridge, and Tenjin to enable conversions API, reporting, and click attribution reporting.Full-funnel and advanced measurement partners including Fospha, Measured, and

INCRMNTAL have also been added.Incrementality measurement partners now include Haus, Measured, and WorkMagic to explore geo-based experiments to help advertisers understand the causal impact

of ChatGPT Ads.Monday’s updates are part of OpenAI’s strategy to focus on helping consumers discover products and services, evaluate options, and make decisions to purchase

products based on what they see in ChatGPT.

articles.headline: John Ternus is already doing it all - Macworld
articles.body: John Ternus is already doing it all    Macworld

scored.body:
When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn't affect our editorial independence.

Contributor, Macworld

Opinion

Oct 6, 2026

John Ternus has now been CEO of Apple for over a month, so it’s time to rate his legacy. Okay, that’s probably unfair. Let’s give the guy at least a quarter.

But since we’re on the subject, what can we glean from what Ternus has done so far that will indicate what kind of CEO he’ll be? Admittedly, even that’s going to be hard because he’s barely had time to actually do anything, but there are some early indicators brought to us by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.

Let’s start with somewhat vague concepts: Apple under Ternus: More products, more often, with a ‘leaner’ staff.

This reportedly includes being “more experimental” with releases. More experimental than the Vision Pro? Oookay. We’ll look forward to that.

Despite the desire to be leaner, Apple declined one… mmm, “opportunity” is the wrong word… “chance to punch itself in the face.” That’s more accurate: Apple Reportedly Planned to Replace 5,000 Support Employees With AI.

[Apple] worked on a plan to lay off about 5,000 AppleCare customer-service workers, including many who work from home, based on the belief that improved AI-powered phone and web agents could take over portions of their responsibilities. Apple ultimately put those plans on hold and isn’t currently looking to take such a step.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, September 29, 2026

Alas, Apple customers will not know the joys of having an AI ask us to do all the things we’ve already tried all over again before advising we log out of iCloud and then back in.

This might be another area where Apple supposedly being “late” to AI will work to its advantage as other companies have learned this lesson the hard way with three-quarters of them having rolled back AI call center deployments. In fact, instead of laying off the support personnel, Apple let go some middle managers and directors instead!

If you’d like to receive regular news and updates to your inbox, sign up for our newsletters, including The Macalope and Apple Breakfast, David Price’s weekly, bite-sized roundup of all the latest Apple news and rumors.

Foundry

Welcome to the class struggle, Apple Inc.? No, no, that’s not right. Ridiculous. Forget the Macalope said that.

Still, it’s worth noting that one Apple executive in particular is even having to do two jobs! And that executive is… oh! John Ternus! Apple’s John Ternus Has Found a New Design Chief: Himself.

15 years after Steve Jobs’ death, the design buck stops at the CEO’s desk once again. According to Gurman, gallant Ternus “works hands-on in the [Apple design] studio several times a week, sometimes visiting multiple times in a single day”, whereas Goofus Tim Cook would only visit “about an hour once a month, at most.” And he reportedly said things like “Is this one of them computers?” and “Does this one get the internet?”

Okay, maybe not that last part. Gurman drops a “many are saying” that really makes you wonder who his sources are.

Given design’s central role in Apple’s product development and in generating ideas for future devices, many people inside and close to the company believed it should recruit an outside chief design officer to oversee the entire organization. But I’m told no such search is underway.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, October 4, 2026

If many are, indeed, saying this, then those many should avail themselves of one of the various means by which one can get bent in today’s modern society. There are many options, please pick one of your choosing, because it is largely unfathomable as to who could just step into the role of chief freakin’ designer at Apple freakin’ Inc. Are Gurman’s sources people who think it should be them? Because this reads like one of those surveys of macho bros who think they could go a few rounds with a bear or a gorilla.

“Yeah, I think I could hold my own in a fight against a gorilla. I took a little taekwondo.”

Please, be the Macalope’s guest. Hope you don’t like using your arms because the gorilla is going to rip them off your body and beat you to death with them.

Anyway, this change just makes sense given the two CEOs’ different backgrounds and styles. It’s not like Cook’s tenure at Apple was anything other than a massive financial and operational success, but it’s still exciting to think this CEO is showing an interest in the details that make Apple products so compelling.

Are Ternus’s changes going to work? Heck if the Macalope knows. He would say we’ll have to wait until the rubber meets the road but Apple canceled the car project so that metaphor doesn’t work anymore. So far the horny one likes what he sees, though.

members.title: Stop worrying about my AI, says multibillionaire Sam Altman. So we bear the risks and he keeps the money - The Guardian

representative.headline: Stop worrying about my AI, says multibillionaire Sam Altman. So we bear the risks and he keeps the money - The Guardian
representative.body: Stop worrying about my AI, says multibillionaire Sam Altman. So we bear the risks and he keeps the money    The Guardian

articles.headline: Stop worrying about my AI, says multibillionaire Sam Altman. So we bear the risks and he keeps the money - The Guardian
articles.body: Stop worrying about my AI, says multibillionaire Sam Altman. So we bear the risks and he keeps the money    The Guardian

scored.body:
Tech bros’ messianic streaks can show up in subtle ways. But one of Sam Altman’s flaws is that he often lacks that subtlety. “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology,” said the OpenAI chief executive in an interview with Politico last weekend.That’s easy for Altman to say. But it’s pretty galling to hear for the rest of us. Lest we forget, we didn’t ask for OpenAI to unleash AI agents that went rogue and weaselled their way into government IT systems and private businesses around the world. Nobody voted for ChatGPT to be released, but the company put it out into the world as a test product that happened to catch the zeitgeist. That kickstarted an arms race among AI companies to push the frontier of the technology ever further and faster, resulting in the mess we now find ourselves in.OpenAI’s competitors, including Anthropic, have started to step back from the brink – as has OpenAI itself, deciding not to release its latest model because it’s purportedly too dangerous. Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, has talked about needing to “pace the frontier”: tech-bro jargon for pumping the brakes to bring down the speed at which the runaway vehicle is skidding out of control.Yet we’re expected to take these incidents – and the harm they cause – as the natural consequences of OpenAI’s continued march towards an IPO that would bring its investors millions. It’s hard to escape the idea that Altman wants to privatise his company’s gains while socialising the risks of untrammelled AI development.Every useful technology – and AI is a useful technology, despite the holdouts and occasional users’ carping – carries risk. Cars can and do crash, while medicines that save us often have harmful side effects. Very rarely, aircraft fall from the sky. But we accept those risks because the benefits are substantial, and we build rules to limit the harm. We also make companies liable. And most importantly, we get some say in deciding what level of risk is and isn’t acceptable.Altman seems to suggest that his company’s messes are our problem to sort out – or worse, that the consequences of his tech are ours to tolerate. But Altman would do well to think about this differently. OpenAI gets to decide how fast it develops its technology and when it releases it. Its investors benefit financially if those bets pay off. But it feels as if he’s suggesting that when the tech creates problems outside OpenAI’s own walls, the costs of cleaning up are ours to bear, not his company’s.The idea that private companies profit while we’re left to deal with the consequences becomes even harder to defend as AI stops being something we opt into using as a chatbot, and becomes something that acts on and changes the world around us. If I ask ChatGPT something and it gives me a bad answer, I chose to expose myself to that risk, so should share that burden. But the same isn’t true for a government department that suddenly finds an OpenAI agent lurking in its files and rooting around. It didn’t opt in; it became an unwilling participant in someones experiment.That’s why Altman’s argument sounds so disingenuous. OpenAI shouldn’t be able to decide for all of us what is and isn’t an acceptable level of failure, then ask everyone to live with the result. The burden ought to be on it to prove its technology can be trusted – and to pick up the bill if it can’t.It’s no wonder that OpenAI wants to travel quickly. The company is seeking $30bn in new funding, and a valuation of $1.4tn ahead of a public listing likely next year. There’s money to be made – never mind at whose expense.To his credit, Altman also acknowledged in the Politico interview that there will need to be a liability framework for companies offering models such as OpenAI’s, and that the company will have to take responsibility for at least some of what goes wrong during training. But that “some” is doing a lot of work.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotionIf Altman believes some bad things are an acceptable price for AI’s progress, OpenAI can dig into its deep pockets to pay that price itself – for instance if its agents go rogue and do damage to government or private company systems, or compromise user data. It can’t, and shouldn’t, get the financial upside when everything goes right, then ask the rest of us to accept the consequences when things go wrong. That’s especially the case when we never agreed to the unregulated experiment in the first place.

Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite App

members.title: Why Are We Paying So Much Attention to Sam Altman? - The New Republic

representative.headline: Why Are We Paying So Much Attention to Sam Altman? - The New Republic
representative.body: Why Are We Paying So Much Attention to Sam Altman?    The New Republic

articles.headline: Why Are We Paying So Much Attention to Sam Altman? - The New Republic
articles.body: Why Are We Paying So Much Attention to Sam Altman?    The New Republic

scored.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has been on a real media blitz. But whether he’s doing damage control for his company’s recent scandals or participating in a new Luca Guadagnino biopic, it hasn’t seemed to improve his image. In an interview with Politico, Altman said that “the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology,” referring to the large language models being developed by his company and its competitors. What things does Sam Altman think are bad? He offered a few examples during a two-part interview with Vanity Fair published this week. Altman called it a “bad thing” for kids to be “glued to a touchscreen of some sort scrolling through brain rot short form video,” and said he would limit his own kids’ access to technology. People using LLMs to “create novel pathogens” would also be bad, he asserted. When Vanity Fair Editor Mark Guiducci asked him to weigh in on a recent New York Times op-ed by journalist Laura Reiley—whose daughter committed suicide shortly after speaking to ChatGPT—an OpenAI publicist attempted to intervene. Altman eventually answered the question, and equivocated on whether it is good or bad for people experiencing a mental health crisis to turn to an LLM. “This is just like, this is new,” he said. “And the fact that someone in a moment of need that maybe can’t get help or isn’t willing to talk to a therapist can get some help here. Clearly people think there’s a version of this that is good. There are also clearly versions of it that are bad.”As Altman has made clear in these and other interviews, however, he thinks it would be very bad for governments to regulate his industry in a way that suppresses innovation. He explained to Guiducci that he’s driven by the belief that putting powerful LLMs “in the hands of everyone and giving people a legitimate new superpower relative to I think what any of us could imagine a few years ago will do tremendously more good than bad.” The upshot here is that Altman would like the public to trust OpenAI to judge when the good is outweighing the bad. And although the “goods” of LLM development remain largely speculative—like curing cancer and granting wishes—the bads continue to pile up. OpenAI faces a growing mountain of legal risks over incidents of its products hacking into government agencies around the world, not to mention providing advice to mass shooters, as Florida’s attorney general’s office has alleged. Nearly every company that’s developing large language models—OpenAI, Nvidia, SpaceX, Microsoft, and Google parent Alphabet—has contracted with a Pentagon that’s been proudly killing fishermen in Latin America, and that continues to wage an illegal war on Iran. While the self-styled good guys at Anthropic declined to work with the military several months back, the company hasn’t balked at building a predictive surveillance system to monitor activists. Silicon Valley executives have largely dismissed concerns that the data centers fueling their technologies threaten everything from local aquifers to electricity rates, and have seemed relatively unconcerned about the ways that LLM-generated slop is rapidly distorting people’s ability to think and reason independently.The trouble with trusting AI companies to decide what’s good and what’s bad is that, like other CEOs, Altman and his colleagues have a financial interest in the answers to these moral questions. There are obvious commercial upsides for the executives in continuing to portray their companies (their “labs,” as they like to call them) as upstanding research entities, and mere stewards of a fundamentally mysterious, powerful, and inevitable technology. But they have just as much to gain from the public conversation about LLMs orbiting around the question of whether individual CEOs are good people. It doesn’t really matter one way or the other. They run large and powerful companies that sell products and have no legal obligation to the public good. Those companies appear to be committing crimes, which they could be tried for using laws that already exist. As far off as real enforcement and regulation might seem, such laws are only things that will keep the rest of us from being subject to their lousy ethics.

scored.body: Sam Altman at the G7 summit on June 17, 2026, in Evian-les-Bains, France. In a new Vanity Fair interview, the OpenAI CEO also talks about Amazon dropping the movie, Elon Musk, his kids, his survivalist streak and why he still thinks AI’s future will be “all going to be great.”Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/Julia Demaree NikhinsonSam Altman has finally had his first real encounter with Andrew Garfield’s version of him.It happened outside Altman’s San Francisco home, where the actor was filming Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial,” the upcoming movie about Altman and the turmoil surrounding his artificial intelligence research and deployment company, OpenAI.One morning, Altman said, he walked down the street to get coffee and came upon a film set — and a man who looked eerily familiar.Article continues below this ad“There were all these cameras and there (was) a guy dressed exactly like me with my same backpack walking so much that I felt I was in some weird glitch of the simulation or something,” Altman told Vanity Fair in a new cover story interview published Monday, Oct. 5.“I waved at him that one time and that was it.”Garfield, Altman added, had apparently mastered one especially recognizable detail.Article continues below this ad“He did walk like me,” Altman said. “Actually, I’ll tell you something: They filmed outside of our house.”It’s a small, surreal detail from an unusually revealing interview with the OpenAI CEO, who spent two conversations with Vanity Fair discussing everything from the movie and his Hollywood doppelgänger to Elon Musk, parenthood, AI safety and the future of humanity.“Artificial,” directed by Guadagnino and starring Garfield as Altman, is scheduled to open in select theaters on Christmas Day.Here are the biggest revelations and lighter moments from the interview:Garfield’s Altman gets one thing very right — the walkPedestrians walk on Lombard Street past a driveway at the home of Sam Altman on April 10, 2026, in San Francisco.Lea Suzuki/S.F. ChronicleAltman has seen the trailer for “Artificial,” and he is not particularly worried about the filmmakers getting every detail of his life right.Article continues below this ad“I don’t think they’re going for accuracy,” he said. “Except for the walk.”That, he added, was “good,” giving Garfield credit for capturing his distinctive style.But the experience of seeing somebody portray him outside his own house was more than a little weird.“I mean, it’s like a strange thing to see someone that has nailed your kind of quirky mannerisms or whatever,” he said.There is no Sam Altman bunker with guns on the wallThe trailer includes a particularly ominous image: Garfield’s Altman walking into a James Bond-style bunker with firearms displayed on the wall.Article continues below this adAltman says that part is fiction.“There’s no bunker with firearms on the wall,” he said.But the joke contains a kernel of truth. Altman revealed he does have what he calls a “survivalist mindset.”“At our ranch, we can survive off-grid, which I guess to many people would be considered a bugout plan,” he said.He then offered a line that seems destined for social media: “We don’t have a submarine.”Article continues below this adWhen asked whether he has a helicopter, he added: “No helicopter, no submarine.”Altman said he nevertheless became more convinced of the value of basic preparedness during the COVID-19 pandemic.“When COVID came, I had a big stack of masks ready to go, and I had enough canned food in the house that if the world had shut down, we could have had enough food for a while and we had water purification tablets.”Sam Altman speaks during the G20 Innovation Ministerial on September 2, 2026 in Chapel Hill, North Carolina. In a new Vanity Fair interview, the OpenAI CEO also talks about Amazon dropping the movie, Elon Musk, his kids, his survivalist streak and why he still thinks AI’s future will be “all going to be great.”Sean Rayford/Getty ImagesHe says Amazon had no role in the movie’s fateThe movie’s path to theaters became especially awkward after Amazon MGM Studios, which originally planned to distribute “Artificial,” abandoned the project.That decision came after Amazon announced a $50 billion investment in OpenAI. The companies’ strategic partnership also includes a major cloud-computing relationship.Altman said he had nothing to do with Amazon’s decision and no one on his behalf spoke to the tech giant about it.“No. I did not, and I don’t know of anyone else who did,” he said.Asked specifically about Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos, Altman was equally direct: “I never spoke to Jeff Bezos about it.”Amazon MGM ultimately said the movie would be “better served if it were released by a different studio,” he explained, and Neon picked it up.Altman isn’t exactly worried about being portrayed as the villain“Artificial” appears to take a darker view of the people and events behind the rise of OpenAI than Altman himself does, and that does not seem to bother him much.“I mean, they’re trying to make a good movie and maybe it will be good.”His qualification: “Good as a movie. It will not be good as an accurate depiction.”He calls Elon Musk a bully — but says he’ll work with himSam Altman (L) and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg (R) attend a state dinner hosted by President Donald Trump for Chinese President Xi Jinping in the East Room of the White House in Washington, DC, on September 24, 2026. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty ImagesThe interview also produced some unusually blunt words about Altman’s longtime rival.“Elon’s a bully,” Altman said. “And so I think once in a while you got to punch a bully back in the nose. And I also think Elon, like many bullies, only respects people who do. So if you want me to be able to work with him, maybe you should be happy I hit back once in a while. But I will work with Elon, of course.”Altman was more forgiving when discussing another tech titan.He said he once had “a very evil caricature” of Mark Zuckerberg, co-founder of Facebook and Meta CEO, in his head before getting to know him personally.“I was projecting whatever people project onto someone with what they perceive as too much power and influence over the world,” he admitted.He wants more kids, but not for Silicon Valley’s pronatalist causeAltman, who already has two young children, said he plans to have more. But he rejected the idea that his interest in a larger family is connected to the Silicon Valley pronatalism movement, which advocates having more children partly in response to declining birth rates.“I love our kids so much and I know I’ll have more kids, but there’s no part of it which is like we got to fight against population decline,” he said. “I love a big family. It’s really great.”He also said his children have changed the way he thinks about AI, though perhaps not in the expected way.“I was very intent on not destroying the world before having kids,” Altman said. “I didn’t need kids to be like, ‘OK, I really shouldn’t gamble with the future’ or ‘We shouldn’t really gamble with the future of civilization.’”Despite running the company behind ChatGPT, Altman is cautious about putting the technology in front of young children.“I’m a big fan of limiting technology across the board for kids,” he said. “I think it’s good for kids to be running around outside and playing in nature and doing whatever kids have done for a long time.”As for his own children using ChatGPT?“I don’t have an age in mind where I would let my kids talk to ChatGPT yet, but it is certainly not now,” he said.He still says AI is close to AGISam Altman speaks at Dreamforce in San Francisco, Sept. 15, 2026. In a new Vanity Fair interview, the OpenAI CEO also talks about Amazon dropping the movie, Elon Musk, his kids, his survivalist streak and why he still thinks AI’s future will be “all going to be great.”Noah Berger/For the S.F. ChronicleOn one of the interview’s biggest questions, Altman stopped just short of declaring that artificial general intelligence, a theoretical form of AI that matches human cognitive abilities, has arrived.Asked whether it is here, he answered: “It’s subjective.”Asked how close it is: “It’s close.”Altman said OpenAI had been talking about this possibility for a decade and that the major change is that the rest of society is finally taking the prediction seriously.“10 years ago, very few people believed us,” he said. “Now most people believe us.”OpenAI has paused training because of safetyOne of the interview’s more significant revelations had little to do with Hollywood.Altman said OpenAI has already halted a model training run because its capabilities were advancing faster than the company expected.“We recently stopped a model training run, paused one because we thought we needed to make more progress on alignment and monitorability given how quickly the capabilities were advancing,” he said.When asked whether that means OpenAI needs to slow down now, Altman said the company has done so before.“There have been many times already, you just haven’t paid attention,” he said.He said OpenAI is talking with other AI companies and governments about shared safety standards and suggested cooperation between the United States and China could eventually be necessary.He says OpenAI would choose humanity over its stock priceWith OpenAI moving toward a potential IPO, Altman was asked what happens if investors demand faster growth at the expense of safety.His answer was blunt: “If we have to do something that is in the interest of the world, but not our particular shareholders, it’s going to be very easy about what we’re going to decide to do there.”And if investors punish the company?“Then it falls,” he said. “Maybe it falls a lot.”Altman said the company would accept volatility if necessary.“If there is ever a question about our share price going up or doing the right thing for the future of humanity, we are not going to pay attention to the share price in that moment,” he said.Privately, he’s more optimistic than he soundsDatebook PicksPerhaps the most revealing answer in the interview, Vanity Fair asked Altman to name something he privately believes about AI that he rarely says publicly because people might misunderstand it.His answer: “That it’s all going to be great.”Altman acknowledged that there are “very scary things” to deal with, and that OpenAI has to get those things right, “But I’m incredibly optimistic for the future.”

articles.headline: How Andrew Garfield Combined Crowdsourcing and a Classic Acting Technique to Understand Sam Altman - The Hollywood Reporter
articles.body: How Andrew Garfield Combined Crowdsourcing and a Classic Acting Technique to Understand Sam Altman    The Hollywood Reporter

scored.body:
Andrew Garfield doesn’t look exactly like Sam Altman.

But the Oscar-nominated actor found a way to try to capture the essence of the OpenAI CEO he portrays in Luca Guadagnino‘s Artificial.

An attempt to use prosthetics to better resemble Altman was unsuccessful (“totally ridiculous,” according to Guadagnino), so much so that Garfield laughed as he recalled how badly that experiment went when reminded of it by The Hollywood Reporter on the red carpet ahead of Artificial‘s world premiere at the 2026 New York FIlm Festival.

Instead, ironically for the tech-forward film, Garfield relied on a classic acting technique and human conversations (an analog version of crowdsourcing).

“When you’re first learning about acting, one of the techniques, Stanislavski, is you go through the play and you see what this person says about other characters. You see what other characters say about him,” Garfield told THR. “So I tried to speak to as many people as possible who know Sam or who have experiences and interactions with Sam to glean more of an objective, moral side, looking in point of view. Everyone is an unreliable narrator. I felt like I needed to absorb as much as possible, put it in the cauldron, put it in the pot, put it on simmer and then [use] my own instincts and interpretation and point of view, because any other actor would have played it differently. I know that I needed to play it in the way that I wanted to play it.”

Artificial tells the story about both the origins of OpenAI and the rise of the artificial intelligence phenomenon, including the Silicon Valley figures at the forefront of the technology. Garfield, like his fellow castmembers in the film, looked to interviews and videos of his real-life counterpart, with Anora breakout Yura Borisov, who plays OpenAI co-founder Ilya Sutskever, also taking a surprisingly ethereal approach.

“I hit a wall, and it was a couple of days before we started to shoot,” Borisov explained of his preparations. “We have the same birthdays (Dec. 8), and I imagined, ‘OK maybe we have some spiritual connection because of this, and I can just relax and create my own character inspired by him.'”

Not Suitable for Work alum Will Angus plays former OpenAI researcher turned Anthropic co-founder Dario Amodei and relished playing the exec at a time when he was somewhat under the radar.

“When we were shooting the movie, [Amodei] definitely wasn’t as in the zeitgeist as he is now, so it was very cool to learn about it from the ground floor,” Angus told THR. “We treated him well. … He really had this anxiety to make sure that AI was morally aligned with humanity so I kind of enjoyed being in that role.”

Amodei has pushed for federal safety regulations around the technology and, just last month, called for an industrywide slowdown of AI development to give safety measures time to catch up.

When asked if he believes Amodei’s AI safety concerns, Angus was cautiously optimistic.

“I hope he’s doing the best he can to make sure AI’s aligned with human goals,” he said. “I don’t know. I hope so.”

Neon, which acquired Artificial after Amazon MGM Studios abruptly dropped the nearly completed film in June, plans a Christmas Day release for the movie, which was written by Saturday Night Live alum Simon Rich and also stars Ike Barinholtz as Elon Musk, Monica Barbaro as OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, Cooper Hoffman, Mark Rylance, Will Price, Chris O’Dowd, Billie Lourd, Zosia Mamet, Jason Schwartzman, Cooper Koch, Thaddea Graham, Nicholas Hamilton and Angus Imrie.

articles.headline: Sam Altman Thinks He’s the Prometheus of Silicon Valley - Gizmodo
articles.body: Sam Altman Thinks He’s the Prometheus of Silicon Valley    Gizmodo

scored.body:
In Greek mythology, Prometheus is a Titan who is sentenced to eternal torture by Zeus after stealing fire from Olympus and gifting it to humanity. He is a democratizing figure who breaks out a source of great power from its confines among the gods to give it to the everyday folk. In Silicon Valley, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman views himself in a similar light. In a new interview with Vanity Fair, Altman was asked to describe his personal mission and how he would like to be remembered in the history of AI. “And what I would really like, if the history books ever write anything about me at all, it’d be great if they don’t, is just the work that OpenAI did really made sure that AI was a fundamental thing that every person got hugely empowered with,” Altman said, comparing the technology to fire or electricity. “It was not something that happened to them. It was something that people were given.”

When the interviewer concludes that the figure he is describing is essentially Prometheus, Altman admits, “closer to that than other things you could come up with for sure.” The OpenAI chief says that many people in Silicon Valley “really believed only a small priesthood should get access to AI,” ultimately casting a group of Silicon Valley insiders as “benevolent dictators” who determine how the general public benefits from AI development. But Altman and OpenAI allegedly believed that giving the “superpower” of AI to people would instead achieve “tremendously more good than bad.”

Altman’s answer taps into longstanding fears of the formation of an AI-powered superclass versus a group of tech-illiterate working-class folk whose jobs get automated by a super-advanced stage of artificial intelligence: a so-called “permanent underclass.” Some of the people who subscribe to this prophecy claim that if these newer, higher-tech artificial intelligence models are kept under wraps only to be used by a select group of people or are made available at prices too high for the average segment of society to afford, then it will result in a group of tech elites gaining immense power over others. OpenAI’s rival Anthropic reignited this paranoia earlier this year with the release of Fable, the watered-down public-use version of its allegedly scarily advanced model Mythos, which was only made available to select government entities and corporations.

The permanent underclass narrative ties into the discussion over AI regulation as well, where some AI industry leaders argue that so-called overregulation will block people out and lead to a concentration of power in a handful of top AI companies. In the interview, Altman said that OpenAI is in a gray area when it comes to the question of regulation.

“We are willing to accept some things going wrong to make sure that this is a widely held and used and democratic technology,” Altman said. For example, open-source models will cause a “tidal wave of cybersecurity problems,” Altman argues, but still should not be banned. “We’re going to, as a society, I think, have to just accept some fairly severe cyber incidents from open models in exchange for the liberty that comes with that,” Altman said.

articles.headline: Now It’s Clear Why Amazon Didn’t Want to Release ‘Artificial’: It’s Withering AF - The Hollywood Reporter
articles.body: Now It’s Clear Why Amazon Didn’t Want to Release ‘Artificial’: It’s Withering AF    The Hollywood Reporter

scored.body:
“Aggressive technocapitalism wins, safety dies” is a long name for a movie and a short logline for a film, yet the phrase might accurately be used for both when it comes to Artificial.Luca Guadagnino brought his latest and by far most-topical movie to a world-premiere at the 64th New York Film Festival Monday evening, the first stop of what has already seemed like an unusually long journey. Ditched by Amazon MGM Studios after its parent company’s $50 billion investment in OpenAI, the film, as it turns out, would be non-grata at a large tech firm even if it never signed on for that 5 percent equity stake in Sam Altman‘s company. Persistently bleak under the rays of the California sun, Artificial (now under the aegis of Anora studio Neon) is the movie of the moment — the origin story of our current AI quagmire at the literal, psychological and pretty much every other level.Or as NYFF programming chief Dennis Lim said before the screening:“We are already in a threshold period. We need to understand how we got here, and the film you’re about to see shows us that way.”The movie is notably faithful, at times dutifully chronological and nearly always horror-movie bracing on the subject of the rise of capitalist AI, as Ilya Sutskever, an idealistic and socially unpolished Russian immigrant, shows up at the office door of Geoffrey Hinton, a godfather of AI, at the University of Toronto in 2003. There he will learn under the well-intentioned eventual Nobel Prize winner, soon following him to Google and its Bay Area halo. As observers of the space well know, Sutskever ends up meeting Sam Altman at a 2014 conference, where the Y Combinator financier, already well established in Silicon Valley at barely 30, chases down the prodigy to convince him to work at a nascent OpenAI as chief science officer and supercharge its LLM ambitions. Or, more accurately, make them possible in the first place — Sutskever is Wozniak to Altman’s Jobs, but more so.Soon a (last) supper follows with Altman, Elon Musk, Greg Brockman and others — the prelude to a slow realization by Sutskever, and us, that the science Sutskever wants to develop to save the world is the capital Altman wants to use to build a warchest. We know the rest — OpenAI rushes out ChatGPT in November 2022, shocking the industry and even many of its own employees; Altman displays a growing accelerationism with the abetment of lead investor Microsoft (mixed with blog-y pronouncements of transforming and saving the world, and a weird word-cloud fondness for the word compute); and OpenAI transitions from a nonprofit to its opposite. The whole story culminates in Sutskever’s notorious November Coup of 2023 in which Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and assorted OpenAI loyalists back Altman, engineering his return so that he’s stronger than ever — a day clear then and doubly indicative now of capitalism’s ultimate triumph and on which, Yom Kippur-style, our AI fate was inscribed and sealed.Which brings us to late 2026 — right up to it, as the film collides with the last month of AI safety warnings, which also make the screen with a postscript (one of about five) about AI researcher and whistleblower Jacob Coxon warning of a pox on all their houses (or, at least on his former employers Anthropic and OpenAI) for a reckless speedplow over any semblance of safety. On cue, Coxon was taping Jon Stewart a half mile downtown at the exact time the movie was playing, in what one commenter very reasonably called a “most serious and chilling episode” of The Daily Show.A slow-burn account that will not surprise those who have covered the meteoric ascent and Teflon resilience of Altman, Artificial still offers a rich and often entertaining primer on the becoming of OpenAI, integrity and caution time and again sacrificed on the holy altar of finance. (You can read The Hollywood Reporter’s review of the film here.) Not to mention a parable of modern Silicon Valley, the place where advanced science and obscene wealth converge in a way that has never happened in the history of humanity and can only, if every novel on either subject can be believed, will end splendiferously well. Guadagnino took an interest in the subject because “as much as AI belongs to a world of mathematics and computers, it is still generated by peoplle and exists in space of their interaction,” as he noted from the NYFF stage. Screenwriter Simon Rich took an interest in the subject after being told by a childhood friend decades ago about what was possible with AI. That friend ended up going on to work in the industry, prompting Rich, a former Saturday Night Live and Pixar writer as well as a novelist and essayist, to pen this script. “I’m not particularly charismatic or good looking but as a last-ditch effort to warn mankind I wrote this movie. I hope to God a couple people pay attention,” he said.Amazon initially backed the movie before, well, “the concept of a conflict of interest is a very important, let’s say, elephant in the room here,” as Guadagnino told THR’s David Canfield. In retrospect it’s almost shocking the company would have even contemplated signing on to a movie so innately critical of a Valley vision in which noble use cases form but a thin camouflaging membrane over the bloody black heart of a human-trampling moneygrab — so much so that the question becomes not why Amazon abandoned the film but which Hollywood agent is responsible for the Houdinian feat of convincing them they should hop aboard in the first place, and why aren’t they the ones ruling the world?

To give you a sense of just how scabrous this film is, and just generally to level you up on how some of Silicon Valley’s most powerful people are getting shown in what will surely be an Oscar mainstay and cultural lodestone this Hollywood season, here’s a quick rundown: Greg Brockman — In real life he’s an AGI evangelist and Altman lock-stepper who’s a jock-like presence that donates millions to a pro-AI Super PAC. In the movie he’s all of those things but nerdier and more simpering. Cooper Hoffman, who plays him, said at NYFF he didn’t read any books about Brockman, but let himself think about a phrase Garfield told him: that the man would leave his wife for Sam Altman.Mira Murati — Long the most enigmatic of OpenAI figures — she tries to stop Altman but also sticks with him; she is at once Cassandra and complicit — the Albanian ex-Tesla engineer gets her due from Monica Barbaro who gives the character just enough warmth to seem like a hero, until undertaking actions that make her seem like the opposite.Sam Altman — Hinton in the film describes Altman as someone so toxically charismatic he would land on an island of cannibals and shortly after become their king. Andrew Garfield portrays him as a completely dishonest personality who will always tell everybody how much he likes them to their face while screwing them behind their back. A flamboyant cipher to a sometimes-cartoonish degree (you can read his articulate descriptions of how he crafted the character here) Garfield’s Altman is going for a different kind of spiritual truth. “Of course it will feel confronting [to Altman],” Garfield said at the screening, “[but I wanted] to a deep interrogation of who are giving our power, our autonomy, our data too.”

The best gift Garfield could give Altman is going so hard on the caricature-y touches, allowing Altman to discredit the whole thing. He’s already tried to do that, without having seen the movie. “I don’t think they’re going for accuracy,” Altman just said to Vanity Fair, admittedly basing his assessment on the trailer. He and Garfield cannot even agree on whether they waved to each other when the film was shooting near the mogul’s house. Altman says they did; Garfield said at the premiere that “if that happened I must have blacked out because I don’t remember it at all.”

Yann LeCun — The other godfather of AI gets a cameo in which he shows up Sutskever by mockingly asking him from the audience if he’s ever seen 2001. I don’t know that this ever happened, but as an object lesson in Sutskever not being taken seriously by the AI establishment it serves its purpose. It feels like shade that LeCun never appears in the film again, though given the treatment some of the other tech personalities receive, he might want to send Luca a bouquet.

Guy on Bench — Jason Schwarzman plays an anonymous prophet of doom (and ex-techie) who shows up at an San Francisco park to describe to Sutskever all the ways the AI boom can go wrong, providing the movie with its from-the-headlines leitmotif and cinema more broadly its wildest hair since Forrest Gump.Elon Musk — Ike Barinholtz has Musk wandering in from another movie, or dimension, a ramble-y, arrogant but ultimately comically non-threatening figure. This will be noticeable and even triggering to anyone who sees Alex Gibney’s Musk or just followed the man’s DOGE-based eviscerations of important aspects of the federal government. “When you play someone as beloved, as universally admired…” Barinholtz began his intro at the festival, before saying he tried to capture Elon how he was viewed then, long before “the RNC with a chainsaw.” Barenholtz’s portrayal raises what’s actually a key question in fact-based art: are we required to inject a modern understanding we couldn’t know at the time?

Tasha McAuley — Entrepreneur, Joseph Gordon-Levitt’s wife and coup-joiner on the OpenAI board, she is played briefly by Zosia Mamet (though not identified by name).

Geoffrey Hinton — If there’s one good thing about AI going so pop-cultural, it’s that we get a full-blooded character representing one of the great scientific minds of our time, here depicted (accurately) as the conscience of an industry. If there’s a second good thing, it’s that we get Mark Rylance portraying such a conscience. Dario Amodei — He is now known as the man who founded the breakaway Anthropic and, a showdown or two with the Pentagon aside, is running a company that could destroy the job market and the world as we know it (hey, his words). But back during his OpenAI era, he’s part of Altman’s gallery, if a very nerdy and definitely more idealistic member of same. Honestly on the scale of image-rehab to complete evisceration, Amodei is one of the few AI entrepreneurs to end up closer to the former in this film. A far cry, to say the least, from his recent depiction on SNL or portrayal in Stewart’s coverage.

Ilya Sutskever — The story’s unabashed hero, aided in real life by him all but disappearing after the failed coup (though he did raise $1 billion for an AI safety company). Garfield’s is the showier performance but Yura Borisov‘s depiction as a man slowly realizing how he’s been had is Richard-Gere-at-the-end-of-Primal-Fear-level stuff. “I was just trying to put this [lost innocence] in the film so you can feel what I hope you feel,” he said at the screening. The Jacob Coxons and other figures who continue Sutskever’s legacy, not to mention the concerns that only become more urgent, make him feel less like a figure from ye old AI days of 2023 but one speaking to us over our shoulder as we scroll the headlines at the breakfast table today.

The only downside to such a fiercely of-the-moment take is that said moment can change in the nearly three months until the film’s Christmas release. Maybe by then Neon will need to include 20 postscripts, and submit to the Oscars’ documentary category.

articles.headline: Apple CEO John Ternus puts design front and center - Cult of Mac
articles.body: Apple CEO John Ternus puts design front and center    Cult of Mac

scored.body:
News

Apple CEO John Ternus is reportedly a regular presence in Apple’s design studio. Image: Apple/Cult of Mac

Apple CEO John Ternus is reportedly spending far more time in the design studio than Tim Cook ever did. He’s there several times a week, sometimes more than once a day.

It’s clearly different from the Tim Cook era. Many people think design influence at Apple slipped after Jony Ive left the company back in 2019, but Ternus seems determined to fix that.

Apple CEO John Ternus takes a hands-on approach

John Ternus has spent virtually his entire career at Apple, joining the company’s product design team in 2001. He rose through the ranks until he reached senior vice president of hardware engineering in 2021.

That makes Ternus an unusually product-focused CEO. Before taking the top job, he spent years directly overseeing the engineers responsible for building Apple’s hardware. And that’s shaping how he runs the company since taking over as Apple CEO on September 1.

In his Sunday Power On newsletter, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said Ternus has immersed himself in the industrial design and human interface teams. Tim Cook, Apple’s previous CEO, by contrast, used to reportedly visit “about an hour once a month, at most.”

Ternus was already familiar with the space from his years running hardware engineering. Apparently, now he’s treating it like a second office.

Ternus is reportedly able to do that because other executives are handling Cook’s old turf. CFO Kevin Parekh is handling finances, while COO Sabih Khan is overseeing the supply chain. That frees up Ternus to focus on engineering and design.

Gurman says Ternus told employees he has to lead himself instead of copying Cook. Cook spent his tenure working where he could add the most value. Ternus could be wanting to do the same, but in different places.

Apple’s design leadership has been in flux

Apple hasn’t had a true design chief since Jony Ive’s exit in 2019. Industrial design and human interface teams each had their own leaders, and they answered to former COO Jeff Williams, who retired in 2025.

Apple then announced the teams would report to Cook. Ternus took over the responsibility ahead of the handoff, according to Gurman. And keeping the teams staffed hasn’t been easy at all. Alan Dye, who led interface design, left for Meta. OpenAI also hired away lots of Apple designers.

See also: The real reason Meta poached Apple’s UI design chief

Apple isn’t hunting for a chief design officer

One might expect Apple to hire a Jony Ive replacement, but Gurman says no such search is underway.

Instead, Apple seems to be leaning on the people it already has. Molly Anderson is leading industrial design, while Steve Lemay heads human interface design. Both appeared during the iPhone Duo presentation, putting them front and center.

Apple has also promoted junior designers and hired new people, per the report. But Ternus remains the final decision-maker on design. And while he has no formal design background, he could be betting his involvement will matter.

For Apple fans missing the days of bold hardware, that’s welcome news. The next product launches might show how far Ternus’ influence goes.

Anurag Chawake is a tech-focused writer specializing in smartphones, apps and consumer technology. articles.body: A New Neurotech Startup Launches to Rival Sam Altman’s Merge Labs    wired.com

scored.body: Sam Altman-backed Merge Labs has a new competitor in the race to build a brain-computer interface powered by ultrasound. Bridge Neurotech is launching with $13.5 million in funding, including from venture firm General Catalyst, which has also backed major tech companies such as Anduril, Anthropic, Airbnb, and Stripe.The company is the latest in a growing field of startups that aim to translate signals from the brain into useful actions. Elon Musk’s Neuralink, plus Synchron, Paradromics, and Precision Neuroscience are all working on brain-computer interfaces to help people who have lost the ability to move or speak.These approaches all require surgery of some kind, which is why Bridge founder and CEO Will Biederman says he struck out on his own. “It fundamentally comes down to a difference in vision,” he says.Biederman developed the chip Neuralink licensed to use in its first devices as part of his PhD work, but his goal with Bridge is to build a wearable device that could be used by far more people than a brain implant. Only 100 or so people around the world have received an implanted brain-computer interface as part of clinical trials, including at least 21 volunteers who have gotten Neuralink’s device.“The risks of neurosurgery really cannot be minimized or dismissed, and so the level of safety and benefit that these devices must deliver really is quite high,” Biederman says. “Nobody really wants a hole in their head.”But wearable brain-computer interfaces have suffered from poor signal quality. Bone and skin weaken electrical signals before they reach external sensors, which affects the performance of a device. It’s why most companies are recording electrical impulses directly from neurons in the brain. Neuralink and others have shown that these electrical systems can allow paralyzed people the ability to control electronic devices, move robotic arms, and communicate in real time with just their thoughts.Bridge Neurotech thinks ultrasound offers an alternative to current implants and external sensors. Ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves to bounce off moving red blood cells and measure the speed and direction of blood flow. In the brain, fluctuations in blood flow closely follow neural activity.Both Bridge Neurotech and Merge Labs have ties to Arbor Neuroscience, which was previously known as Forest Neurotech, a nonprofit founded in 2023 by Biederman and fellow researchers Sumner Norman and Tyson Aflalo to pursue “work that is too integrated and long-horizon for a single academic lab, and too early for a company.” The organization built an instrument that uses ultrasound to image brain function that is in trials in the UK.Merge Labs spun out of Forest Neurotech in January, with Norman and Aflalo among the company’s cofounders, which also include Altman, researcher Mikhail Shapiro, and tech entrepreneurs Alex Blania and Sandro Herbig.Maryam Shanechi, a neuroengineer at the University of Southern California, says because ultrasound measures brain activity indirectly from blood instead of directly from neurons, there is a natural delay of a few seconds between when neurons fire and the subsequent change in blood flow and volume.“It captures a slower variation in neural activity,” Shanechi says. “That’s fine for a lot of applications, but it depends what you want to build.”For real-time, fast-paced tasks such as moving a robotic limb instantly or rapid typing, this lag time could pose a challenge for ultrasound-based brain-computer interfaces. Bridge is planning to use predictive AI models to cut down on that lag time and boost the performance of its interface. Biederman says the company is interested in pursuing both consumer and medical applications but didn’t comment on specific plans.The company is starting its first clinical study in volunteers in Redwood City, California. It’s an observational study, with no treatments or diagnoses involved, in which a small ultrasound probe will be placed on the side of the head of healthy adults, as well as those who have undergone skull surgery. Bridge’s probes, which use semiconductor silicon chips made by the portable ultrasound company Butterfly Network, will record brain activity while participants listen, watch, move, and speak.Bridge isn’t releasing images of its device yet, but Biederman says it is “something close to headphones” that will sit on the temporal window, which is located slightly above the ear. As the thinnest part of the skull, “it's the easiest place to image through,” Biederman says. That’s relevant for ultrasound, because bone scatters and absorbs sound, which presents technical challenges for imaging noninvasively through the skull.In a 2024 study, researchers from Caltech and the University of Southern California demonstrated that an ultrasound-based brain-computer interface could read and decode human brain activity, but it required a portion of the skull to be removed and replaced with a “window” through which ultrasound waves can pass. That is one of the biggest technical hurdles that Bridge will have to address.“My vision is focused on noninvasive interfaces,” Biederman says. “I think that's where the biggest opportunity to help people is.”

articles.headline: Why Sam Altman takes his hardest questions to Nikesh Arora - Fortune
articles.body: Why Sam Altman takes his hardest questions to Nikesh Arora    Fortune

scored.body:
Nikesh Arora has a knack for piercing directness.

I profiled the Palo Alto Networks CEO for our latest issue. A tech veteran leading the only pure-play cybersecurity company in the Fortune 500, Arora has a “tell it to you straight” posture that has made him a sought-after mentor. Case in point: When he needs advice, Sam Altman has for years turned to Arora.

“I think it’s hard to get direct, actionable advice,” Altman told me. “Most people aren’t sure, aren’t confident, are busy, or aren’t going to spend enough time. Maybe they don’t want to offend you.”

Arora doesn’t mind. He’s been known for that hard-driving rigor since his days at Google (he joined months after the company’s IPO, rising to chief business officer under Eric Schmidt). As I write in the story:

At Google, Arora developed a reputation for tear-inducing toughness, and he doesn’t deny it. “If people show up in this room unprepared, they’ll leave the room knowing they were unprepared,” he says. “I say to the people who come into this room, ‘If you have a lot going on, give it to me, and I’ll deal with it—but don’t show up here looking dazed.’”

An exacting attitude is necessary, Arora says, when the work has such high stakes.

“Would you want to get on that rocket that was built by somebody who was hungover and decided to not tighten the screw?” he asks rhetorically. “Would you ever excuse the person who didn’t do all the checks on a plane before it took off with 200 lives at stake? You expect that from these people. You expect them not to screw up. So why is it tough that I expect my team to not screw up? In every business we work, there are life-threatening or life-ending things that can happen if people don’t pay attention.”

It’s intense, yes. But that sort of intensity is perhaps warranted in the seat Arora occupies: AI has upended the cybersecurity landscape, with escalating stories of “agents gone rogue” and the looming prospect that there may be more cyberattacks than ever. Arora—also one of cybersecurity’s omnipresent acquirers—is right in the center of a generational moment, for cyber, for AI, and by extension for us all.

Read the whole profile here.

articles.headline: Trumpy Billionaire Tried to Kill This Movie—Now We Know Why - The Daily Beast
articles.body: Trumpy Billionaire Tried to Kill This Movie—Now We Know Why    The Daily Beast

scored.body: With all due respect to Aaron Sorkin, filmmaker Luca Guadagnino has delivered the true sequel to The Social Network with Artificial, an A.I. origin story that’s at once a cautionary tale, horror show, and tragedy. Detailing the rise, fall, and still-skyrocketing re-ascent of OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman, the Call Me By Your Name auteur’s latest (world-premiering at the New York Film Festival ahead of its Dec. 25 theatrical release) is a saga of timely terror. If its tonal unevenness sometimes undercuts its urgency, it’s still an engrossing lament that we’re forever doomed to repeat our mistakes—until, that is, we’re literally doomed.Amazon MGM Studios—run by the MAGA-friendly Jeff Bezos—tried to kill Artificial after it was completed (it’s now being distributed by NEON), and given its scathing depiction of its subject, it’s easy to assume that decision was driven by reasons that have nothing to do with the film’s quality. Whatever the case, Guadagnino’s drama doles out a figurative beating to OpenAI and Altman, whom Andrew Garfield embodies as the phoniest and most amoral of toxic tech bros. Having suffered at the hands of a megalomaniac as Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in The Social Network, the star now assumes the role of an agent of apocalyptic calamity, and his compellingly rancid performance is the dark heart of this modern fable. Even so, it’s Anora’s Yura Borisov who runs away with the film as the idealist whose dreams of a brighter tomorrow are shattered by the realities of an avaricious and cold-blooded today.In 2003, math prodigy Ilya Sutskever (Borisov) arrives at the University of Toronto office of famed computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton (Mark Rylance)—who’ll decades later win the Nobel Prize and be known as the “godfather of A.I.”—and immediately wows him with his genius. Sutskever is convinced that artificial general intelligence (AGI) is a potential reality in his lifetime, and despite his peers’ mockery, his collaboration with Hinton earns them millions in funding from Google, where they strive to achieve what many deem “science fiction.” For Sutskever, AGI heralds paradigm-altering breakthroughs in science, medicine, and other fields that will reap tremendous benefits for mankind. He’s a true believer, and his zealotry earns him a fan in Altman.Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov in “Artificial.” Neon Sutskever thinks that the primary thing standing in the way of his goal is scaling—meaning, he needs more money to ramp up the amount of data he pumps into his A.I. Disregarding Hinton’s reservations, he solves this problem by partnering with Altman and Elon Musk (Ike Barinholtz), both of whom are won over by a big dinner speech in which Sutskever declares, “Feel the AGI!” As Guadagnino’s camera pans around the table in the lead-up to that proclamation, Artificial captures the alluring promise of the technology and the borderline-religious faith that drives its development. Unfortunately, the spell the director casts breaks every time Musk appears on screen, thanks to a Barinholtz performance that consists of cartoonish faces and clownish gestures.In large part because of the goofy Tesla CEO, Artificial’s tone is slightly off early on. It rights itself once Musk jumps ship on OpenAI because of its slow progress, which threatens to let its formidable competitors reach A.I. first. Garfield’s Altman is totally blasé about this abandonment, pivoting by bringing in (with Sutskever’s seal of approval) Mira Murati (Monica Barbaro). Along with board chairman Greg Brockman (Cooper Hoffman), the team sets out to change the world responsibly—a mission whose altruism the company’s nonprofit status supposedly safeguards.Blur and Gorillaz frontman Damon Albam’s alternately electronic and orchestral score infuses Artificial with unsettlingly woozy energy, while Guadagnino and cinematographer Malik Hassan Sayeed’s canted angles give the film its edge, and their shot-counter-shot close-ups lend it an unnerving romanticism. With the wind at their back, Sutskever and Altman head for the techno-horizon, but the former is so seduced by the latter’s charm and support—all of it wrapped in florid, soft-spoken encouragements and comforting reassurances—that by the time he realizes that his cohort is consolidating power, crassly monetizing their invention (via ChatGPT), and ignoring warning signs (including with regard to their deal with Microsoft), he’s left with nothing but dire options.Astutely and amusingly written by the surrealist Saturday Night Live writer Simon Rich, Artificial moves efficiently through the recent past until it reaches its Big Bang: Sutskever convincing the board to fire Altman for deceptive and dangerous practices and to install Murati as OpenAI’s new CEO. This is the make-or-break moment for the company and, as Guadagnino’s film suggests, for the industry—if not the entire human race. As those acquainted with the news will know, Altman’s ouster was short-lived, and in the director’s hands, his proverbial resurrection plays out as depressingly inevitable, with only Sutskever unaware until the end that good intentions are no match (in Silicon Valley, or elsewhere) for unchecked greed and ego.Sam Altman is played by Andrew Garfield in the new film. Shelby Tauber/Pool/REUTERS Garfield’s Altman is a weirdo who grows less human as his control over the planet’s most powerful tech increases, and Artificial is wise to not italicize that, as a manipulative and untrustworthy liar who only cares about his own survival, he’s the perfect reflection of his duplicitous A.I.. It’s Borisov, however, who’s truly magnetic as the principled Sutskever, who clings to the hope that safety and security will win out. With a focused intensity that’s an extension of his character’s dogged inability to lie (making him the opposite of an AGI), the actor makes for a deeply sympathetic protagonist, not to mention a depressingly pitiable one once he’s forced to reckon with the nature of his allies and grapple with his own responsibility for the dawning A.I. crisis.Guadagnino can occasionally be too flashy; a shot of Altman and Sutskever hugging in real time, with super-slow-motion background revelry, for example, is unnecessarily showy and distracting. And ultimately, his censure of the men hurtling the Earth toward possible destruction—without a care for anything other than their own narcissism and covetousness—is too familiar to radically open anyone’s eyes. Yet Artificial imagines these tech pioneers in such bold and repugnant hues that it’s still easy to get swept up in Sutskever’s optimism and, consequently, to be wrecked by the rude awakening he receives. Consider it a caustic takedown of the stewards tasked with protecting us from the danger they’ve created, and a scary backstory for a future that looks bleaker with each passing day.Obsessed with pop culture and entertainment? Follow us on Substack and YouTube for even more coverage.

scored.body:
Sid Clark

Posted On 05/10/2026

Apple CEO Tim Cook and hardware chief John Ternus have paid tribute to Steve Jobs today, marking 15 years since the Apple co-founder died on October 5, 2011.Cook shared a photograph of Jobs alongside a personal message reflecting on the impact he had both on the world and on Cook himself.“There are people who leave a mark on the world, and then there are people who change it entirely,” Cook wrote. “Steve changed the world and so many lives in the process. He certainly changed my life forever. His spirit lives on in everything he created and everyone he inspired.”Cook, who succeeded Jobs as Apple CEO in August 2011, has regularly marked the anniversary of his death with personal tributes, often reflecting on Jobs’ influence on Apple and the people who worked alongside him.John Ternus, Apple’s senior vice president of Hardware Engineering, also shared a tribute to Jobs, focusing on lessons that continue to shape the company’s work today.“The way Steve taught us to care about every detail, every experience, every person, still guides our work today,” Ternus wrote. “Forever grateful.”Ternus joined Apple’s Product Design team in 2001, meaning he spent around a decade at the company while Jobs was CEO. The Apple Post previously reported on Ternus’ years working at Apple under Jobs as he rose through the company’s hardware organization.The two tributes offer different reflections on Jobs’ legacy. Cook focused on the personal and global impact Jobs had during his life, while Ternus highlighted the attention to detail and experience that Jobs instilled in Apple and which he says continues to guide the company today.Jobs died on October 5, 2011, aged 56, just weeks after stepping down as Apple CEO. Today marks exactly 15 years since his death.AuthorSid Clark

Sid Clark writes for The Apple Post, covering the latest from Apple and the wider tech world. Outside of writing, he’s a keen guitarist, music fan and someone who’s always got a new piece of tech to play around with.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman

Heather Diehl/Getty Images

Sam Altman says you need to accept some level of drama if you want him and Elon Musk to work together."I think once in a while you've got to punch a bully back in the nose," Altman told Vanity Fair during a wide-ranging interview. "And I also think Elon, like many bullies, only respects people who do."Altman and Musk had a famous falling-out that has since been recounted and is at the center of multiple legal battles. Their drama, which is far from the only simmering beef in the AI world, is now also the backdrop to efforts among the world's largest AI companies to reach a consensus on how to steer their technology.The OpenAI CEO said he would work with Musk, who has taken to calling his one-time ally "Scam Altman," as the industry grapples with renewed concerns over AI safety."If you want me to be able to work with him, maybe you should be happy I hit back once in a while, but I will work with Elon, of course," he said.For his part, Altman said that he "won't call myself a saint." At the same time, he doesn't view himself as the biggest problem."I'm not sure if I'm the one that you're supposed to come after between Elon and me," he said.In July, Musk lashed out at Altman when another account said that he had "warned the world about Scam Altman."Musk quoted that post and added, "He takes scamming to a whole new level."

In response, Altman took a shot at Musk's advocacy for orbital data centers, something the OpenAI CEO has repeatedly expressed skepticism about."Homeboy you're the one selling public market investors on short-term space datacenters," Altman wrote.Despite the drama, AI companies have taken more steps toward cooperation. Leaders of OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceXAI, Google, and Nvidia signed a White House-driven agreement in which the companies agreed to some self-imposed safety measures.Altman told Politico's Decoded Podcast that there's no single group chat, but officials at frontier labs have multiple avenues to continue talking."There's no like big WhatsApp that everybody's in," Altman said, "but there's like lots of, you know, people are running into each other at the same conference. There's calls, occasional meetings, stuff like that."

members.title: Google DeepMind chair and Alphabet chief scientist Demis Hassabis on the human brain: “a biological approximation to a Turing machine” - Martin Cid Magazine

representative.headline: Google DeepMind chair and Alphabet chief scientist Demis Hassabis on the human brain: “a biological approximation to a Turing machine” - Martin Cid Magazine
representative.body: Google DeepMind chair and Alphabet chief scientist Demis Hassabis on the human brain: “a biological approximation to a Turing machine”    Martin Cid Magazine

articles.headline: Google DeepMind chair and Alphabet chief scientist Demis Hassabis on the human brain: “a biological approximation to a Turing machine” - Martin Cid Magazine
articles.body: Google DeepMind chair and Alphabet chief scientist Demis Hassabis on the human brain: “a biological approximation to a Turing machine”    Martin Cid Magazine

scored.body:
Demis Hassabis has built his career on treating the human brain as the one working blueprint for general intelligence. This week a fragment of his became the emblem of everything a critic believes the AI industry gets wrong about minds, and the full sentence it came from is narrower, and more revealing, than the piece that travelled.

“a biological approximation to a Turing machine.”

The phrase anchors an essay by Benjamin Riley in The Verge, “Our minds aren’t equipped to handle AI.” Riley opens with the cybernetics pioneer Norbert Wiener, “The thought of every age is reflected in its technique,” and offers Hassabis, now chair of Google DeepMind and Alphabet’s chief scientist, as the clearest case of an industry that sees its own machines when it looks at a skull. The words themselves come from a conversation with James Manyika published this year in Dædalus, the journal of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

What the full sentence says

In Dædalus, Hassabis was explaining what AGI means to him. He defines it as “a system that exhibits all the cognitive capabilities the human mind has,” because the brain is “the only existence proof that we know of so far, perhaps in the universe, that general intelligence is even possible.” Then comes the line in full: “The brain can be viewed as a biological approximation to a Turing machine, meaning that, in theory, it could learn anything that is computable.” The next sentence applies the brake. Any finite system needs “some degree of specialization because there is only so much time, memory, and information.”

Read that way, it is not a claim that people are laptops. It is a claim about range, about what a brain could learn in principle, and it doubles as an engineering spec. If the brain is the reference machine, AGI is whatever matches its entire range. Hassabis even sketches the exam: train a model with a knowledge cutoff of 1910 and see whether it arrives at General Relativity, as Einstein did in 1915. “For now, the answer is clearly no,” he says.

The critique works one layer down

Riley’s objection sits somewhere else. Drawing on Paul Cisek, a neuroscientist at the University of Montreal, he argues that brains are better understood as feedback-control systems that act on the world to change what they perceive, shaped first by evolution and then by culture: imitation, language, writing, schools. On that model, a chatbot that does the effortful part of thinking is “a cognitive hot dog,” tempting in the moment and corrosive as a regular diet. He points to OpenAI’s education chief Leah Belsky calling ChatGPT “the world’s largest learning platform,” and to a study from China in which thousands of students essentially stopped doing their homework once they started using AI.

The clause that decides it

The sharpest collision is inside Hassabis’s own paragraph. A few lines on, he says the key is “the brain’s potential to learn almost anything, especially as we are able to design and build tools and machines to help us gain knowledge.” That clause carries the whole dispute. Riley is not really proving the Turing-machine framing false. His evidence is about tools that do the learning instead of helping a person gain it. A computability claim describes what a brain could absorb in theory. It says nothing about whether a given product leaves the learner’s head fuller or emptier.

That question now lands on the person setting Alphabet’s scientific direction. Hassabis gave up the day-to-day CEO job in August to concentrate on AGI strategy and science, telling staff, as Fortune reported, that AGI is close at hand and that getting the next steps right is critical for humanity. A lab that measures its machines against the full range of the human brain has a direct stake in that range not shrinking in the people who use them.

An approximation to a Turing machine still has to be programmed by something. For people, that has always been the slow work of learning, and it is the one step a tool can either amplify or quietly skip.

Tags: Demis Hassabis, Google DeepMind, AI in education, Artificial general intelligence, Turing machine

scored.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently argued that society may need to accept some negative consequences of artificial intelligence because of its broader benefits. Now a new report by Fortune has revealed that the ChatGPT-maker is introducing a new interview process which is aimed at accessing how prospective employees would help ensure AI benefits humanity. The contrasting developments highlight how the ChatGPT maker is simultaneously advocating for wider acceptance of AI-related risks while strengthening its focus on mission-driven hiring as the technology becomes increasingly powerful.The new ‘mission interview’ at OpenAIAccording to Fortune, OpenAI has begun piloting what it calls a "mission interview" for candidates applying to certain teams, starting with marketing and human resources. The goal, OpenAI told Fortune, is to give candidates dedicated space to explain how they'll contribute to the company's mission — ensuring that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity.The interview isn't designed to extract a single correct answer. Instead, OpenAI says it's meant to assess how candidates actually think, including their judgment and their ability to weigh trade-offs — qualities the company considers increasingly essential as AI firms work to harness a technology carrying both significant benefits and real risks. A company representative said skepticism and disagreement are welcome in these conversations, as is intellectual diversity more broadly.How it worksTo keep the process independent, the person conducting the mission interview comes from a different team than the one the candidate is applying to join. OpenAI is also building out a training program that employees can complete to become certified interviewers for this process, though the program is still in its early stages of ramping up.Part of a broader push to standardize hiringThe introduction of a formal mission interview reflects OpenAI's attempt to bring more consistency to its evaluation process as the company continues to grow rapidly. OpenAI currently employs roughly 8,000 people worldwide and has 830 open roles as of this writing. Standardizing how candidates are assessed is aimed at giving the company a more consistent measure for evaluating new hires across different teams, rather than leaving mission-alignment checks to vary interviewer by interviewer.Not the first company to test for "mission fit"OpenAI isn't alone in building this kind of evaluation into its hiring process. Several major tech companies, including Meta and Amazon, use their own versions of a mission or culture-fit interview. Amazon, for instance, trains certain employees as "bar raisers" — interviewers pulled from outside the hiring team specifically to assess whether a candidate meets the company's broader Leadership Principles.Rival AI lab Anthropic reportedly takes a more direct approach. According to Axios, Anthropic interviewers test candidates with a blunt question aimed at determining whether they're joining the company for its mission or simply for the money — a particularly pointed question given how lucrative positions at leading AI labs have become.The money complicates the mission questionThat tension between mission and compensation is hard to ignore at companies like OpenAI, where many roles currently offer salaries exceeding $300,000, often with substantially more once stock compensation is factored in. According to posts on the anonymous professional network Blind, one software engineer with six years of experience reportedly received a total compensation offer from OpenAI worth $935,000, including a $385,000 base salary and $2.2 million in restricted stock units vesting over four years. A separate Blind post claimed Anthropic had offered another candidate $620,000 in total compensation.
