articles.body: When Is OpenAI Going Public? Sam Altman Just Delayed the IPO Timeline    South Florida Reporter

scored.body:
The company behind ChatGPT has already taken its first official step toward going public — and if you’ve ever used the chatbot to write an email, plan a trip or settle a debate, this initial public offering (IPO) will affect you one way or another.

But investors hoping to buy shares of OpenAI will probably have to wait a while.

CEO Sam Altman said in September that the company is delaying its IPO while it addresses growing concerns about the safety of increasingly capable AI models. At OpenAI’s DevDay conference, Altman explained that the firm needs “to be able to make confident safety claims” before moving forward with a listing, according to reporting from The Verge.

That’s a notable shift from earlier this year, when the company confidentially filed its S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Reports back then suggested the IPO could make its debut as early as September. A 2027 debut now seems to be the closest possibility based on Altman’s comments.

Regardless of when exactly the OpenAI IPO lands, here’s what you should know before reaching for your brokerage app.

How OpenAI’s IPO could affect ChatGPT

OpenAI faces a costly problem: Building and maintaining artificial intelligence models requires enormous computing infrastructure. The company has made significant data-center spending commitments that will require substantially more revenue to support.

Going public would give OpenAI access to a much larger pool of capital because it would open the company to public stock markets instead of relying mainly on private investors, venture capital firms or internal cash flow. But it also means the company would have to answer to shareholders, which has implications beyond Wall Street.

When consumer tech companies go public, the pressure to grow revenue and hit quarterly targets can reshape the products people rely on. Netflix, for example, raised subscription prices repeatedly and cracked down on password sharing starting in 2022, while Reddit expanded monetization efforts around its API and advertising business ahead of its IPO in March 2024.

ChatGPT currently offers a free tier alongside its paid plans, but as a public company, OpenAI will face scrutiny over whether it’s doing enough to monetize its over 1.2 billion weekly active users — of which only around 50 million are paid subscribers. That could result in changes to what’s free and what’s paywalled.

What is OpenAI worth?

OpenAI said in March that it closed a $122 billion funding round where it was valued at $852 billion, making it one of the most anticipated IPOs in years. For context, that’s larger than the market cap of most Fortune 500 companies.

Its potential valuation has climbed considerably since then. The company is now discussing another private funding round of at least $30 billion at a valuation of roughly $1.4 trillion. The talks are still preliminary, but Bloomberg reported the new funding could serve as bridge financing while OpenAI delays its IPO.

These numbers matter for investors because they set expectations. Retail investors buying OpenAI stock once it goes public will likely be paying a premium on top of an already enormous valuation, and the company has yet to prove it can generate profits at a scale that justifies that valuation.

Is OpenAI profitable?

OpenAI revenue has grown sharply since it first announced its IPO. The company’s annual recurring revenue is nearing $70 billion, according to Axios; that’s up more than 70% since the beginning of the third quarter.

But rapid growth in revenue doesn’t mean OpenAI is profitable. Its net losses reportedly climbed to $42 billion in 2025, and the company doesn’t expect to reach profitability until around 2030.

OpenAI also faces growing competition from Anthropic, the makers of Claude, which generated $11.5 billion in revenue in the second quarter of 2026 and also filed confidential IPO paperwork. More recent reporting suggests that pace has since climbed above $100 billion annually.

What investors should consider before an OpenAI IPO

Whether OpenAI is worth investing in will largely depend on your risk tolerance. High-profile tech IPOs have a mixed track record: Uber, Lyft and Rivian, for example, all debuted with enormous valuations and delivered rocky early returns for investors who bought in at launch.

OpenAI also has an unusual corporate history. It launched as a nonprofit research lab, converted to a for-profit structure to raise capital and only recently completed the structural changes legally necessary to pursue a public offering.

A lawsuit filed by co-founder Elon Musk challenging that conversion went to trial this year. A jury sided with OpenAI on technical grounds and the judge dismissed Musk’s claims, clearing what had been the biggest legal obstacle to going public. (Musk separately launched a major IPO of his own for SpaceX.)

The S-1, once public, will be the most important document for investors to read before making any decision. Until then, the company’s targeted valuation is mostly just a number — not a verdict on what OpenAI is actually worth to shareholders.

How to invest in OpenAI before its IPO

Retail investors can’t directly buy the company’s stock yet because it’s still private. But there are several ways to invest in OpenAI indirectly.

Microsoft is the clearest example. The software giant has invested heavily in OpenAI and built its technology into products like Azure, Bing and Copilot. Nvidia has also benefited from rising demand because companies like OpenAI rely on its chips to train and run AI models at scale.

Investors can also gain exposure through ETFs that hold large positions in AI-focused companies, including major tech firms tied to the growth of generative AI infrastructure.

Some private-market platforms occasionally offer access to pre-IPO OpenAI shares, though those opportunities are generally limited to accredited investors (people or institutions that meet certain income or wealth requirements set by financial regulators) and often come with high minimum investments and added risk.

scored.body: Apple CEO John Ternus, who recently stepped into the top leadership position after guiding the company’s hardware engineering teams across multiple device generations, has shared how an iconic Steve Jobs philosophy continues to dictate Apple’s design standards – even on its most budget-friendly devices. Speaking soon after the launch of the MacBook Neo earlier this year, Ternus revisited one of his favourite stories about the late Apple co-founder, illustrating how attention to unseen details remains the foundation of the company’s product line.The ‘carpenter's lesson’Ternus recounted a quiet moment involving Jobs moving a bedroom dresser away from the wall.“Steve was moving a piece of furniture, a chest of drawers, and pulled it away from the wall and looked at the back and was just reflecting on the carpenter who had made it beautiful. It finished the back as beautifully as the rest of it, even though nobody was going to see it right and I think about that all the time because I think that perfectly exemplifies what we do here,” he said.The mindset of treating internal components and unseen surfaces with the same engineering precision as the exterior casing has been a foundational rule of Apple hardware since the earliest Macintosh models. Ternus connected that design ethos directly to the MacBook Neo, pointing out that cost-effective pricing does not mean cutting corners on aesthetic or structural integrity.“We've been talking about the MacBook Neo. Here is our most affordable Mac we've ever made, and it's absolutely beautiful. And if you open it up and look inside, it's just as beautiful,” Tetanus said.“And that's true about all products – an iPhone Pro Max or a MacBook Pro or an iPad Pro, but it's also true on a MacBook Neo,” he added, suggesting that Apple applies the exact same standards to its entry-level hardware.For Ternus, continuing to obsess over hidden details provides a clear roadmap for where the company is headed under his tenure.“That's what we do, and so, it's just been really good just to think about that and reflect on that because that is probably the best kind of clue as to where we're going in the future. We're going to keep pushing in that same way,” Ternus said.

scored.body:
Tech fascist, end times harbinger, and general slime-ball Sam Altman has experienced a glitch in the matrix. And left with the most… bizarre takeaway.

In a conversation with Vanity Fair on Sunday, Altman broke his silence on Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s upcoming film about the five-day period when Altman got ousted from his company, OpenAI, and then reinstated. Andrew Garfield will play Altman.

Although Altman hasn’t been sold on the movie as an accurate telling of what happened in those five days of his life, he identified one part of the movie he can get onboard with: Garfield mastering his walk. (A walk that seems hardly signature being his most recognizable quirk?? Altman is never beating the robot allegations.) He and Garfield haven’t met, and Altman says he’s largely been able to ignore Artificial‘s looming release. Mostly.

Speaking to the outlet, Altman said he was surprised to step out of his San Francisco home (we’re picturing something modest, provincial, very un-oligarchical) and find the crew of Artificial mid-shoot. His biggest clue was Garfield, walking that damn walk and carrying Altman’s (allegedly) signature backpack. The two Altmans—one an Oscar-nominated actor with beautiful hair (2.0); the other who delights in coparenting his baby with ChatGPT (1.0)—then reportedly crossed paths and shared a wave. As Altman 1.0 and Altman 2.0 (allegedly) locked eyes, it is not confirmed nor denied if thousands of birds fell out of the sky with a desperate screech, or computers around the world glitched simultaneously, or if a giant portal to a technological netherworld opened up.

Altman 1.0 described the moment as “really weird.” “I mean, it’s like a strange thing to see someone that has nailed your kind of quirky mannerisms or whatever.” Yes, quirky is the word I’d use to describe to describe a guy who, when asked about the risks of a technology he created, said “the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology.” ~Quirky!~

Per an interview he did with Esquire, Garfield’s portrayal of Altman will be primarily based on court transcripts, interviews, and external research. He plans to move carefully in Altman’s world, partially out of fear of a Jungian “shadow self” that he has to connect with to play someone so dark, and partially for not-so-favorably portraying an extremely powerful person. He emphasizes it’s not his goal to villainize anyone, but let the villainy—er, quirk—speak for itself. Stay safe, Andrew!

articles.headline: Sam Altman Is Going to Try to Play Artificial Cool - Vulture
articles.body: Sam Altman Is Going to Try to Play Artificial Cool    Vulture

scored.body:
By

Fran Hoepfner,

a senior news writer who covers pop culture and the internet

Photo-Illustration: Vulture; Photos: Getty Images

If you are an exorbitantly wealthy tech CEO who happens to have a movie coming out about you this fall, there are lots of different ways you can act. You can be Elon Musk and post, uh, Twitter poems about it. You can be Mark Zuckerberg and have a secret email exchange with Jeremy Strong. Or you can be Sam Altman, who has decided that of all the ways you can play off the bizarre sensation of having a possibly scathing biopic come out about you, the best way to act is that it’s all, just, you know, whatever. He cares, duh! But not that much. Not too much! He’s normal about it, in a very California way. He’s not like other tech CEOs. He’s a chill tech CEO. Right?

In a new, wide-ranging interview with Vanity Fair, Altman addressed the forthcoming Luca Guadagnino film Artificial, starring Andrew Garfield as Altman, by being, to quote an old meme, “very demure.” “I mean, they’re trying to make a good movie, and maybe it will be good,” he says, adding that it “will not be good as an accurate depiction.” Except for one thing, of course, which is his signature weird walk. “One morning I was walking down the street to get coffee and there were all these cameras and there was a guy dressed exactly like me with my same backpack walking so much that I felt I was in some weird glitch of the simulation or something,” Altman explains, which is about as sharp an endorsement as any for Garfield’s performance in the film. Regarding any of the movie’s more controversial beats, however, Altman shrugs it all off. The fact that Amazon dumped the movie because of its alleged connection to OpenAI? “I never spoke to Jeff Bezos about it,” Altman answers. About the shot in the trailer where Garfield’s Altman goes into a bunker with a bunch of guns? “That’s an example of an inaccuracy, but I did look kind of cool,” he says, which is a canny non-joke that is almost funny enough to deflect the later conversation topic of Altman being a prepper (or, “I have a survivalist mindset,” as he says).

Altman’s low-key response is the anomaly, but it’s not necessarily less concerning than threats of lawsuits given the ongoing anxieties around the work being done at OpenAI. Lest we forget, Mark Zuckerberg showed up on SNL when Jesse Eisenberg played him in The Social Network, and now he’s, uh, dressing weird while Meta is expected to pay out more than $17 billion in settlement money for social-media addiction claims. So Altman can chill for now, if that’s his goal, but it doesn’t necessarily make his tech any less scary.

Sam Altman Is Trying to Play Artificial Cool

articles.headline: ‘Having Their Say’ in AI. Altman, AI Researchers & Big Tech. ARD #178 - AI: Reset to Zero
articles.body: ‘Having Their Say’ in AI. Altman, AI Researchers & Big Tech. ARD #178    AI: Reset to Zero

scored.body: It is Tuesday, and today’s theme is ‘having their say’ on things that matter in AI. Getting your turn to speak on something that matters, putting it on the record, saying it the way you want it, once and for all. We all want to do that, and AI is no different. In this AI Tech Wave, three groups had their say in the past few days, each in their own way.OpenAI’s Sam Altman, with a lot of words, to a lot of different outlets, in just a few days. A group of AI researchers who left the leading labs, having their say on the safety issues around AI. And Meta and Microsoft, speaking with their budgets on where they want to go versus the frontier AI models. Then the Gadget AI, where app developers are having their say on Apple’s first foldable iPhone.Sam Altman went on a media blitz this weekend, on top of his posts on X. On Saturday, he posted that he is very uncomfortable with people ascribing religious force to AI models, or surrendering human judgment to them, and called it a real safety issue, per Axios in ‘OpenAI’s Altman: Ascribing religion to models a “safety issue”’. The religious element comes in because The New York Times reported that Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah has been meeting with religious leaders again, on whether AI models could be conscious, and how to give them morals. You may recall I wrote about his meetings with the Vatican a few months ago, in ARD #84.Altman had a particularly interesting interview with Politico, in ‘Sam Altman to Decoded: “The world should accept some bad things happening” for the benefits of AI’. He said there is a lot of daylight between OpenAI and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei. He also said one lab in San Francisco should not hold the most powerful AI and dole out the benefits, calling that a completely unacceptable trade-off. And he drew a line at catastrophic risks, like a serious loss of control to AI.Then came a two-part cover interview in Vanity Fair, with Altman at the top of its New Establishment list, in ‘Sam Altman Sees the Future. Are We In It?’ Part 1 and Part 2. He went into a lot of detail on how OpenAI thinks about its opportunity set, its IPO timing (not in a rush, with the nonprofit still governing), and its latest frontier model, Astra 6.1, which OpenAI delayed because it would have tipped too far toward accident risk.MP Take: Altman is taking this time to position himself and his company versus Anthropic, which is going public imminently, likely before Thanksgiving, as I wrote in ARD #176. That is why he is on a media barrage: to position himself relative to the conversations he knows he will have with the same investors meeting with Sam and his team over the next few weeks. It paves the road on some of those issues and differences.By itself, ‘accept some bad things happening’ sounds sensational. But his broader point is that most technologies have dual uses. Every technology, from fire to the wheel, has had downsides for society. In that context, it is not a dramatic statement. And no one is going to disagree that one lab should not hold the most powerful AI.The core issue is that both Anthropic and OpenAI are threading the needle. They are running a pragmatic course between growing revenue toward eventual profits, building compute and getting their share of the capital dollars, while being as careful as possible. That is across a laissez-faire US market, a much more controlling Europe, and open source competition from China. So the daylight between the two is real, but far narrower than the rhetoric suggests. Both want the upside of AI while mitigating the downside. That has been true since I wrote about ‘A Tale of Two AI Essays’ from Sam and Dario two years ago, in RTZ #508.Sources: Axios, ‘OpenAI’s Altman: Ascribing religion to models a “safety issue”’ · Politico, ‘Sam Altman to Decoded: “The world should accept some bad things happening” for the benefits of AI’ · Vanity Fair, ‘Sam Altman Sees the Future. Are We In It?’ Part 1 · Part 2.For longtime readers: RTZ #508, ‘A Tale of Two AI Essays’ · ARD #84, ‘Pope Leo XIV’s AI Encyclical + Anthropic’s Three Questions’ · ARD #162, ‘All Together Now’ in AI · ARD #176, ‘Come Hell or High Water’ in AI.New York Magazine, with Asterisk magazine, sat down with eight people who left OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind, in ‘What Would You Do If Your Employer Could Destroy the World?’. They include Jacob Coxon, the 27-year-old who got a lot of attention when he quit Anthropic last month, after working to make its models more capable, as I noted in AI-RTZ #1206. Around the same time, an Anthropic alignment lead, Evan Hubinger, put the odds that AI could kill all humans at over 10% within a decade.The others left for different reasons, from the pace of AI progress to the Pentagon, job losses and the data center bets. Former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo says companies cannot be trusted to regulate themselves. Miles Brundage, OpenAI’s former head of policy research, now audits AI companies, because you don’t want the companies checking their own homework.MP Take: this is not unusual in AI. It is just the latest set of folks saying what they want to say. Remember that the doom versus boom arguments have been there from the very beginning, going back at least to Elon Musk and Larry Page’s 2015 falling-out over the risks versus the benefits of AI. This is a decade-plus debate, unlike anything in prior tech waves, and nothing will be resolved in the next few quarters. It will take years, because we have to see what AI actually ends up doing.I have been in the camp of people like Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, and China, as I discussed in AI-RTZ #1208: build the technologies carefully and methodically, year by year. Like any tech wave, it will take a long time to figure out the true benefits. And I still believe we will have ample time to control the downsides, without a whole mega set of policies. You generally cannot anticipate what technologies are going to be used for. They always surprise on the upside in their impact, from the PC to the internet to mobile phones, social media and cloud. AI is going to be no different, and it will take years to figure this out.Sources: New York Magazine, ‘What Would You Do If Your Employer Could Destroy the World?’.For longtime readers: AI-RTZ #1208, ‘The AI Existential Risk Essays, US vs China’ · AI-RTZ #1206, ‘OpenAI’s “Alien Mind” Essay, & Asimov’s Three Laws’ · RTZ #996, ‘Resurgent AI Fears from AI Researchers’ · ARD #160, ‘Not So Fast’ in AI.Meta and Microsoft are working actively to kick their Claude habits, per The Information in ‘Meta and Microsoft Push to Kick Their Claude Habits’. They are two of Anthropic’s biggest corporate customers, and both are cutting how much their own staff use Claude. They are token managing how much Claude gets used in their shops, not only for cost or competitive reasons, but because there are a lot of options, including their own models: Meta’s Muse line, and Microsoft’s MAI models plus others they partner with.At Microsoft, internal spending on Claude was on track for at least $1 billion this year. That is now down by more than a third. Microsoft recently made OpenAI’s models the default for its internal coding, which is cheaper for Microsoft to run given their commercial relationship, and each division now manages a token budget. At Meta, the number of employees using Claude Code fell by half, from about 60,000 to about 30,000. Part of that is layoffs, but mostly it is Meta’s own coding tools, running on its own Muse models.Remember, both are still big Claude users, and will be represented in Anthropic’s S-1 numbers on revenue growth. Microsoft’s payments to Anthropic for Claude features in its customers’ Copilot keep rising, so its total spending with Anthropic is roughly flat.MP Take: these are, as you would expect, the logical moves by these companies to manage their costs and their dependencies, thinking through the tactical and strategic implications of how they invest in and use AI models, frontier and otherwise. That shows up in the budgets. There will be a lot of ebbs and flows, and it is important to track, especially for those looking at Anthropic’s IPO, likely between now and Thanksgiving. It extends what I wrote about in June, when Microsoft picked a side versus the frontier AI models in AI-RTZ #1127, and the ‘Us vs Them’ dynamic in enterprise AI in ARD #111. And it is the reverse of the ‘tokenmaxxing’ boomlet at Meta earlier this year, in AI-RTZ #1118.Sources: The Information, ‘Meta and Microsoft Push to Kick Their Claude Habits’.For longtime readers: AI-RTZ #1127, ‘Microsoft picks a side vs Frontier AI models’ · ARD #111, ‘Us vs Them’ Comes to Trillion $+ Enterprise AI & more · AI-RTZ #1118, ‘Meta steps back from AI “tokenmaxxing”’.MP Take: we are seeing clarity from specific individuals, founders and CEOs like Sam Altman, from the people who are critical of and fearful of AI, and from the big companies figuring out with their budgets what they are saying about the big models themselves. Everyone is having their say, in words and in actions. And that is important to track and understand.A little fun here. Developers are leaning into Apple’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, before it is even out, per Axios in ‘iPhone Duo app-makers are having fun with the fold’. Pre-orders start October 16, with the phone in stores October 23. It is Apple’s first folding phone, years after Samsung, now on its eighth Fold, and Google’s Pixel Fold.This is the first time developers seem to be getting excited about what they can do with a folding phone, and they are showing a lot of creativity. One independent developer recreated a Walkman, in very clever ways, with real Walkman sounds and a fold-open cassette door. One San Francisco hackathon alone produced 73 Duo projects, from an accordion where folding faster plays louder, to a beat machine and a pop-up book.MP Take: it is fun to see, and something we have not seen as much as I would have anticipated with the many folds on the Android side. But it is Apple, and Apple does provide the software tools, the inspiration and the operating system, and developers are leaning in. As Steve Ballmer famously chanted, ‘developers, developers, developers’, as I wrote in 2023. Early adopters like yours truly, and whoever tries one at an Apple Store or Best Buy, will have fun checking out these apps. I am all for it.Sources: Axios, ‘iPhone Duo app-makers are having fun with the fold’.For longtime readers: AI: ‘Developers, Developers, Developers!’ · AI-RTZ #1113, ‘Apple Intelligence & Siri AI hum with “Google & Nvidia” inside’ · ARD #159, ‘Beyond the Moon’ in AI · RTZ #958, ‘Samsung vs Apple global “AI” smartphone race’.What do I relish most about a folding phone?My behavior is consistent with how most people use them: most of the time, they don’t open the phone. What I relish is that at any moment I could, and have a screen the size of an iPad mini. Most of the time it is just a phone that stays in my pocket. It is the luxury of knowing you could use it that way. That is one of the most underappreciated parts of the experience.It is like my love for the iPhone Air, a lot lighter and thinner than the iPhone 18 Pro Max: it is what is not there that is fun to relish.What has been the most disappointing thing about foldables so far?The creative apps developers are building for the Duo are exactly what has been missing over the last half decade or so. Developers made sure their apps open across the two screens, and that you can share two apps on a screen. But I have not seen creative things done. Even Samsung’s mobile chief said in January that foldables grew slower than expected, partly for lack of apps suited to the design, as I noted in RTZ #958. In a market of billions of smartphone users, millions of foldables have been sold. It shows how early these things are, despite years of annual models, and how slow some of this is when the technology is way ahead of users and developers.Meta and Microsoft, two of Anthropic’s biggest corporate customers, are cutting how much their own staff use Claude, per The Information.MP Take: they are token managing how much Claude gets used in their shops. Not only for cost or competitive reasons, but because there are a lot of options, including their own models.Developers are leaning into Apple’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, from a Walkman app to dozens of hackathon projects, before it even ships.MP Take: this is the first time developers seem excited about what they can do with a folding phone. Fun to see, and overdue.Researchers who left the leading AI labs are having their say on AI risks. The doom versus boom debate will take years to settle.MP Take: I am in Jensen Huang’s camp. Build the technology carefully and methodically, year by year, and we will have ample time to control the downsides.Sam Altman told Politico the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of AI, and that no single lab should hold the most powerful AI.MP Take: sensational by itself, but not in context. Every technology since fire and the wheel has had dual uses.Today’s AI-RTZ #1231, ‘The Agent to Agent ‘a2a’ Web Arrives’ is Part 2 of our three-part series, ‘From Apps to Agents’. It is about the AI agent web arriving, and how it interacts with the app environment, e-commerce and more.AI Ramblings Daily on AI-RTZ is here to think through AI and reset. Together.Tomorrow, we will be back with ARD 179 and AI-RTZ #1232, Part 3 of the series.Thanks for joining us, AI Curious Folk. Stay tuned.Axios, ‘OpenAI’s Altman: Ascribing religion to models a “safety issue”’, Oct 3, 2026Politico, ‘Sam Altman to Decoded: “The world should accept some bad things happening” for the benefits of AI’, Oct 4, 2026Vanity Fair, ‘Sam Altman Sees the Future. scored.body:
TikTok is bringing its ad network beyond its own app to U.S. advertisers and opening up campaign management to third-party AI platforms, the company announced at Advertising Week New York 2026.

The “TikTok Ad Network” (TTAN) lets U.S. advertisers extend campaigns beyond TikTok to reach audiences across what the company describes as a premium network of nearly 400,000 apps worldwide. TTAN is fully integrated into TikTok Ads Manager and includes brand safety and placement controls.

Alongside the network expansion, TikTok said its “Model Context Protocol” (MCP) tool for advertisers is now available as a connector across several AI platforms and registries, including Claude, Kimi, Manus, Perplexity, Replit, Snowflake, Tencent WorkBuddy, and the IAB Tech Lab Agent Registry. Built on the open “Model Context Protocol,” the tool allows developers to build AI agents directly on top of TikTok’s ads ecosystem to plan, launch, and manage advertising workflows with fewer manual steps. TikTok said advertiser use of the MCP tool for campaign activation and management has grown more than 200% since launch, citing internal data from July through September 2026.

“The TikTok MCP is indispensable to our AI-powered campaign workflows, including how we build campaigns, upload creative, and analyze performance. TikTok is a leader in helping brands leverage AI to grow,” George Velonias, Head of Growth Marketing at Wayfair Canada, said in a blog post.

The announcements were part of a broader set of AI-powered advertiser tools TikTok unveiled at the conference, spanning commerce, lead generation, and creative automation. On the commerce side, TikTok introduced “Buy Direct,” an in-app checkout tool that lets users complete purchases from the For You feed without leaving the app, and “Shopping Assistant,” a conversational AI agent built into multiple TikTok touchpoints that provides real-time guidance on product details, shipping, sizing, and availability. The company also introduced “Agentic Leads,” an AI agent for lead generation available through TikTok Direct Message and on advertiser-owned websites.

On the creative side, TikTok is automating its “Search Ads Campaigns” through Smart+, which extends automation to keyword and creative selection in search ads buying. A related feature, “Smart+ Creative Selection,” consolidates creative sourcing, including advertiser assets, Symphony’s AI-generated creatives, and creator content, into a single approval workflow. TikTok is also expanding GMV Max, its automated ad solution for TikTok Shop sellers, to factor in costs such as affiliate commissions, coupons, and referral fees when optimizing campaigns.

“AI is transforming how advertiser content is created and scaled,” said David Kaufman, Global Head of Monetization Product Partnerships at TikTok. “With our suite of solutions, we are bringing together AI, automation, and creativity to help advertisers improve performance while reducing effort.”

TikTok cited a PF Global economic impact report published last week finding that activity on the platform helped generate $81 billion in GDP for U.S. businesses, with 54 million Americans reporting a purchase after watching a TikTok video.

articles.headline: SDKs emerge as key gateway to AI advertising as in-app ad market hits $400 billion - The Economic Times
articles.body: SDKs emerge as key gateway to AI advertising as in-app ad market hits $400 billion    The Economic Times

scored.body: The software development kit (SDK) has emerged as the key control point in the $400 billion in-app advertising market and could give independent adtech platforms an early advantage in the next wave of advertising across AI assistants, lockscreens and agentic commerce, according to a new report by Analysys Mason.The report, The SDK Advantage: How independent adtechs won mobile and are positioned to win AI-native advertising, argues that platforms such as AppLovin, InMobi and Liftoff, which built large SDK footprints across mobile apps, are best positioned to capture advertising on emerging AI-native consumer products.In-app advertising reached around $400 billion in 2025, growing 10.8% year on year and reaching five times its 2017 level, according to the report. It accounted for roughly a third of the $1.18 trillion global advertising market, while users spent more than 90% of their smartphone time inside apps.The shift is significant because traditional web advertising tools have limited applicability inside apps. Apps do not use cookies and are isolated from one another, while Apple’s ATT opt-in rate is around 35%. Safari and Firefox block third-party cookies by default, and Google retired its Privacy Sandbox in October 2025.As a result, first-party signals collected through SDKs have become the most dependable basis for targeting, the report said.The report argues that installed footprint, rather than simply advertising technology, has become the key competitive moat. Independent SDKs can reach up to 44% of Android and 31% of iOS app downloads.AppLovin’s $1.05 billion acquisition of MoPub is cited as an example of deals focused on acquiring installed footprint rather than just technology.The economics of that footprint can be significant. AppLovin generated $5.48 billion in advertising revenue in 2025, up 70%, with an adjusted EBITDA margin of around 82%, according to the report.At the same time, advertising remains heavily concentrated among the largest online platforms. Google, Meta and Amazon account for 70-75% of global online advertising spend, even though the open internet represents around 60% of online time.For publishers, the economics of in-app advertising remain more fragmented: of every $100 spent by an advertiser in-app, publishers receive about 50-55, the report said.The next opportunity could come from AI-native products. The report argues that advertising will become increasingly important as AI products scale because every query carries an inference cost and subscriptions alone may not cover those costs at consumer scale.Published pricing indicates that inference costs have fallen by more than 99% since 2023, potentially making free, ad-supported AI viable.Unlike conventional digital advertising, however, this emerging inventory will not necessarily have a webpage or ad tag. It will instead need to be accessed through code already sitting on the device—potentially strengthening the position of adtech companies with established SDK footprints.“Apps broke the advertising playbook built for the web,” Ujjwal Chaudhry, Partner at Analysys Mason, said. “Without cookies, tracking a user across apps no longer works, and the SDK has become the one place where the audience, the ad and the result can all be measured.”Chaudhry said the next wave of advertising would sit across lockscreens, AI assistants and agentic checkout.“AI products are costly to run, and advertising is the most scalable way to keep them free for consumers,” he said, adding that independent platforms with the widest SDK footprints were best placed to capture this new supply.According to the report, each successive shift in advertising has widened the lead of independent SDK-first platforms rather than resetting the competitive landscape.

articles.headline: I asked Gemini to fix my Pixel issues; here's what actually worked - Android Police
articles.body: I asked Gemini to fix my Pixel issues; here's what actually worked    Android Police

scored.body:
Published Oct 6, 2026, 11:00 AM EDT

Ali has spent more than a decade covering consumer technology, with a knack for looking beyond the specs, tinkering with software, and uncovering the bigger stories behind Android, Google, Apple, and everyday devices.

Over time, my Google Pixel had built up a handful of small annoyances, the kind of issues you notice at first but never really sit down to fix them properly. Gemini has silently become useful for everyday troubleshooting like this, not only for asking trivia questions or writing emails. This brought me to ask about four separate issues instead of googling each one separately like I normally would. Some of the answers were straightforward and immediately useful, but others only helped partially. Either way, it beat digging through settings menus and guessing what might be causing each problem.

Battery drain had no obvious cause

Gemini found the actual culprit in battery usage

The first issue I discussed with Gemini was battery drain, which had gradually crept up enough that I couldn't pinpoint the exact reason. I asked Gemini why my Pixel was draining battery significantly faster than usual and how I could figure out what was causing it. It walked me through checking battery usage and flagged a power-hungry app running in the background. It also suggested changing my settings for that app instead of giving generic battery-saving tips. I opened Settings > Battery > Battery usage, tapped the app Gemini flagged, and turned off the Allow background usage toggle under Manage battery usage. I did that for all the apps that I didn't use every day. I tested the fix over the next few days to see if it made a difference, and it did. The improvement was not dramatic, but it was noticeably better than before I made the change. It was a win for my Pixel and me.

Notifications had gotten completely out of hand

Fewer interruptions without going fully silent

With every new service I join, or when I'm surfing the web and creating accounts, my emails get flooded with promotional marketing material. The same approach applies to X accounts. Over the past few years, I have followed many people on X and selected push notifications for most of them for news purposes. Now, it feels like my Pixel never catches a break, and neither do I. I'd been putting this off for months, so I asked Gemini to find a solution. I asked the AI-powered assistant, "My Pixel gets too many notifications. What can I do to make it less annoying?" Gemini pointed me toward finding the apps that are bringing in the most notifications through Notification History, along with app-specific notification categories. Notification history, found under Settings > Notifications, showed me which apps were sending the most alerts, and each app's notification categories let me switch off only the ones I didn't need. I tamed my notifications in the Settings app by turning off app-specific notifications and random notifications. By the end, the distractions and interruptions were reduced. Now, I only receive notifications that matter to me and that I actually want to see and keep. This was more of a targeted fix than a blunt one.

My storage was full, and I didn't know why

A guided cleanup instead of random deleting

My Pixel's storage was getting full, and I wasn't sure what was taking up so much space. That's a frustrating spot to be in, because deleting the wrong thing is worse than deleting nothing at all. Since all my photos are stored securely in Google Photos, I shouldn't worry about device storage filling up. Gemini walked me through it and explained which apps and files were taking up the most space and which of them were safe to remove. In Settings > Storage, I could see what each app and file type was taking up, so I cleared the biggest ones. That separation was useful for me, as I'm always unsure about app data and which of them are important. I freed up a hefty amount of space without deleting anything important.

My connection kept dropping, and nothing looked wrong

Gemini narrowed it down before I reset anything

The last issue was the most irritating one, because it came and went randomly. My Pixel always struggles to stay stable and keeps trying to switch between Wi-Fi and mobile data, even though my other devices work fine. What made it hard to deal with was that nothing appeared broken, and it was hard to put my finger on what was going wrong. Other devices kept working fine, which made me realize that the problem wasn't originating from the router. I asked Gemini why my Pixel keeps losing its internet connection, even though other devices are working fine, and what I should check.

It asked me to change a few network settings and do the usual restarts and resets, but first it helped me narrow down the problem, which saved me from resetting everything. I checked Wi-Fi and mobile data separately to see which one was causing the trouble. The fix was turning off Adaptive connectivity under Settings > Network & internet, along with the option to switch to mobile data automatically, so my Pixel stopped jumping between the two.

Gemini is now my first stop for fixes

None of these fixes were dramatic, and my Pixel doesn't feel like a different phone; it still functions the same and performs the same functions as normal. What changed is that I now have a starting point for issues that used to mean a lot of scattered searching. The battery fix was the most modest of the four issues, as it was better than before but not a major comeback. The notifications, storage, and connection fixes did what I needed them to do. If you try this yourself, being specific in the question matters. I described what was happening and what I noticed, and the answers were more targeted than a generic troubleshooting list. This holds real value for me. Gemini doesn't have to solve everything for me; it just needs to tell me what the real problem is and where to look first. For me, that's precisely what it did pertaining to these four problems.

scored.body:
Published Oct 6, 2026, 7:30 AM EDT

Abhinav pivoted from a career in banking to pursue his first love in writing. Even while working full-time, he continued contributing as an editor-at-large, a role he has held for more than 7 years. A lifelong tech enthusiast who has built three gaming and productivity powerhouse PCs since 2018, his passion for technology keeps him closely following the semiconductor industry, from NVIDIA and AMD to ARM. His MSc dissertation explored how artificial intelligence will reshape the future of work, reflecting his curiosity about the wider social impact of emerging technologies.

I've spent some time reflecting on my LLM usage habits, and, inevitably, three names from the biggest cloud AI providers were on my list. ChatGPT and Claude, which together covered a broad chunk of my daily workflow and the menial things that I used to spend a lot of my time on. Each brought something to the table that others don't, which had me convinced for the longest time that there simply wasn't one model capable of replacing all three. There was a price to this convenience, of course. Both the services offered $20 Pro or Plus plans, and having subscriptions to both of them was eating into my spare change. Naturally, I tried looking for a local model that could handle everything I was throwing at the cloud models, and to my surprise, I found one that could handle most, if not all of it.

Qwen 3.8-27B changed how I saw local AI

It does the job of two subscriptions and costs me nothing

Before using Qwen 3.8-27B, I'd assumed it meant settling for something smaller and possibly less intelligent than a cloud model that I was replacing. Perhaps that's why running Qwen 3.8-27B felt like it defied all expectations I had surrounding local AI. The UD-IQ4_XS build from Unsloth is a 13.3GB download that fits on my 4070 Ti Super (with 16GB of GDDR6X VRAM) with context room to spare at 16K context window, and llama.cpp serves it over localhost at speeds that stop being a complaint after a few minutes of use. The model holds about 33.7 tokens per second across runs, and in a Pygame test where I asked it to build a working Snake game in a single file, it did exactly that in one shot. Plain text queries give no room for complaint either, as the model is excellent at the sort of ordinary summarization and analysis work that I usually go to a cloud model for.

ChatGPT was the easiest to replace

Most of what I use it for doesn't need a model running in a data centre

One of the things I use ChatGPT for most often is grammar checking and tidying up my emails, and on the off chance something verbose lands in my inbox, pulling the key details out of it. On rare days, I might even use it to trim down bloated sentences when I get too carried away, or turn a rough thought filled with jargon into something I can communicate more effectively. I also rely heavily on sentiment analysis when I'm researching products and services. I'll often go through dozens of user forums and discussion threads to understand how consumers are reacting to a particular product, service, or pricing change and then use an LLM to codify that information. Those are all tasks that a local model can handle without breaking a sweat, and that's something I learned only after a few days of using the Qwen and Gemma family of models. To put this to test, I fed Qwen 3.8-27B a deliberately rambling email about PC component prices with a dozen figures scattered through it. The model was able to pull every number and categorize it into a clean table, and that was enough for me to be convinced that it's a model that can take down a subscription from my bank statement.

Claude is brilliant, until it tells me to go away

Five-hour limits are counterproductive for something iterative like coding

Anthropic's frontier models are undoubtedly better at coding, and if you don't believe me, you'd only have to go through a dozen tests I've put them through against Google and OpenAI's models. One might even argue that the rise of Claude changed developer workflows permanently, and it'd be a reasonable argument. I use it much the same way, particularly when I'm working on Python projects that require a lot of back-and-forth. The problem is that Anthropic's models come with a lot of limits and guardrails, even for customers like myself who would happily pay $20 a month for some extra usage and performance from its top models. It's no surprise that tweaks to get past Claude's rate limits or to mitigate them as far as possible have their own dedicated tutorials these days. The biggest problem that anyone who relies on Claude faces is that when the five-hour limit runs out, there isn't much you can do besides use your credit card to make it work again, which is a charge on top of a subscription. Waiting for the limit to reset completely destroys the tempo of an iterative coding project, because by the time I'm back (five hours later), I have to go through the thread again and try to pick up where I left off, potentially losing ideas for refining whatever app I was working on.

That's a problem that's almost entirely fixed by running a local model. Qwen running locally has no five-hour wall, no weekly cap, and no overage bill that piles up and stares at me at the end of the month. I can leave it iterating on a project overnight if I want, and the only cost will be the 285W the GPU draws from the wall. As an added advantage, nothing I send to Qwen leaves my PC. That goes for both my half-written apps and the benchmarking data, none of which touch a server that another organization controls the retention policy for.

llama.cpp

Llama.cpp is an open-source framework that runs large language models locally on your computer.

Qwen models are free, but they are priceless in the right workflow

Qwen 3.8-27B doesn't exactly top the benchmark charts, but for the simple things that I need an LLM for, it absolutely does not have to. Although I found the model that fits the needs of my workflow (and my GPU's VRAM) perfectly, there's a perfect model out there on Hugging Face for every card, from the Gemma family that runs comfortably on my 16GB laptop to smaller Qwen builds that would run on even older hardware. All of them cost nothing besides the hardware they run on, so there's no reason not to tinker and give them a go.

scored.body:
July 27, 2026 26 min read

Anthropic and OpenAI have spent 2026 converging on the same idea from opposite directions: let an AI agent write, test, and ship code with less hand-holding. Claude Code does it from your terminal, one reviewed action at a time. Codex does it from a cloud sandbox, working through a task queue while you do something else. Both now charge exactly $20, $100, and $200 a month at their three main consumer tiers, which makes the pricing page nearly useless as a tiebreaker.What Is Claude Code?What Is OpenAI Codex?Claude Code vs Codex at a GlancePricing Compared: Claude Code vs Codex PlansTotal Cost of Ownership: Modeling a Real Team’s Monthly BillBenchmark Performance: SWE-Bench, Terminal-Bench, and SWE-LancerWhat the Benchmark Gap Actually MeansArchitecture Face-Off: Terminal-Native vs Cloud SandboxContext Windows and Token EfficiencyDo Other August 2026 Tests Confirm the Gap?Extensibility: CLAUDE.md vs AGENTS.mdReal-World Adoption: Who’s Actually Using These ToolsSecurity, Compliance, and Enterprise Readiness7 Use Cases: When to Choose Claude Code vs CodexMigration Guide: Moving Between Claude Code and CodexClaude Code: Pros and ConsCodex: Pros and ConsThe Verdict: Claude Code vs Codex in 2026Related CoverageFrequently Asked QuestionsIs Claude Code or Codex cheaper?Which has a bigger context window, Claude Code or Codex?Can I run Claude Code and Codex on the same project?Does Codex work without a ChatGPT subscription?What model actually powers Claude Code and Codex right now?Is Codex safe to let run unattended on my codebase?Do I need CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md files, or does the agent work without them?Which tool is better for a solo developer on a budget?Does the 23% cost gap apply to my monthly subscription bill?Does Morph’s August 2026 test contradict Firecrawl’s 23% cost gap?What happens if my team exceeds its plan’s usage cap?

So the real comparison has to happen somewhere else: benchmark scores, token efficiency, architecture, and who is actually shipping production code with each tool. Anthropic itself put a number on that last question in February 2026, disclosing that Claude Code had reached a $2.5 billion annualized revenue run rate and was serving more than 300,000 business customers. This piece pulls together SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench results, current pricing for every tier, a Microsoft Research study of tens of thousands of engineers, and a practical migration path for teams trying to decide between Claude Code and Codex, or wondering whether they need both.

Both tools sit at the center of a broader shift in how software gets written this year: fewer engineers typing every line themselves, more engineers reviewing and directing an agent that drafts the first pass. Claude Code and Codex are the two most-discussed options in that shift, and the fact that their pricing pages now read almost identically only raises the stakes on getting the rest of the comparison right.
