Add Now

What Is Claude Opus 5.5, and Why It Changes the API Math

Claude Opus 5.5 is the first model in Anthropic’s new Claude 5.5 family, aimed at long-running agentic coding and knowledge work rather than quick chat replies. The model ID is claude-opus-5-5, a fixed string with no date suffix, which matters because it means you don’t need to chase a new snapshot name every quarter the way you did with earlier Opus releases. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 performs at roughly the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most tasks while running at 40% lower cost, and it leads Anthropic’s own benchmark table on SWE-bench Pro at 89.9%, ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 (81.3%), Claude Fable 5.1 (81.2%), and the older Claude Opus 5 (79.2%), according to BenchLM’s October 2026 SWE-bench Pro leaderboard.

Three changes make the Claude Opus 5.5 API worth a dedicated setup guide instead of a one-line model-string swap. First, pricing dropped to $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, down from $5/$25 for Opus 5, according to Anthropic’s Claude Platform release notes. Second, the model runs with a 1-million-token context window and up to 128,000 output tokens by default, no special header required. Third, Opus 5.5 uses always-on adaptive thinking instead of an opt-in extended-thinking flag, so the model decides how much reasoning effort a request needs, defaulting to a medium effort level unless you tell it otherwise.

None of that means Opus 5.5 is the right model for every call. If you’re already happy with Claude Sonnet 5.5’s API setup for well-scoped tasks like bug fixes or document drafting, keep using it. Opus 5.5 earns its keep on multi-hour agentic jobs, large-codebase refactors, and anything that benefits from genuinely long context rather than a clever summary of it.

It also matters that Opus 5.5 arrived alongside a usage-limit change on the consumer side. Anthropic raised five-hour usage limits on Pro, Max, Team, and seat-based Enterprise plans at the same time it cut API pricing, a signal that the company expects developers to run more, not fewer, Opus-class calls now that the per-token cost has dropped. If your team has been rationing Opus usage to control spend, this release is the point to revisit that budget rather than keep the old restrictions in place out of habit.

Prerequisites and Requirements

You don’t need much to follow along with this Claude Opus 5.5 API setup, but get the versions right before you start, because the Claude Python SDK moves fast and older releases don’t expose every Opus 5.5 parameter.

An Anthropic Console account at console.anthropic.com with billing enabled (a credit card or prepaid credit balance)

Python 3.9 or later, or Node.js 18 or later if you prefer TypeScript

The official anthropic Python package, version 0.45.0 or later (run pip show anthropic to check)

A terminal with curl for quick API tests before you write any code

Roughly 90 minutes for the full walkthrough, including the working project at the end

Optional: an AWS, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Azure account if you plan to deploy through Bedrock, Vertex AI, or Foundry instead of calling Anthropic’s API directly

One thing worth deciding up front: how you’ll track spend. Opus 5.5 is cheaper than Opus 5, but a 1-million-token context window makes it easy to accidentally send a huge prompt and get an unpleasant invoice. We’ll set spend limits in Step 13, but keep it in mind while you’re testing.

Steps 1-4: Account, API Key, SDK Install, and Your First Call

Step 1: Create Your Anthropic Console Account and Generate an API Key

Sign in at the Anthropic Console, add a payment method under Billing, and open the API Keys section. Click “Create Key,” name it something you’ll recognize later (for example, opus-5-5-digest-tool), and copy the value immediately. Anthropic only shows it once. Store it as an environment variable rather than hardcoding it anywhere:

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-api03-your-key-here"

Add that line to your shell profile (.zshrc, .bashrc, or equivalent) so it persists across terminal sessions, and never commit it to a repository. If you’ve ever pushed a key by accident, rotate it from the same Console page before moving on.

Step 2: Confirm Billing Tier and Initial Rate Limits

New accounts start on usage Tier 1, which caps requests per minute and tokens per minute at conservative levels while Anthropic verifies payment history. Tier limits increase automatically as your account accrues spend and age, and you can check your current tier and exact numbers on the Console’s Limits page. The retrieved documentation doesn’t publish a single universal Tier 1 number for Opus 5.5 specifically, since limits are account-specific, so check your own dashboard rather than assuming a figure from a blog post.

What you can plan around is the general shape of the tier system: Anthropic ties higher tiers to cumulative spend and account age, not to a one-time application or approval form. That means the fastest route to a higher ceiling is simply running real traffic consistently rather than firing one large test batch and hoping it bumps you up overnight. If you know you’ll need high throughput on day one, for example to process a backlog of thousands of documents, it’s worth spreading that first batch across a few days instead of one, so you don’t bounce off a rate limit the moment you need it least.

Step 3: Install the Official SDK

Install the Python SDK in a virtual environment so it doesn’t collide with other projects:

python3 -m venv venv

source venv/bin/activate

pip install --upgrade anthropic

If you’re working in Node.js instead, swap in npm install @anthropic-ai/sdk. Both SDKs expose the same model parameters, so the rest of this guide applies either way, with syntax adjusted for your language.

Step 4: Make Your First Call to Claude Opus 5.5

With the key exported and the SDK installed, send a minimal request to confirm everything is wired up correctly:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

message = client.messages.create(

model="claude-opus-5-5",

max_tokens=1024,

messages=[

{"role": "user", "content": "In two sentences, what changed in Claude Opus 5.5?"}

]

)

print(message.content[0].text)

print("Input tokens:", message.usage.input_tokens)

print("Output tokens:", message.usage.output_tokens)

Running that script should return a short answer plus token counts in the terminal, something like:

Claude Opus 5.5 dropped pricing to $4/$20 per million tokens, cut 20% from

Opus 5's $5/$25 rate, while adding a 1-million-token context window and

always-on adaptive thinking by default.

Input tokens: 16

Output tokens: 41

If you see an authentication error here, jump ahead to the troubleshooting section before continuing. There’s no point debugging prompt caching on a connection that doesn’t work yet.

Step 5: Understand Claude Opus 5.5 Pricing Before You Build Anything

Pricing drives every architecture decision you’ll make with this model, so get the numbers straight before writing production code. Claude Opus 5.5 bills at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens for standard requests, a 20% cut from Claude Opus 5’s $5/$25 rate, according to Anthropic’s own model overview documentation. Prompt caching and batch processing both apply additional discounts on top of that base rate, which we’ll use directly in Steps 8 and 9.

Pricing TierInput (per 1M tokens)Output (per 1M tokens)Notes

Standard$4.00$20.00Base rate, no caching or batching

Prompt cache write (5-minute)$5.00—One-time cost to cache a prompt segment

Prompt cache write (1-hour)$8.00—Longer TTL for repeat sessions

Prompt cache read$0.20—5% of standard input price, a 95% discount

Batch API$2.00$10.00Flat 50% discount, asynchronous processing

A quick worked example: if you’re sending a 50,000-token codebase as context on every call and only the user’s question changes, the first call costs roughly $0.20 for that context segment at standard input pricing. Cache it, and every subsequent call against the same context costs about $0.01 for the cached portion instead, a difference that compounds fast once you’re running hundreds of queries against the same repository in a single afternoon.

Step 6: Put the 1-Million-Token Context Window to Work

Claude Opus 5.5 ships with a 1-million-token context window enabled by default and a maximum output of 128,000 tokens per response, per Anthropic’s release notes. That’s enough to load a mid-sized codebase, a full legal contract set, or months of support tickets into a single call without chunking. The catch is that a 1-million-token prompt at $4 per million tokens still costs about $4 just to send once, so this capability is most valuable when you reuse that context repeatedly, which is exactly what prompt caching is for.

Here’s how to load a large file set into a single request:

import os

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def load_codebase(directory, extensions=(".py", ".js", ".md")):

chunks = []

for root, _, files in os.walk(directory):

for name in files:

if name.endswith(extensions):

path = os.path.join(root, name)

with open(path, "r", errors="ignore") as f:

chunks.append(f"--- {path} ---\n{f.read()}")

return "\n\n".join(chunks)

codebase_text = load_codebase("./my-project")

response = client.messages.create(

model="claude-opus-5-5",

max_tokens=4096,

messages=[

{"role": "user", "content": f"Here is a full codebase:\n\n{codebase_text}\n\nSummarize the architecture in 10 bullet points."}

]

)

print(response.content[0].text)

For anything beyond a quick test, don’t send raw context on every call. Structure the request so the large, unchanging part sits first and gets cached, which is exactly what Step 8 covers.

Step 7: Configure Adaptive Thinking Effort Levels

Unlike earlier Claude models that required an explicit extended-thinking flag, Opus 5.5 uses always-on adaptive thinking. The model decides internally how much reasoning to apply, and Anthropic reports it defaults to medium effort. At that default setting, Anthropic says Opus 5.5 scores 52.5% on its internal agentic benchmark, ahead of Claude Fable 5.1’s 51.8% at maximum effort and Claude Opus 5’s 46.6% at maximum effort, according to Anthropic’s Claude Opus product page. That’s a meaningful detail: Opus 5.5 at its default setting already beats older models running at their hardest setting.

For latency-sensitive applications like a chat interface, you can bias toward speed by keeping prompts tightly scoped and avoiding unnecessary context. For batch research or refactor jobs where correctness matters more than response time, give the model room to reason by increasing max_tokens and letting it work through the problem rather than truncating output early. Anthropic’s documentation doesn’t currently expose a manual per-effort token budget override for Opus 5.5 the way older thinking-mode flags did, so the practical lever you control is prompt design and output budget, not a hidden reasoning-depth parameter.

Step 8: Cut Costs by Up to 95% With Prompt Caching

Prompt caching is the single biggest cost lever available on Opus 5.5. Mark a block of your prompt as cacheable, and Anthropic stores it for either 5 minutes or 1 hour depending on which TTL you request. Every subsequent call that reuses that exact block pays the $0.20 cache-read rate instead of the $4 standard input rate, a 95% discount. For a deeper walkthrough of caching strategy across providers, see our LLM prompt caching setup guide; here’s the Opus 5.5-specific implementation:

response = client.messages.create(

model="claude-opus-5-5",

max_tokens=2048,

messages=[

{

"role": "user",

"content": [

{

"type": "text",

"text": codebase_text,

"cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}

},

{

"type": "text",

"text": "What security issues do you see in the authentication module?"

}

]

}

]

)

print("Cache creation tokens:", response.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens)

print("Cache read tokens:", response.usage.cache_read_input_tokens)

Run that same request five more times with different follow-up questions appended after the cached block, and only the small, variable part of the prompt bills at full price each time. In practice, teams running repeated queries against the same large document or repository report their effective cost per query dropping by an order of magnitude once caching is wired in correctly.

Step 9: Batch Large Jobs at 50% Off

If your workload doesn’t need an answer in real time, the Batch API cuts both input and output pricing in half, bringing Opus 5.5 down to an effective $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. That’s the right tool for overnight jobs like summarizing a week of support tickets, re-indexing documentation, or running a bulk code review across every file in a monorepo.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

batch = client.messages.batches.create(

requests=[

{

"custom_id": f"file-{i}",

"params": {

"model": "claude-opus-5-5",

"max_tokens": 1024,

"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": f"Review this file for bugs:\n\n{file_text}"}]

}

}

for i, file_text in enumerate(file_contents)

]

)

print("Batch ID:", batch.id)

print("Status:", batch.processing_status)

Poll client.messages.batches.retrieve(batch.id) until processing_status reads ended, then pull results from the batch’s results URL. Batches typically complete within hours, not minutes, so this pattern fits scheduled jobs far better than user-facing requests.

Step 10: Deploy Through AWS Bedrock, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Foundry

If your company already routes AI spend through a specific cloud vendor for procurement or compliance reasons, Opus 5.5 is available on all three major platforms with slightly different model identifiers. On Amazon Bedrock, the native model ID is anthropic.claude-opus-5-5, with regional variants like us.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5, eu.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5, and a global.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5 routing option, according to AWS’s Bedrock model card documentation. Microsoft Foundry uses the simpler claude-opus-5-5 identifier, matching Anthropic’s own API.

import boto3

import json

bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-east-1")

response = bedrock.invoke_model(

modelId="us.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5",

body=json.dumps({

"anthropic_version": "bedrock-2023-05-31",

"max_tokens": 1024,

"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this quarter's error logs."}]

})

)

result = json.loads(response["body"].read())

print(result["content"][0]["text"])

One important detail: AWS bills model usage separately from Bedrock itself, so Opus 5.5 charges appear under the model provider line in AWS Cost Explorer, not under a generic Bedrock line item. If your finance team is auditing cloud spend, point them there directly instead of letting them search for “Anthropic” in the main billing dashboard.

Steps 11-12: Build a Complete Project — A Long-Context Repo Digest Tool

Now put all of the above together into something you’d actually use. We’re building repo-digest, a command-line tool that loads an entire codebase, caches it, lets you ask unlimited follow-up questions against that cached context for the next hour, and falls back to the Batch API if you point it at a folder of files to review in bulk instead of a single interactive session.

Step 11: Write the Core Digest Script

# repo_digest.py

import os

import sys

import anthropic

MODEL = "claude-opus-5-5"

MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS = 3_000_000 # roughly 750K tokens, safely under the 1M limit

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def load_codebase(directory, extensions=(".py", ".js", ".ts", ".md", ".go")):

chunks = []

total_chars = 0

for root, _, files in os.walk(directory):

if "node_modules" in root or ".git" in root:

continue

for name in files:

if name.endswith(extensions):

path = os.path.join(root, name)

try:

with open(path, "r", errors="ignore") as f:

text = f.read()

except OSError:

continue

if total_chars + len(text) > MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS:

print(f"Warning: truncating at {path}, context limit reached")

return "\n\n".join(chunks)

chunks.append(f"--- {path} ---\n{text}")

total_chars += len(text)

return "\n\n".join(chunks)

def ask(codebase_text, question, ttl="1h"):

response = client.messages.create(

model=MODEL,

max_tokens=4096,

messages=[{

"role": "user",

"content": [

{"type": "text", "text": codebase_text, "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": ttl}},

{"type": "text", "text": question}

]

}]

)

return response.content[0].text, response.usage

if __name__ == "__main__":

directory = sys.argv[1]

question = sys.argv[2]

codebase = load_codebase(directory)

answer, usage = ask(codebase, question)

print(answer)

print(f"\n[cache_write={usage.cache_creation_input_tokens} cache_read={usage.cache_read_input_tokens} output={usage.output_tokens}]")

Run it with python repo_digest.py ./my-project "What's the biggest architectural risk in this codebase?". The first run pays the cache-write price for your full codebase; every follow-up question you ask within the hour against the same directory reads from cache at $0.20 per million tokens instead of $4. A first run against a mid-sized repository looks something like this in your terminal:

The biggest architectural risk is the shared database connection pool in

db/pool.py, which isn't thread-safe but is imported directly by four

background workers in workers/. Under concurrent load this will eventually

produce connection leaks rather than a clean error, making it hard to

diagnose in production. Recommend wrapping access in a queue or moving to

a connection-per-worker model.

[cache_write=187420 cache_read=0 output=612]

Ask a second question against the same directory a few minutes later, and the usage line flips: cache_write=0 cache_read=187420 output=..., confirming you just paid $0.20 per million tokens for the context instead of $4. That swing from write to read is the entire value proposition of this pattern, and it’s worth watching those two numbers directly in your logs rather than trusting that caching is working silently in the background.

Step 12: Add a Batch Mode for Bulk File Review

# batch_review.py

import glob

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def submit_batch(file_pattern, question="Review this file for bugs and style issues."):

files = glob.glob(file_pattern, recursive=True)

requests = []

for i, path in enumerate(files):

with open(path, "r", errors="ignore") as f:

content = f.read()

requests.append({

"custom_id": f"{i}-{path}",

"params": {

"model": "claude-opus-5-5",

"max_tokens": 1024,

"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": f"{question}\n\nFile: {path}\n\n{content}"}]

}

})

batch = client.messages.batches.create(requests=requests)

print(f"Submitted {len(requests)} files as batch {batch.id}")

return batch.id

if __name__ == "__main__":

import sys

submit_batch(sys.argv[1])

Running python batch_review.py "./my-project/**/*.py" queues every matching file at the 50%-discounted batch rate, then you poll for completion the next morning. For a 400-file repository, that’s the difference between an interactive session costing real money in an afternoon and a scheduled job that costs half as much while you’re asleep.

Step 13: Add Error Handling, Retries, and Spend Monitoring

A script that works on your laptop will eventually hit a rate limit, a timeout, or an overloaded endpoint in production. Wrap every call in retry logic with exponential backoff rather than letting a transient error kill a long batch job:

import time

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def ask_with_retry(messages, max_retries=5):

for attempt in range(max_retries):

try:

return client.messages.create(

model="claude-opus-5-5",

max_tokens=2048,

messages=messages

)

except anthropic.RateLimitError:

wait = 2 ** attempt

print(f"Rate limited, waiting {wait}s...")

time.sleep(wait)

except anthropic.APIStatusError as e:

if e.status_code == 529:

wait = 2 ** attempt

print(f"Overloaded, waiting {wait}s...")

time.sleep(wait)

else:

raise

raise RuntimeError("Max retries exceeded")

For spend monitoring, set a hard monthly limit in the Console’s Billing section before you run your first batch job, and check the Usage dashboard daily while you’re still tuning prompt sizes. A 1-million-token context window is powerful, but it’s also the easiest way to turn a $20 testing session into a $200 one if a loop accidentally re-sends the full codebase on every iteration instead of relying on the cache.

Claude Opus 5.5 vs Sonnet 5.5 vs Opus 5 vs Fable 5.1: Which Should You Use?

Picking the wrong model in this family is the fastest way to overpay or underperform. Here’s how the four most relevant Claude models compare as of October 2026:

ModelInput / Output Price (per 1M)Context WindowSWE-bench ProBest For

Claude Opus 5.5$4 / $201M tokens89.9%Long-running agentic coding, large-codebase work

Claude Sonnet 5.5$2 / $101M tokens81.3%Everyday tasks, bug fixes, well-scoped jobs

Claude Opus 5$5 / $251M tokens79.2%Legacy deployments not yet migrated

Claude Fable 5.1Not disclosed in standard pricing tables1M tokens81.2%Maximum-capability reasoning where cost is secondary

The practical takeaway: Opus 5.5 now beats Fable 5.1 on SWE-bench Pro while costing less than Opus 5 did, which is why Anthropic markets it as matching Fable-tier output at Sonnet-adjacent economics. Our coverage of how Opus 5.5 matches Fable 5.1 at 60% less cost digs deeper into that specific comparison if you’re deciding between the two for a production workload. Worth noting too: rival releases from OpenAI have specifically targeted this price point, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna reportedly undercut Opus 5.5 by as much as 50% on list price, so benchmark your actual workload rather than picking a model on pricing alone.

How Claude Opus 5.5 Stacks Up Against GPT-6 Astra and Gemini

Anthropic isn’t the only company shipping long-context, agent-focused flagship models right now, and it’s worth a quick gut check before you commit a production pipeline to Opus 5.5 alone. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra and Google’s Gemini 4 Argon both target the same category of multi-step, tool-using work, and all three now ship context windows at or near the 1-million-token mark, which has quietly become table stakes for a flagship coding model in late 2026 rather than a differentiator. Our earlier breakdown of GPT-6 Astra vs Gemini 4 Argon vs DeepSeek covers the pricing and benchmark gap between those three in detail.

Where Opus 5.5 tends to separate itself is in the combination of adaptive thinking that’s on by default and a batch discount that stacks with prompt caching, which lets a well-architected pipeline hit genuinely low per-task costs without sacrificing the reasoning quality that agentic workloads need. If your evaluation criteria are purely benchmark score per dollar, run the same representative task through all three APIs with your own data before standardizing on one, since published benchmarks rarely match the specific mix of code, documents, or tickets your pipeline will actually process. A $20 test across three providers is cheap insurance against locking into the wrong model for six months.

5 Common Pitfalls When Migrating to Claude Opus 5.5

1. Assuming the old extended-thinking flag still applies. Opus 5.5 uses always-on adaptive thinking, so a thinking parameter block written for an older Claude model may be silently ignored or rejected. Check your request payload against the current Opus 5.5 schema before deploying.

2. Sending the full context on every call instead of caching it. This is the single most expensive mistake in this guide. If you’re not using cache_control on the static part of your prompt, you’re paying full price for the same tokens over and over.

3. Using the wrong model ID on Bedrock vs. direct API. claude-opus-5-5 works against Anthropic’s own API, but Bedrock needs the prefixed anthropic.claude-opus-5-5 or a regional variant. Mixing these up produces a model-not-found error that has nothing to do with your actual code logic.

4. Treating batch jobs as synchronous. The Batch API doesn’t return results immediately. If your code polls in a tight loop expecting a sub-second response, you’ll burn through rate limits checking a job that’s still queued.

5. Ignoring the 5-minute vs. 1-hour cache TTL tradeoff. The 5-minute cache write is cheaper ($5/MTok vs. $8/MTok) but expires fast. If your users ask follow-up questions more than five minutes apart, you’ll pay the cache-write cost again on what should have been a cache-read. Match the TTL to your actual usage pattern.

Troubleshooting Guide: 8 Common Errors and How to Fix Them

1. “authentication_error: invalid x-api-key.” Your environment variable isn’t being picked up, usually because you set it in one terminal tab and are running the script from another. Run echo $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the exact shell session you’re testing from.

2. “model_not_found: claude-opus-5-5.” Your SDK version predates this model’s release. Run pip install --upgrade anthropic and confirm the version is 0.45.0 or newer.

3. “rate_limit_error” on the very first request. New accounts start on Tier 1 with conservative limits. Check your Console Limits page; the fix is usually to wait for tier upgrades tied to account age and payment history, not a code change.

4. Cache reads showing as zero in usage. This almost always means the cached block isn’t byte-for-byte identical to the previous call. Even a trailing whitespace difference breaks the cache match. Log the exact string you’re sending and diff it against the prior request.

5. “overloaded_error” (HTTP 529) during peak hours. This is a temporary capacity signal, not a bug in your code. Implement exponential backoff as shown in Step 13 rather than failing the request outright.

6. Context window errors despite being under 1M tokens. Remember that token count isn’t the same as character count. A rough rule of thumb is four characters per token for English text, but code and non-English text can run higher. Use the SDK’s token-counting endpoint before assuming you’re under budget.

7. Batch job stuck in “in_progress” for hours. This is normal for large batches. Anthropic doesn’t guarantee a specific completion window, so build your pipeline to poll periodically (every 15-30 minutes) rather than expecting near-real-time results.

8. Unexpectedly high bill despite using caching. Check whether you’re using the 1-hour TTL but issuing requests more than an hour apart, or whether a bug in your loop is regenerating the cached block with a dynamic timestamp or ID embedded in it, which breaks cache matching silently on every single call.

Securing Your API Key in a Real Deployment

Everything in this tutorial so far assumes a single developer running scripts locally, which is fine for testing but not how a production key should live. Once you’re ready to deploy repo-digest or anything like it beyond your own laptop, move the key out of shell environment variables and into a proper secrets manager, whether that’s AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault, or even your CI/CD platform’s built-in encrypted secrets store. Pulling the key at runtime from a secrets manager means it never sits in a .env file that could end up committed by accident, and it means rotating a compromised key doesn’t require redeploying every service that uses it.

Scope keys narrowly where Anthropic’s Console allows it, create a separate key per service or environment (one for staging, one for production, one for the nightly batch job) rather than sharing a single key across your whole stack, and set a conservative spend limit on each one individually. If a staging key leaks, you want the damage capped at whatever staging-level spend limit you set, not your entire organization’s monthly budget. It’s a five-minute setup step that turns a potential incident into a minor inconvenience.

Advanced Tips for Production Deployments

Once the basic setup is solid, a few patterns separate a demo from something you’d trust in production. Structure your prompts so the largest, most stable content (codebase dumps, policy documents, historical logs) always comes first in the message, with the smallest and most variable content (the actual user question) last. This maximizes your cache hit rate because Anthropic’s caching matches on a prefix basis, not an exact full-string match.

For agentic workflows that run for extended periods, don’t let the model’s context grow unbounded across a long conversation. Periodically summarize earlier turns and replace them with the summary, keeping your effective context well under the 1M ceiling even on sessions that would otherwise run for hours. This also keeps your per-call cost predictable instead of climbing linearly with conversation length.

If you’re running mixed workloads, route by task complexity rather than defaulting everything to Opus 5.5. A simple pattern: use Claude Sonnet 5.5 for the first pass on a request, and only escalate to Opus 5.5 if the task is flagged as complex (multi-file refactor, ambiguous requirements, security-sensitive code). This tiered approach, discussed in our Sonnet 5.5 model comparison, can cut blended API costs by 40-60% compared to sending every request to the flagship model.

Finally, if you’re building anything that runs autonomously for long stretches, look into Anthropic’s broader agent tooling rather than hand-rolling your own loop. Our Claude Agent SDK walkthrough covers the higher-level framework Anthropic ships specifically for multi-step, tool-using agents, which handles a lot of the state management this tutorial’s manual scripts don’t.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Claude Opus 5.5 cheaper than Claude Opus 5?Yes. Opus 5.5 bills at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, versus $5 and $25 for Opus 5, a 20% price cut on standard requests. Anthropic separately describes the model as 40% cheaper to run overall, a figure that factors in efficiency gains beyond the listed per-token rate.

What’s the exact model ID I should use in my code?Use claude-opus-5-5 for Anthropic’s direct API. On AWS Bedrock, use anthropic.claude-opus-5-5 or a regional variant like us.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5. On Microsoft Foundry, the ID is claude-opus-5-5, matching Anthropic’s own naming.

Does Claude Opus 5.5 support the same context window as Claude Sonnet 5.5?Yes, both models ship with a 1-million-token context window by default and a maximum output of 128,000 tokens, according to Anthropic’s documentation on Amazon Bedrock model availability.

How much does prompt caching actually save in practice?Cache reads cost $0.20 per million tokens, which is 5% of the $4 standard input rate, a 95% discount. The savings scale directly with how often you reuse the same cached context within the TTL window you choose (5 minutes or 1 hour).

Can I use Claude Opus 5.5 for free to test it first?Anthropic doesn’t offer a standing free API tier for Opus 5.5; you need billing enabled on your Console account before generating an API key. New accounts typically get a small initial credit, but check your own Console dashboard for current promotional credit, since this changes over time.

Is Opus 5.5 better than Claude Fable 5.1 for coding tasks?On SWE-bench Pro, Opus 5.5 scores 89.9% versus Fable 5.1’s 81.2%, per BenchLM’s October 2026 leaderboard. Anthropic’s own benchmark separately shows Opus 5.5 at its default medium effort setting outperforming Fable 5.1 at maximum effort, which suggests Opus 5.5 is now the stronger coding option for most teams.

What happens if I exceed the 128,000 output token limit?The API truncates the response at that ceiling. For tasks that genuinely need longer output, break the job into sequential calls, feeding the prior output back as context for the continuation, rather than expecting a single call to exceed the documented maximum.

Should I migrate existing Opus 5 code to Opus 5.5 immediately?In most cases, yes, since it’s a straight price cut with better benchmark scores and the same context window ceiling. The main thing to verify first is whether your code relies on an explicit extended-thinking parameter that behaves differently under Opus 5.5’s always-on adaptive thinking model.

scored.body:
Credit: Lucas Gouveia / Android Police | voronaman / Shutterstock

Published Oct 6, 2026, 6:58 AM EDT

I've been covering Android and other mobile technology for close to ten years now, with a specific interest in phone accessories, e-readers, and what makes each individual phone different from another. I delight in looking at the phone market from as many angles as possible, and while my opinions may be odd, at times, they're always from the heart as much as the head.

I have a background in the mobile accessories world, which explains my odd enthusiasm for cases and things that clip onto smartphones.

I worked for Digital Trends from 2017 to 2025.

Sign in to your Android Police account

Google Gemini's Call for Me is expanding from just business calls, into personal calls, according to details seen in the latest updates. This would mean Gemini would be capable of calling your nearest and dearest, and while the functionality looks to be on the limited side, Call for Me will be able to ask simple questions and relay messages. Of course, whether you want to give up talking to your friends and family, so a robot can is another question entirely.

Call for Me may soon mean you never need to make another call again

But is that really a good thing?

Call for Me debuted last month on the Pixel 11, and it has a simple premise: Gemini makes calls to businesses for you, making or changing appointments, so you don't have to call yourself. The reception was mixed, to say the least. While some appreciate the time-saving elements here, others are keenly aware of how this sort of technology further increases isolation and loneliness within society. Plus, who wants to talk to robots instead of people? This news comes from a new update to the Phone app, which Android Authority was able to dig into. These screenshots show some examples of what Gemini may be able to do in the future, and it includes options for calling "John" or "Mom", and delivering a message or asking a simple question. While it's not spelled out in the hacked build, it's a clear implication that Call for Me is prepping to go beyond businesses and expand into personal calls. It also looks as if there's an option to bar the AI from calling you, but good luck getting your mom or grandmother to turn that setting on. This feature isn't available yet, and testers weren't able to get it working, even with their hacked builds.

Auto Call Screening

Look, I hate making phone calls as much as anyone else, but this technology does give me pause. I use Call Screen in order to filter out spam and nonsense calls all the time, and to some extent, those people deserve to speak to a robot instead of a human. But a blameless receptionist at the local salon? The last thing they need is to talk to Gemini fifteen times a day. Extending that to talk to your friends and family takes that to another level. While using Gemini can save some time for you, it's going to be bluntly obvious to the person being called that you don't care enough about them to talk to them yourself. Instead, you made them talk to a robot instead.

There are many jokes made about tech billionaires and companies not being real people, and actually being lizards or aliens in disguise, but stuff like this genuinely does make me wonder whether there's some truth in that. There's no confirmation this feature will ever see the light of day, of course, but it's clear proof Google is working on adding it.

scored.body: I teach special education students across elementary, junior, and senior high — each with a different disability, mental age, and learning style. The hardest part is the weight of individualization: every student needs their own learning program, and abstract instructions mean very little without visual support.Using Gemini on our classroom Chromebooks, I generate simple visual guides — like a child holding a pencil or opening a book — so students who cannot read can immediately understand what they are seeing. The most moving changes are my students who cannot write using voice prompts to speak to Gemini, generating their own images and expressing their ideas. It has, quite literally, given a voice to those who cannot write.Together with colleagues, I'm building an AI-powered app that unifies special education planning and programming. For us, AI isn't just about saving time — it’s about ensuring a student’s disability no longer determines how much they get to learn.

articles.headline: Claude Sonnet 5.5 Medium vs High vs Max: Which Effort Setting Is Worth the Cost? - Kingy AI
articles.body: Claude Sonnet 5.5 Medium vs High vs Max: Which Effort Setting Is Worth the Cost?    Kingy AI

scored.body:
I would start Sonnet 5.5 at Medium for a clearly scoped coding task, move to High when the work needs more investigation, and reserve Max for problems where a comparison shows that the extra effort improves the result. Choosing Max for everything can turn an inexpensive model into an expensive workflow.

The cost gap is substantial in one independent evaluation. Artificial Analysis reports $0.59 per Intelligence Index task at Medium, $1.12 at High and $7.67 at Max. Max scores higher on that index, but costs about 13 times as much as Medium. Those are benchmark-specific task costs, not prices for your next bug fix. Medium results, High results, Max results.

There is also a default-setting difference worth checking before you compare results: Sonnet 5.5 starts at Medium in Claude apps and Claude Code, and High on the Claude API. Anthropic documents both in its Sonnet 5.5 announcement.

Our Astra vs Sonnet 5.5 comparison and Sol 6.1 vs Sonnet 5.5 comparison cover model choice. This guide covers the setting you should evaluate before changing models.

Sources and benchmark snapshot checked October 5, 2026. Setup examples follow official documentation and have not been tested against a paid API or a logged-in Claude session for this guide. Task examples and worked budgets are illustrative; benchmark measurements belong to the named evaluator.

What Medium, High and Max change

Effort controls how much work Claude puts into a response, including thinking, answer text and tool calls. It is a behavioral control rather than a fixed allowance of reasoning tokens. Max still operates within request limits such as max_tokens; it does not authorize an unlimited API bill. Anthropic effort documentation.

Sonnet 5.5 supports five levels: Low, Medium, High, Xhigh and Max. Anthropic recommends Medium for well-specified agentic coding and multistep tool work, High for harder or longer tasks, and an evaluation before adopting Xhigh or Max. For latency-sensitive chat, it suggests Medium or Low. Sonnet-specific effort guidance.

Here is how I would apply that guidance. The examples are suggested starting points, not measured completion rates.

On small screens, scroll tables sideways to see every column.

Task

Start with

What to check before raising effort

Implement a specified feature with clear acceptance criteria

Medium

Does the implementation meet the brief and pass relevant checks?

Diagnose an intermittent bug across several files

High

Does the explanation fit the evidence, and does the fix address the cause?

Draft a document from an organized source packet

Medium

Are claims supported and calculations correct?

Resolve conflicting requirements or a difficult technical decision

High

Does the answer identify the tradeoffs and material exceptions?

A recurring hard problem that High leaves unresolved

Compare Xhigh and Max

Does either improve accepted results enough to cover the added time and cost?

A longer answer is easy to notice. An overlooked edge case is harder to notice. Set your acceptance criteria before reading the output, so an impressive explanation does not substitute for a working result.

For a bug fix, that might mean a reproduction that fails before the change and passes afterward. For a research memo, it could mean supported claims, correct dates and a calculation another person can reproduce. For a document, include the required sections and the intended audience in the brief.

The defaults depend on where you use Sonnet

Product

Sonnet 5.5 default effort

Claude apps

Medium

Claude Code

Medium

First-party Claude API

High

Sources: Anthropic's launch announcement, Claude Code model configuration, and Sonnet API model overview.

An explicit setting, a saved preference or an organization policy can affect what you see. Record the active setting instead of assuming that every Sonnet session starts the same way. When comparing a Claude app response with an API response, set matching effort deliberately and account for the tools and context each product supplies.

Sonnet 5.5's effort scale is also recalibrated relative to Sonnet 5. Anthropic recommends retesting the levels on your own tasks when upgrading. A familiar setting name does not guarantee a familiar token bill. Sonnet 5.5 prompting guide.

Independent results show why Max needs a reason

Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index v4.3.2 provides separate Sonnet configurations. All three rows below retain the evaluator's Default Fallback label.

Sonnet 5.5 effort

Intelligence Index

Weighted cost per index task

Output tokens across the index run

Medium

41

$0.59

31 million

High

47

$1.12

52 million

Max

56

$7.67

420 million

Sources: Artificial Analysis Medium, High and Max pages, checked October 5.

High costs about 1.9 times Medium in this evaluation mix. Max costs about 6.8 times High. Its higher composite score establishes a capability gain on that index, while the cost shows why a blanket Max policy deserves scrutiny.

The index points are not success percentages. Its weighted task costs account for benchmark token use and caching assumptions, and the campaign-wide output totals are not tokens for one request. The rows also include fallback behavior; they do not isolate Sonnet with fallback disabled. See the evaluator's benchmark methodology.

Anthropic flags a since-fixed structured-output bug in the prerelease Sonnet deployment used for two Artificial Analysis knowledge-work tests. That caveat remains relevant when interpreting the launch-era results; a current page alone does not establish that every affected test was rerun. Launch footnotes.

Use these figures to decide which configurations to test. Budget a live workload from its own usage records, including failed attempts, tools and review time.

Max can lose to Xhigh

Anthropic reports Sonnet 5.5 at 52.1% on FrontierCode 1.1 at Xhigh and 46.2% at Max. Its launch footnote attributes the lower Max result in part to review activity that caused timeouts or changes outside the requested scope in two examined cases. The benchmark grades whether a change could be merged without human edits. Anthropic's results and explanation.

That is one benchmark and one harness. It is enough to reject the assumption that increasing effort always improves the result.

If High produces a valid patch, Max needs to improve something you value: a missed failure mode, a stronger implementation, fewer repairs or better performance on the hard cases. Extra files, extra commentary and extra checks have value only when they serve the task.

I would include Xhigh in an evaluation before standardizing on Max. Keep the same brief, tool permissions and acceptance checks. Count a timeout or an unnecessary change as a problem rather than crediting the model for doing more work.

How to change effort in Claude apps

Select Sonnet 5.5, click the model name beside the send button, open Effort, and choose a level. Anthropic says the change applies from the next response. The menu identifies a recommended default. Claude Help Center instructions.

Thinking and effort are separate controls, but Sonnet 5.5's thinking cannot be turned off in the Claude apps. A missing expected model or effort option on an Enterprise account may reflect an administrator's restriction. Higher effort consumes more tokens and can use up your allowance sooner. The help page does not establish a fixed number of messages you gain by choosing Medium.

For ordinary iterative work, try Medium with a concrete brief. Move up when the answer misses requirements or fails a check. Keep subscription allowances separate from the API dollar examples below; our ChatGPT Pro vs Claude Max guide covers the plan decision.

How to change effort in Claude Code

Select Sonnet 5.5 through /model, then set the level directly:

/effort medium

Use /effort high or /effort max to compare other settings. The session header shows the active level. You can also launch a session explicitly:

claude --model claude-sonnet-5-5 --effort high

On current versions, typing a Low-through-Xhigh level after /effort saves it for later sessions. For a session-only choice, open the /effort slider and confirm with s; that behavior requires v2.1.257 or later. Max applies to the current session unless set through the effort environment variable. It is not accepted as a persisted effortLevel or per-model settings value. Organization caps can limit the applied level. Claude Code configuration documentation.

Check the header after changing settings, especially on a managed account. This gives you an observable configuration to record alongside the result.

How to set effort in the Claude API

Set output_config.effort explicitly. This Python example uses Anthropic's Messages SDK and the verified model ID. It assumes the SDK is installed and an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is available in your environment.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(

model="claude-sonnet-5-5",

max_tokens=4096,

output_config={"effort": "medium"},

messages=[{

"role": "user",

"content": (

"Compare two approaches to adding retries to a background job. "

"Cover duplicate execution, failure handling and how to test it."

),

}],

)

print("Stop reason:", response.stop_reason)

print("Usage:", response.usage)

for block in response.content:

if block.type == "text":

print(block.text)

The example follows the Sonnet 5.5 migration guide. It sends one text request; it does not execute tools or implement a coding agent. Change medium to high, xhigh or max for a separate evaluation. No beta header is required for top-level effort.

Give thinking and the answer room to finish

The example's 4,096-token ceiling suits a small demonstration, but can truncate a demanding response. Thinking shares the output budget with the visible answer. Sonnet's standard maximum is 128,000 output tokens. Model limits, Thinking and billing.

Anthropic recommends a 128,000-token ceiling and streaming for agentic coding. Its SDK supports collecting a final message from a stream:

with client.messages.stream(

model="claude-sonnet-5-5",

max_tokens=128000,

output_config={"effort": "high"},

messages=[{

"role": "user",

"content": "Analyze the attached implementation and test evidence.",

}],

) as stream:

message = stream.get_final_message()

print(message.stop_reason)

print(message.usage)

Replace the sample message with the actual implementation and evidence; this snippet does not attach files. A high ceiling permits more output and therefore more spending, but does not force the model to consume it. Choose the ceiling your application can afford. Agentic coding guidance, SDK streaming pattern.

Check stop_reason before accepting a result. max_tokens signals truncation, tool_use requires the tool workflow to continue, and end_turn means the model finished its response. Even end_turn still needs your task's acceptance checks. Stop-reason documentation.

Avoid incompatible thinking settings

Sonnet 5.5 rejects thinking: {"type": "disabled"}. To remove up-front thinking, use thinking: {"type": "between_tools"} at Low, Medium or High. That combination is rejected at Xhigh and Max; use adaptive thinking there by omitting thinking or setting its type to adaptive. Migration rules.

Keep adaptive thinking for the initial effort comparison so you change one control at a time. Testing between_tools can be a separate latency experiment.

Changing top-level effort between requests invalidates cached message blocks. Sonnet supports a cache-preserving per-message effort change in beta, requiring adaptive thinking and the mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01 header. Use the documented per-message format when implementing that behavior, and inspect actual cache usage. Cache invalidation rules.

API prices and a worked budget

Sonnet 5.5's first-party Standard API prices are the same across effort levels:

Token category

USD per million tokens

Ordinary input

$2.00

Billable output

$10.00

Five-minute cache write

$2.50

One-hour cache write

$4.00

Cache read

$0.20

Source: Anthropic pricing. Thinking is billed as output even when its text is hidden. Thinking documentation.

Consider two hypothetical single requests, each using 100,000 ordinary uncached input tokens. One generates 20,000 total billable output tokens; the other generates 100,000. Their calculated bills are $0.40 and $1.20. These examples exclude tools, retries, regional modifiers and tax. They do not predict which effort setting will generate either output count.

The $0.80 difference equals 48 seconds of human time at an assumed $60 an hour. If the larger request saves more than that in review or repair and meets the same quality bar, the extra spending could be worthwhile. If it produces the same usable result, the smaller request has the cost advantage.

An agent job can contain many requests. Add every attempt, cache operation and applicable tool charge before comparing costs. For a batch of jobs, divide total spending by the number of accepted results. Report unresolved jobs alongside that figure so a low completion rate cannot hide behind a low average bill.

When to try Opus or Astra instead

If Sonnet repeatedly fails to plan a difficult task, resolve ambiguity or sustain the work, compare a different model alongside higher Sonnet effort. Anthropic's Sonnet prompting guide points to Opus for the hardest long-horizon work. Our Sonnet vs Opus 5.5 comparison covers the cost and capability tradeoff.

Use Astra vs Sonnet when your task fits Astra's evaluated strengths, and Sol 6.1 vs Sonnet for the less expensive OpenAI alternative. OpenAI also recommends reserving Xhigh and Max for cases where representative evaluations justify their cost and latency. OpenAI deployment guidance.

Matching effort names across models do not equalize computation, cost or capability. Compare complete configurations and the deliverables they produce.

A small evaluation you can reuse

Choose representative work: a routine task, a difficult task and a case that previously failed. For each, write the acceptance checks before running it. Use fresh sessions or the same starting repository state so one configuration does not inherit another's solution.

Run Medium and High with identical briefs, files, tool access and thinking mode. Include Xhigh and Max on the difficult cases.

Record the model ID, active effort, output ceiling, fallback policy, total usage and elapsed time to a usable result.

Grade the deliverables against the same checks. Include failed attempts, unexpected edits and human repair time.

Repeat ambiguous cases before treating a small difference as reliable.

For coding, require a check that exercises the change. Anthropic documents that Low effort can sometimes skip verification, so make the required test or build explicit in the task. Higher effort still needs an observable result. Coding verification guidance.

Keep Medium for work it finishes acceptably. Route demonstrated failures to the setting or model that resolves them, and revisit that policy when the model or your workload changes.

articles.headline: Google just replaced Gemini Gems with Skills. Here's how to use and master them - Android Authority
articles.body: Google just replaced Gemini Gems with Skills. Here's how to use and master them    Android Authority

scored.body: Khamosh Pathak / Android AuthorityAdd Android Authority on Google: Google introduced Gems way back in mid-2024, before the agentic AI obsession. Gems were supposed to be AI helpers with a personality and a unique goal. You could have a Gem that helped you cook, code, or serve as your language learning partner. They all had their own chat windows and instructions, essentially turning them into mini-apps.But that didn’t work. Gems were their own silos. They could help you complete repeating tasks, sure, but you had to find and open the Gem conversation first. So in true Google fashion, it’s gone, joining the ever-growing graveyard of products Google abandoned. And in its place comes Skills.If you use Claude or Perplexity, you might be familiar with this concept. But if not, here’s a rundown on what’s changing — and how to start using Gemini Skills today.Did you ever use Gems?28 votesWhy Google is moving from Gems -> SkillsKhamosh Pathak / Android AuthorityGems lived in their own silos, in the sidebar, and were trivially easy to forget. When they came out, I played around with them and quickly forgot they existed. The way consumers use AI chatbots has evolved. With a long context window, it makes sense to continue working on multiple aspects of a project in the same chat window. What you want is to use your pre-configured gems and customized prompts anywhere. That’s what Skills does.Once configured, you can call up a skill from any chat, and invoke it using the data from the current chat. And this isn’t limited to a single skill or chat. You can stack up skills, chaining up a step-by-step automation system.For example, you might be working on researching a specific module related to your work or college in a chat. You can use one skill to start the research based on parameters you’ve already narrowed down. Then, another skill can take all that information, format it into an easy-to-read digest, and write it in your own style (based on data from your Google account activity). Yet another skill can then take that digest and send it to your team members via Gmail, or create a Google Doc based on it. This can go on and on, and it’s only truly limited by your unique requirements and workflows.While I don’t use AI for writing (part of my personal AI ethics policy), I do use it for brainstorming ideas, creating unique angles, and doing the menial tasks like generating keywords and SEO descriptions based on my text. And this is where Gemini’s Skills, to me, are really helpful. Previously, I fed my preferences into Gemini’s Memory file, and now, instead of relying on Gemini’s recall, I can give specific instructions for each task.How to build and use your own Gemini SkillsKhamosh Pathak / Android AuthorityHow to make a skill? Well, just ask Gemini. Yes, there is a dedicated Skills page in Settings where you can see recommended skills, ones you’ve created, and even your Gems from the before times.True to its form, Skills is built into the chat interface. So open a chat, type “create a skill for me that does,” and ramble on. You can even use voice typing to give more instructions. As with any AI prompt, the more detailed it is, the better your chances of success.Then, press Enter and let Gemini do its thing. It will create a new skill for you, with detailed instructions, surpassing what you rambled on about. For example, I asked Gemini to create a skill for me that proofreads text. I’m what you call a silly-mistakes writer. In my flow, I might make a silly mistake or two that my eyes gloss over during proofreading. Instead of burdening my editors, I usually use something like Grammarly Pro, Claude, or Gemini to go through the article and point out silly mistakes that I then fix myself (I don’t trust an AI model to just fix typos without introducing new issues in the process).Khamosh Pathak / Android AuthorityGemini made a skill called “draft-proofreader” for me (I can change the name if I’d like). Now, all I have to do is paste in the draft text, use the “/“ command to run the draft, and wait for the results.And here’s a pro tip: If you simply enter the forward slash command in the text box, you will see a list of all your Skills.Khamosh Pathak / Android AuthorityIf you want to be particular about the skills, it’s best to create one manually. Go to Settings -> Skills -> Create Manually. Here, you will see sections to give your skill a name (no spaces between words, hyphens only), add a description, and then add all your detailed instructions.5 Gemini Skills you should tryKhamosh Pathak / Android AuthorityGiven how simple it is to make Gemini Skills, you should try it out for yourself. It will depend highly on my workflow. For me, skills include online research, editing, and writing. For you, it might be about science, technology, arts, or plain idea generation.If you can take repeated action based on a similar dataset or question, you should try to turn it into a skill. Here are some ideas to get you started.Meeting-prep: If you use Gmail, Google Docs, and Meet, you can ask Gemini to create a workflow based on the next Google Calendar or Google Meet session. Based on the meeting, it, can go to your Gmail and surface relevant recent threads and insights from documents related to the project.Repurpose: If you find yourself reshuffling content to fit into different formats, create a skill dedicated to it. Ask Gemini to take a long article or a listicle and format it as an X or LinkedIn post, a script for an Instagram Reel, or a Facebook post.Distiller: Create a skill that pulls in Slack threads, Gmail messages, or documents and presents you with a bullet-point list of main learnings, actionable items, and highlights the decisions already made/tasks already accomplished.De-jargon: Ask Gemini to go through any text (a pitch or an email) and remove all the telltale signs of AI writing (trust me, Gemini already knows). This presents a cleaner prose that you can actually read, like a real human person.Stack skills together: A big side effect of moving from Gems to Skills is that they are stackable. For example, with a command like /fact-check-links + de-jargon on the same prompt, you can ask Gemini to first fact-check all the claims and URLs in an email or as a submission, then run it through an anti-AI filter to give you content that is already cross-checked and down to the basics.FollowThank you for being part of our community. articles.body: Claude Design: How to Create On-Brand Visuals With AI    Social Media Examiner

scored.body:
Want to create professional-looking slides, websites, and animations without hiring a designer or learning complex software? Wondering how to keep every piece of visual content on-brand across platforms?

In this article, you'll discover how to use Claude Design to build a design system, create on-brand visuals, and automate content workflows that used to take hours.

This article was co-created by Jeff Sieh and Michael Stelzner. For more about Jeff, scroll to the end of this article.

What Is Claude Design?

When most people hear “AI” and “design” in the same sentence, they immediately think of generative AI tools like Midjourney or ChatGPT that create images from a prompt. Claude Design does not do that. It does not generate images at all.

Instead, Claude Design is a layout and front-end design tool built by Anthropic. Think of it more like Adobe InDesign than an image generator. It handles the arrangement of fonts, colors, spacing, and visual elements that make a page or a slide look polished and professional.

The layout side of design is what most creators actually struggle with. Anyone can generate an image with a prompt, but composing that image alongside text, white space, and branding elements in a way that looks intentional is a different skill entirely. Claude Design handles that composition.

For solopreneurs and small teams without access to a professional designer, Claude Design serves as an on-demand front-end designer. A front-end designer's job is to design the look and the feel of something, whether that's a website, a slide deck, a PDF, or a landing page. The careful selection of colors, fonts, images, and white space that makes a website look beautiful rather than cluttered is exactly what Claude Design produces.

The platform is accessible through claude.ai by clicking the design button at the bottom left of the screen. The desktop app has the same entry point. The tool is still in Anthropic's labs, so the interface continues to evolve. When Claude Design first launched, it had its own separate usage limits, and users would frequently time out. Now it ties into the general Claude credits, so there is no separate usage meter to monitor.

#1: How to Build a Design System With Claude Design

The single most important step before creating anything in Claude Design is building a design system. A design system is essentially a standard operating guide for how a brand or product should look. It includes fonts, colors, swatches, logos, spacing rules, animation styles, and any other visual element that defines a brand's identity.

Many creators are familiar with Canva's brand kit, which stores a logo and fonts that get pulled into new designs. Claude Design takes that concept further. Rather than just storing assets, the design system considers how those assets should be used across different contexts. It adjusts usage depending on whether the output is a website, a slide deck, or a client-facing PDF.

Because the design system is stored as code, specifically as a Markdown file called design.md, the system is portable. That design.md file can be plugged into any AI model or platform. If the AI landscape shifts and a new tool becomes dominant, the design system can be transferred without starting from scratch.

What’s more, Claude Design supports multiple design systems within a single account. A creator who runs two shows or works with multiple clients can maintain a separate design system for each one, switching between them depending on the project.

Jeff creates design systems for his clients based on their logos and podcast artwork. When he sends a report or even an email template using the client's own design system, the result looks so professional that clients ask how he did it. Building design systems for clients is also a service that can be offered as a paid deliverable.

Building a design system takes about 10 minutes or more. The process begins with providing materials. Logos, color swatches from Pinterest, screenshots from websites, podcast artwork, or any visual reference that represents the desired look can be dragged directly into the interface.

Claude Design will ask clarifying questions during setup. This is by design, as visual preferences are personal and the tool needs specific input to get the system right. The setup process in Claude Design asks design-specific questions that go beyond what Claude Code or Claude Cowork would ask when prompted to build something visual.

Go Deeper Than an Article Can Take You

Join thousands of small-business marketers at Social Media Marketing World — three days of AI, social media, and marketing strategy taught by world-class experts. April 1–3, 2027 in Anaheim.

Every session is pitch-free and built around tactics you can use yourself, no big team required. Your All-Access ticket includes an extra day of workshops, full access to AI Business World, and recordings of everything.

GET MY ALL-ACCESS TICKET — SAVE $790

Jeff Sieh recommends skipping the one-click answer buttons during setup and instead using the open text fields to provide more context. Voice input through a tool like Wispr Flow works especially well here because speaking naturally provides far more detail than clicking preset options.

Providing a website URL during setup is also valuable. Claude Design will scrape the site and pull in not just visual style but also written tone, giving the system a fuller picture of the brand.

The design system doesn't just store colors and fonts. It stores understanding. The more context provided during setup, the more intelligently the system applies that understanding across every output.

When Jeff was building his own design system, he wanted to capture a 1950s and '60s retro-futurism aesthetic, something like The Jetsons meets Fantastic Four. Through workshopping the concept back and forth with Claude Design, he discovered the style was called Googie architecture.

Once he added that term to his design system, Claude Design understood the entire architectural style and began applying it throughout his work, from background elements in layouts to the image prompts it generated for ChatGPT.

#2: How to Interact With Claude Design

The most effective way to interact with Claude Design is to speak to it. Using a voice-to-text tool like Wispr Flow, designers can dictate instructions naturally rather than typing requests or clicking through menus.

Claude Design is essentially a chatbot that also happens to be a designer, so instructions like “I want more white space between the headline and the body text” or “Show me this in a darker color palette” work exactly the way they would if spoken to a human designer.

Requesting Multiple Iterations

One of the strongest techniques for achieving good results is to ask for multiple options at once. Rather than requesting a single landing page design and iterating from there, asking for five different versions at once works far better. Claude Design will generate all five, and then the refinement conversation becomes more productive.

Direct Click-and-Drag Editing

Once a design is generated, elements can be edited directly by clicking and dragging. Text can be retyped, headlines can be repositioned, and spacing can be adjusted manually. These direct edits do not consume any credits, which makes them the most efficient way to handle small tweaks.

#3: Using Skills and Templates in Claude Design

Using Skills Inside Claude Design

Claude Design supports skills, which are reusable instruction sets that modify how the tool operates.

Jeff uses an anti-AI slop skill that ensures all generated text avoids common AI tells, such as excessive hyphens, generic phrasing, and emojis. This skill runs directly inside Claude Design, so the text in every layout is cleaned up during creation rather than in a separate editing pass.

He also uses a voice-matching .md file that has analyzed his emails and writing style, so Claude Design produces text that sounds like him.

Using Built-In Templates

Claude Design includes built-in templates for mobile app design, slides, documents, wireframes, animation, user interface, mockups, resumes, 3D objects, research, HTML emails, color and type pairing, diagrams, and filler. These templates serve as starting points, but the real flexibility comes from combining them with a custom design system. Any template can be generated using any design system, so the output always matches the brand.

The built-in templates shouldn't be treated as boundaries. Anything that can be imagined can likely be built, even if no template exists for it. When a specific capability, such as a camera push-in effect, isn't available, Claude Design can build the tool to create it.

Creating Custom Templates

Claude Design stores projects, design systems, and templates in separate tabs. Templates can be created for any repeating format.

Jeff has built templates for landing pages and even for Ecamm Live scenes, the live-streaming software he uses for Creator News Live. When he needs a new scene layout, the template gives the design system a starting point that already matches his show's visual style.

#4: Creating Assets and Media With Claude Design

Building Websites, Landing Pages, and Software Mockups

Claude Design can produce complete web pages, landing pages, and website mockups. The output is functional HTML that can be deployed directly or handed to a developer for integration.

Jeff uses Claude Design to build web pages for clients and for his own projects. When his link-in-bio service shut down, he pointed Claude Code at the broken tool, referenced his design system, and it built a custom WordPress plugin that automatically pulls in his latest YouTube videos and blog posts, all styled to match his brand.

Tired of Guessing Which AI Moves Matter?

New AI tools and strategies launch every week — and figuring out which ones matter takes hours you don't have.

The AI Business Society filters the noise for you, with expert-led training you can put to work the same day — plus a community of marketers sharing what's actually working.

I'M READY FOR REAL AI RESULTS

For software teams, Claude Design opens up a mockup workflow. For the NoteGo app, Mike’s team created a design system specifically focused on software user interfaces. New features and functions can now be mocked up in Claude Design and reviewed before any code is written. Previously, the developer would build the full feature in Claude Code, only to learn the design needed changes. The mockup step catches those changes before development time is spent.

Creating Animations and Motion Graphics

Claude Design includes animation capabilities that go beyond simple transitions. The tool can produce After Effects-style motion graphics, the kind of high-end animations that traditionally take days to create manually.

The animations Claude Design creates are vector-based and rendered in code rather than as video files. This means they take up almost no storage space and can be embedded directly into websites or other digital content without the file size concerns that come with video.

For a practical example, a five-step instruction process can be animated within the design system. Claude Design figures out how to draw each step using vector animations that render on screen, creating a polished walkthrough without ever generating a video file.

The animation tools can also be used to build custom effects. When a standard slow push-in or pull-back camera move wasn't available, Claude Design offered to build the tool to create that specific effect. It's limited primarily by imagination rather than by a fixed set of capabilities.

Pairing With ChatGPT for Image Generation

Because Claude Design handles layout and composition but not image creation, pairing it with ChatGPT fills that gap.

Claude Design can write image generation prompts that include the exact hex codes from the design system. Those prompts are copied to ChatGPT, which generates images that match the brand's color palette. The images are then dragged back into Claude Design and placed into the layout.

This same approach works with Midjourney. The design system's carousel skill produces two sets of prompts, one formatted for each image generator, so creators can choose whichever platform produces the best results for a given project.

#5: Automating Content Workflows With Your Design System

The real power of a design system emerges when it's connected to automated workflows. Three examples from Jeff's production process demonstrate how far this can go.

Automated Podcast Cheat Sheets

Jeff wanted to create a downloadable cheat sheet for every episode of Creator News Live, something inspired by Amy Porterfield's approach of offering a downloadable resource with each podcast episode. Before AI, this would have required a team and most of a day's work per episode. Now the entire show production takes 30 to 45 minutes, and the cheat sheet is part of that.

The automated system reads the episode transcript, pulls the relevant information, applies the design system to format the cheat sheet, generates a thumbnail, uploads it to Jeff's website, and publishes it as a draft kit ready to distribute. The entire process runs automatically after the show ends. The results can be seen at jeffsieh.com/cheatsheet.

The Carousel Automation System

The carousel workflow is a multi-step automated process built in Claude Code that turns an hour-long show transcript into finished carousel posts for Instagram and LinkedIn.

The system follows this sequence: it takes the transcript, identifies sections that would make strong carousel content using a specific formula (hook, two builds, payoff, and call to action), and then generates dual image prompts, one optimized for Midjourney and one for ChatGPT. Both prompts include the exact hex codes from the design system, so the generated images match the brand colors.

The only manual step is rendering the images in ChatGPT (or Midjourney) and placing them in a designated folder. Once the images are in the folder, the system detects them automatically. A Python script analyzes each image to determine optimal text placement, and then the system builds the complete carousel with alternating dark and light backgrounds.

The output includes the carousel images formatted as a PDF for LinkedIn since LinkedIn uses PDF format for carousel-style posts), individual images formatted for Instagram, captions written specifically for each platform based on the transcript, and the entire package delivered to Slack for the team to review and post.

Video Editing With ChatCut

A newer application pairs Claude Design with ChatCut, an AI video-editing tool (not to be confused with CapCut). ChatCut connects to either OpenAI or Claude Code and allows video editing through voice commands.

Because ChatCut can reference a Claude Design system, all motion graphics, lower thirds, and visual elements generated during the edit automatically match the brand. Jeff edited an entire episode of Creator News Live without touching a keyboard. Every visual element was spoken into existence and matched his design system.

YouTube Thumbnails

When a design system is loaded into a Claude Code project, Claude automatically references it whenever visual assets are needed. Jeff's thumbnail workflow inside Claude Code writes the image prompts with the correct hex codes for ChatGPT without being asked, because the design system is already part of the project. The thumbnails come back matching the brand colors, fonts, and overall aesthetic every time.

#6: Exporting the Design System to Other Tools

The design system can be exported from Claude Design to work across multiple platforms. Although Claude Design lives in its own environment, separate from Claude Code and Claude Cowork, several export options bridge that gap.

The export options available directly within Claude Design include PDF, project HTML (which packages all assets into HTML for developers), PowerPoint, and direct connections to Claude Code, Adobe, Canva, Gamma, and Google Slides. More integrations continue to be added.

The design.md Workflow

For creators who want to use their design system in Claude Cowork or Claude Code, the process is straightforward. Inside Claude Design, ask it to create a design.md file, a Markdown file that contains everything the design system needs. Download that file, then drag it into any project folder in Cowork. From that point forward, any design work within the project automatically references the design system.

The design.md file can also be shared with other AI systems. Because Markdown is a simple, widely understood format, the file works across different AI platforms without conversion or compatibility issues.

Working With Gamma for Slides

Gamma is an AI slide-generation tool that integrates directly with Claude. After building a design system in Claude Design, the system can be tied into Gamma. Slides built through Gamma then automatically use the correct colors, fonts, logos, and other brand elements.

The workflow for a presentation looks like this: outline the talk, have Claude help refine the hooks and structure, then send it to Gamma. Because the design system is already in place, the slides come back fully branded without any manual formatting.

Other Notes From This Episode

Vera Solutions achieves Select partner tier in Claude Partner Network to support responsible AI for nonprofitsHow can Vera support your AI journey?

LONDON , UNITED KINGDOM, October 6, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Vera Solutions has achieved the Select partner tier in the Claude Partner Network Services Track. Organizations advancing the social sector can work with Vera to responsibly design, deploy, and govern Claude across their programs. The Select tier status builds on Vera's role as one of the inaugural implementation partners for Anthropic's Claude for Nonprofits program, launched on December 2, 2025.

Vera's AI work sits within three connected service areas. Advisory Services help organizations make sense of their data, navigate AI responsibly, and build data and tech strategies that fit their context. Implementation Services put powerful and affordable technology and data solutions in place, including AI-powered tools. Enablement Services equip teams to use those systems with confidence, driving long-term adoption and success. Where AI comes into play in these three service areas, Vera's focus is on sustainable and ethical use of AI. AI supports the work and people stay in the loop to review outputs, guide decisions, and stay accountable to the communities they serve.

As a Select tier partner, Vera has a growing number of Certified Claude Architects to support organizations advancing social and environmental impact. For Vera's clients and prospects, this means direct access to a team trained and tested on Anthropic’s suite of Claude products (LLMs, Chat, Cowork, Code, API).

"For 16+ years, we've helped social impact organizations make data-informed decisions. Our philosophy has always been to leverage the best available technology to help organizations solve problems,” said Zak Kaufman, Co-founder and CEO of Vera Solutions. “While we and our clients need to be careful and deliberate in implementing AI, the technology offers opportunities for organizations to save time, gain insight, and deliver more value to communities. Hitting ‘Select’ partner status is a signal that our team is ramping up on AI, and that Vera is meaningfully broadening our impact beyond the Salesforce platform and ecosystem.”

Organizations exploring Claude can talk to Vera's team.

About Vera Solutions

Vera Solutions is on a mission to amplify the impact of the social sector. It envisions a sector driven by transparency, accountability, and data-informed decisions. For 16+ years, Vera has helped leading impact-driven organizations save time, money, and headaches by delivering powerful, flexible technology and data solutions. Vera is a Certified B Corporation and Salesforce Summit Partner, with more than 20,000 social impact professionals using its systems across 195+ countries.

The Claude Partner Network is how Anthropic works with the firms that put Claude into production for customers. The Services Track recognizes partners for building a certified delivery team, delivering Claude use cases for clients, and proving the work through public customer references. Partners advance through Certified, Select, Preferred, and Global Premier tiers.
