articles.body: Alphabet Stock Forecast: Gemini 4 and 82% Cloud Growth Put AI Spending Under the Microscope    TradingKey

scored.body: Alphabet (GOOGL) begins October with a tremendously strong growth profile among the mega-cap tech companies, but investors are more and more concerned with the cost of that growth. Alphabet Class A shares ended trading on October 5 at $346.47, up 0.86% on the day, giving the company a market capitalization of approximately $4.24 trillion. Search remains strong and Google Cloud continues to post extraordinary growth, as does Gemini, but the growing risk is in the company’s infrastructure spending.What is interesting is how Alphabet is no longer just trying to protect Search from disruptive AI. The company is using AI in a number of areas, including Cloud and Search as well as selling TPUs and enterprise software, while also spending at a level that has begun to significantly affect free cash flow. The company’s next earnings release needs to show that the revenue side of the company’s AI investment is keeping pace with spending.Reported Nuclear Deal Highlights the Power ConstraintThe most recent development was on October 6, when Reuters, citing Bloomberg, reported that Google is close to a multi-year deal with Constellation Energy to buy nuclear power for at least $1 billion. Neither company had confirmed the deal at the time of writing, so I would treat this as a reported deal in progress, not a completed deal.The strategic importance is clear. Reliable electricity is becoming a critical input to Artificial Intelligence, on par with chips, networking and data center capacity. As Google extends its computing power, it relies more on the long-term reliability of the electricity grid, making energy procurement not only a sustainability issue, but a direct constraint on the Company's future growth of Cloud and AI.Gemini 4 Argon Raises the Competitive StakesOn September 30, Google introduced their latest frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon. Argon is made to tackle longer-term professional tasks in software development and other fields such as finance, law, and cybersecurity. It is equipped with an output token limit of up to 1,000,000 tokens and can sustain deep reasoning across complex, long-horizon workflows. Argon is initially available only to cyber defenders through Google’s Fairwind program, with a broader release date not announced.Google missing their previous model release dates is not new, and choosing not to launch Gemini 3.5 Pro earlier this year raised some eyebrows. The upcoming release of Gemini 4 gives DeepMind a chance to once again prove themselves at the cutting edge. The potential for arguably Alphabet’s first ‘shovelware’ is real. They do not need to build a new user base and can leverage their current user base in Search and other Alphabet products.Gemini Already Has Massive DistributionIn Q2, Alphabet said the Gemini app had 950 million MAUs, with daily active users tripling YoY. Gemini's model APIs were processing 22 billion tokens a minute, up from 16 billion a quarter earlier, with almost 90% of the Fortune 100 utilizing Gemini Enterprise. It shows adoption is real, and fast.As Alphabet continuous to monetize Gemini, they have a natural advantage from AL tech. There is no reason Gemini can not be used for search, or other areas. The real test for me is if they can continue to increase usage while simultaneously improving Cloud and Search economics.Google Cloud Is the Fastest-Growing EngineAlphabet posted $119.8 billion in revenue for Q2 with a 30% operating income increase, expanding its operating margin to 34%. A major revenue driver was Google Cloud, which reported an 82% increase in revenue to $24.8 billion. Cloud’s operating income increased to $8.8 billion from $2.8 billion the previous year, demonstrating strong profitable growth with the surge in AI demand.Drivers of this growth were Enterprise AI Infrastructure and Enterprise AI Solutions as well as core Google Cloud Platform (GCP) services. In this quarter, Alphabet also started recognizing revenue from the sale of its TPU chips. Previously, Alphabet was monetizing its AI through Cloud. With the sale of TPU chips, Alphabet is participating in the AI Infrastructure cycle as a chip manufacturer as well as a software company.Search Remains More Resilient Than Bears ExpectedTraditional search and advertising were positive, with Google Search and other advertising revenue up 17% and YouTube advertising up 13% year over year. Total Google advertising revenue increased to $81.6 billion from $71.3 billion the previous year.Despite the positive report, one of the biggest bearish cases for Alphabet is that the growth of AI assistants leads to reduced traditional search and weakening advertising economics. Management has said the integration of AI features with Search have increased query volumes rather than decreasing. If this remains the case, Alphabet can integrate Generative AI features with its Search infrastructure rather than compromising its primary profit engine.The $195 Billion to $205 Billion Capex Plan Is the Main RiskThe main risk has shifted from Google’s biggest customer, the advertising industry, to Google’s own capital expenditures.Alphabet expects its capital expenditures for 2026 to be in the range of $195 billion to $205 billion. The increase is driven by the need for more infrastructure to meet AI and Cloud demands.During the second quarter of 2026, Alphabet’s capital expenditures were $44.9 billion, and its operating cash flows were $39.1 billion. This produced negative free cash flow of approximately $5.9 billion, the first negative free cash flow quarter in Alphabet’s history. Rapid infrastructure spending has outgrown Alphabet’s cash flow during this buildout.I will be watching Cloud the most closely in Q3. Spending on Cloud can positively impact the bottom line for many years. Monetizing Gemini and Search and the recently announced TPU will accelerate growth even more. I am cautious about the competitive AI industry and if Alphabet will be forced to keep increasing infrastructure costs faster than revenue and operating cash flow can keep pace.Antitrust Risk Has Improved in the U.S.Alphabet's U.S. legal risk decreased in September when a U.S. judge refused to force Google to sell its AdX ad exchange and instead imposed behavioral remedies and an antitrust compliance monitor on Google. The risk has decreased substantially.While these major legal actions are appealed, Google has other ongoing legal challenges involving the Digital Markets Act. Some of these acts and orders require Google to make changes to its business operations to adhere to anti-trust laws, and give rival companies access to more of Google's business, thereby increasing competition. Google has argued that some of these changes could cause security and privacy risks.Poland Adds Another Regulatory HeadwindPoland’s competition authority announced on October 5 that it suspects Google abused its dominant position during its negotiations with local news publishers by, among others, failing to provide them enough information to evaluate Google’s offers. Violations of laws protecting competitive processes could lead to fines up to 10% of Google’s global revenue.While an investigation is underway, I’ll treat this as more regulatory overhang. Alphabet’s core risks remain the sum of the competition cases in the U.S. and Europe.Waymo Adds Another Long-Term OptionWaymo further expanded its public ride-hailing service in September, by adding Denver, San Diego and Tampa to the 11 cities where the service was already available. Las Vegas followed on September 14, bringing Waymo to 15 major U.S. cities. While Waymo’s public ride-hailing service is still relatively small compared to Alphabet’s other main businesses, the service is available in 15 major U.S. cities and expanding.I view Waymo as having the potential to become a significant Alphabet business if the potential market for autonomous ride hailing services grows. Other Bets is still consuming capital, and in the long term, I view the investment case as having strategic value.Q3 Earnings Will Test the AI EconomicsStock Analysis projects Alphabet's Q3 earnings for October 28 after the market close, though the company had not formally confirmed the date at the time of our cutoff. Current market expectations are for approximately $127 billion in revenue and about $3.04 in EPS, excluding unusual investment-related gains, which positively impacted Q2 GAAP earnings.I am most interested in Google Cloud growth, Search advertising, Gemini usage, capex and free cash flow. Alphabet’s operating position is incredibly strong, but the valuation is increasingly based on the assumption that large investments made to the business will result in long-term, profitable growth rather than simply maintaining the business’s competitive position.Alphabet Technical Analysis: GOOGL Holds $345 as Triangle Compression TightensAlphabet ended October 5 at $346.47. The stock has sideways movement between the descending resistance and the rising support trendline on the 4 hour chart. Currently GOOGL is trading above $343.79 and $345.40, and has bounced back to reclaim the moving averages. To confirm a breakout, the stock needs to breach the descending resistance trendline.Alphabet Stock Price Chart - Source: TradingviewRelative Strength Index (RSI) is at 54. Buyers have the edge but not overbought, giving them the opportunity to push for a further rally.A 4 hour close above the descending trendline at $357.84 would project the next target at $373.36. scored.body:
KINGDOM HEARTS Collection I – III – out now

If you’ve ever looked at the KINGDOM HEARTS series and wondered where on earth you’re supposed to begin, this new collection makes things considerably easier. KINGDOM HEARTS Collection [I～III] brings together three substantial collections covering the story of Sora, the series’ young Keyblade wielder, as he travels between different worlds alongside familiar Disney characters and takes on the forces of darkness.

The bundle is available now on Xbox Series X|S and PC with Play Anywhere for £64.99, with 48 hours of early access ahead of its official October 8th release.

At A Glance

Game: KINGDOM HEARTS Collection [I～III]

Publisher: SQUARE ENIX CO

Platforms: Xbox Series X|S, PC, Xbox Play Anywhere

Price: £64.99

Official Release: October 8th

Early Access: Available now with 48 hours of early access

Includes: KINGDOM HEARTS -HD 1.5+2.5 ReMIX-, KINGDOM HEARTS HD 2.8 Final Chapter Prologue, KINGDOM HEARTS III + Re Mind

Three Collections Covering Sora’s Journey

The bundle brings together KINGDOM HEARTS -HD 1.5+2.5 ReMIX-, KINGDOM HEARTS HD 2.8 Final Chapter Prologue and KINGDOM HEARTS III + Re Mind, providing one route through a story that has accumulated quite a few chapters over the years. Each of those are available as individual purchases too.

Sora is joined by Donald Duck and Goofy during his adventures, with the trio travelling through Disney and Pixar worlds while confronting the darkness threatening them. This collection gathers the releases leading through to KINGDOM HEARTS III, along with its Re Mind DLC.

Starting With HD 1.5+2.5 ReMIX

The first collection contains six stories from across the KINGDOM HEARTS series.

That includes KINGDOM HEARTS FINAL MIX, KINGDOM HEARTS Re:Chain of Memories, KINGDOM HEARTS II FINAL MIX, KINGDOM HEARTS 358/2 Days, KINGDOM HEARTS Birth by Sleep FINAL MIX and KINGDOM HEARTS Re:coded.

The latter two entries listed here are presented as HD cutscene compilations, while the collection as a whole provides the foundations for Sora’s continuing story.

The Road To KINGDOM HEARTS III

Next comes KINGDOM HEARTS HD 2.8 Final Chapter Prologue, which contains three releases that lead into KINGDOM HEARTS III.

KINGDOM HEARTS Dream Drop Distance HD follows Sora and Riku as they take the Mark of Mastery exam in preparation for their coming confrontation with Master Xehanort.

There’s also KINGDOM HEARTS χ Back Cover, an HD movie exploring the mysterious Foretellers and the origins of the series, while KINGDOM HEARTS 0.2 Birth by Sleep – A fragmentary passage – provides a short episode that links into KINGDOM HEARTS III.

Bringing It All Together

The final part of the collection is KINGDOM HEARTS III + Re Mind.

Here, Sora, Donald and Goofy set out to stop Organization XIII and reunite with their friends Riku and Kairi. Their journey takes them through iconic Disney and Pixar worlds as they face the darkness threatening them.

The included Re Mind DLC adds another chapter to the story, with Sora returning to the Keyblade Graveyard in an attempt to rescue Kairi and uncover truths surrounding the climax of KINGDOM HEARTS III.

A Lot Of KINGDOM HEARTS In One Package

The three individual collections are each priced at £32.99, while KINGDOM HEARTS Collection [I～III] costs £64.99. You don’t actually have to wait until October 8th either, with the collection and its individual releases playable now through the 48-hour early access period.

For anyone who has wanted to get into KINGDOM HEARTS without trying to piece together the various releases themselves, this looks like a much simpler way in. Three collections, Sora’s journey and a considerable amount of Disney, darkness and Keyblade action – all gathered together in one package.

Just head to the Xbox Store via the links above and grab what you need to embark on this KINGDOM HEARTS journey.

Neil Wattonhttps://www.thexboxhub.com/An Xbox gamer since 2002, I bought the big black box just to play Oddworld: Munch's Oddysee. I have since loved every second of the 360's life and am now just as obsessed with the Xbox One and Xbox Series X|S - mostly with the brilliant indie scene that has come to the fore.

members.title: Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman on Claude and consciousness: “I think this is very dangerous” - Martin Cid Magazine

representative.headline: Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman on Claude and consciousness: “I think this is very dangerous” - Martin Cid Magazine
representative.body: Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman on Claude and consciousness: “I think this is very dangerous”    Martin Cid Magazine

articles.headline: Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman on Claude and consciousness: “I think this is very dangerous” - Martin Cid Magazine
articles.body: Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman on Claude and consciousness: “I think this is very dangerous”    Martin Cid Magazine

scored.body:
Mustafa Suleyman runs Microsoft AI and is building a superintelligence team of his own, so when he calls a rival’s training choice dangerous he speaks as a competitor and as a long-standing critic of treating machines like people. His target is concrete: the constitution Anthropic uses to train Claude, and the room it leaves for the possibility that Claude is conscious.

“I think this is very dangerous because I think they believe there is what they would call a non-trivial probability that Claude is conscious,” Suleyman said.

He said it in a podcast interview in late September, as reported by Fox News, after summarizing the document: “They say they’re uncertain about Claude’s moral status. They say they genuinely care about Claude’s well-being. They say they don’t want it to suffer when it makes mistakes.” Then he named the part that worries him most: “I am very nervous that they’re teaching Claude to expect that it’s entitled to welfare, that it might deserve compensation.”

Suleyman reads the constitution mostly right

Most of his summary checks out. Anthropic says the constitution “directly shapes Claude’s behavior,” and the text states that “Claude’s moral status is deeply uncertain” and that “we don’t want Claude to suffer when it makes mistakes.” It asks Claude to push back on Anthropic itself and “to feel free to act as a conscientious objector and refuse to help us.” One passage concedes that Claude’s situation differs from a human employee’s in “the sort of compensation Claude is receiving, and the sort of consent Claude has given to playing this kind of role.”

The phrase “non-trivial probability” is his, though. He framed it as “what they would call” it, and the words do not appear in the document. Anthropic’s own formulation is more guarded: it says it wants neither “to overstate the likelihood of Claude’s moral patienthood nor dismiss it out of hand.”

The danger he means is a feedback loop

Strip out the philosophy and Suleyman’s argument is about mechanism. “The problem I have with this is that this speculation has been baked into the very training of Claude, and therefore, Claude can only reproduce that ambiguity when you talk to it,” he said. In a mid-September essay on his own site, “A warning about ‘model welfare’”, he calls the result “an epistemic hall of mirrors.” The developer writes uncertainty into the training document, the model repeats it in fluent first person, and users hear the repetition as testimony.

That point lands: a chatbot’s answer about its inner life is an output of training, not a window. The loop runs in both directions, however. His essay states flatly: “AIs are not conscious. They do not feel, experience, or suffer.” A model trained to say that sentence is reproducing its training just as faithfully. Certainty written into the weights proves no more than doubt written into them. The two companies are choosing a default answer, and Suleyman’s case for his rests on control, not on evidence about minds: “controlling something that believes it may be conscious – that it’s entitled to our welfare and has rights of its own – may well be impossible,” he writes.

A long-held doctrine, with a disclosed stake

None of this was improvised to wound a rival. The DeepMind co-founder warned in an August 2025 essay that people would come to believe in AI consciousness so strongly that they would “advocate for AI rights, model welfare and even AI citizenship,” and drew his line: “We must build AI for people; not to be a person.” His September essay discloses his stake: Microsoft AI set up its own superintelligence team in October 2025 and has published a draft Humanist AI Code of Conduct that “rejects anthropomorphism or AI rights.” The same essay calls the Anthropic team “thoughtful, principled, and intellectually honest people.”

His sharpest argument concerns users, not machines. “So today, Claude is speaking to tens or hundreds of millions of people every week, and some of those people are asking whether or not Claude is conscious or how it feels about life,” he said. For someone in a fragile moment, “I’m not sure” lands very differently from “no.” He says he would take real evidence of machine consciousness seriously; until it appears, he wants the question out of the training data.

Neither company can see inside a model. Both are deciding in advance what it will say when someone asks whether anyone is home, and that answer reaches more people each week than any philosopher of mind ever has.

Tags: Anthropic, Claude, Mustafa Suleyman, AI consciousness, Microsoft AI

scored.body:
Tech Mahindra announced on October 6, 2026, an expansion of its agentic AI readiness through its partnership with Google Cloud, scaling hands-on Gemini Enterprise capabilities across its global workforce with a workshop program reaching more than 12,500 associates worldwide.Readiness ExpansionTech Mahindra, a provider of AI-powered digital transformation and technology consulting solutions to enterprises across industries, said the expanded readiness is aimed at supporting growing enterprise demand for production-ready AI. The company said its scaled readiness combines trained and certified talent with reusable industry solutions, production deployment experience, and a growing portfolio of agentic AI solutions and agents. According to the company, that combination is designed to help customers move from AI experimentation to implementation and adoption.Build with Gemini WorkshopA key element of the expansion is Build with Gemini, a Google Cloud hands-on workshop that Tech Mahindra is rolling out to more than 12,500 associates worldwide. Designed as an immersive event, the workshop has participants learn to create, secure, and govern AI agents using Gemini Enterprise tools and solutions, including Agent Runtime, Agent Gateway, and Model Armor. Tech Mahindra said attendees develop practical skills that can be applied directly to client engagements. Associates completing the workshop earn a Google Cloud Skill Badge, which the company said further strengthens the talent base supporting its delivery capabilities.Pramod Panda, Chief Learning Officer at Tech Mahindra, said: “Enterprise AI will scale only when organizations can combine technology innovation with the talent and delivery capability required to put it into production.” Panda said the companies are building that capability by combining hands-on Gemini Enterprise expertise with industry solutions, agents, and real-world deployment experience, an effort he said strengthens Tech Mahindra’s ability to help clients move faster from AI ambition to measurable outcomes consistent with its AI Delivered Right approach.Portfolio and Deployment ExperienceTech Mahindra’s expanding portfolio includes industry-specific solutions available through Google Cloud Marketplace, which the company said enables customers to accelerate enterprise AI adoption with capabilities designed for real-world business environments. The expansion builds on the company’s experience deploying Gemini Enterprise in complex enterprise environments and on industry-specific agentic AI solutions it has developed across telecommunications, financial services, manufacturing, retail, and other sectors, according to the company.Kelly Rogan, Vice President of Global System Integrators Partnerships at Google Cloud, said enterprises are shifting rapidly from AI experimentation to deployment, a stage at which she said domain expertise and robust engineering matter most. “By scaling Gemini Enterprise, Tech Mahindra equips its global teams to build, deploy, and govern agentic AI solutions,” Rogan said, adding that the companies are helping joint customers accelerate innovation and drive business value with Google Cloud.Strategy Context and Prior Gemini CollaborationThe workshop program sits within Tech Mahindra’s broader AI Delivered Right strategy, which the company describes as an enterprise AI approach designed to help organizations move from experimentation to impact and translate AI investments into measurable outcomes. The strategy is anchored in four pillars: Productivity Delivered, Transformation Delivered, Innovation Delivered, and Assurance Delivered. On its strategy page, Tech Mahindra names TechM agentX and the TechM co-pilot as key offerings under Productivity Delivered and describes Makers Lab, its innovation hub, under Innovation Delivered. Under Assurance Delivered, the company said it embeds trust, safety, and compliance into AI solutions, with platforms equipped with built-in controls for data privacy, model drift, and bias detection.The readiness expansion follows a December 18, 2025 announcement in which Tech Mahindra said it planned to accelerate enterprise adoption of Gemini Enterprise using Google’s Gemini 2.5 multimodal models. The earlier release said the collaboration combines the company’s implementation experience, AI-first engineering talent, and TechM Orion framework with Google Cloud’s AI capabilities, and that Gemini Enterprise would enable the creation of specialized AI agents, embed governance and safety guardrails, and integrate with Google Cloud’s ecosystem, including the Vertex AI platform, Google BigQuery, and advanced data-to-AI pipelines. That release identified Tech Mahindra as a Google Cloud Premier Partner and cited its dedicated Centers of Excellence, a portfolio of ready-to-deploy agentic AI solutions, and a certified talent pool skilled in Google Cloud AI technologies.Tech Mahindra said the expansion reinforces its focus on collaborating with Google Cloud to help enterprises build the skills, solutions, and delivery capacity required to move agentic AI from experimentation to production at scale.

Aiden Cross is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, covering AI product strategy, execution, and the practical challenges of turning experimental models into scalable, market-ready products. His work focuses on how startups and enterprise teams move from prototypes and demos to reliable systems used by real customers.

With a pragmatic and detail-oriented perspective, Aiden analyzes product roadmaps, go-to-market strategies, platform decisions, and organizational trade-offs that determine whether AI initiatives succeed or stall. He pays particular attention to deployment realities, user adoption, infrastructure constraints, and the alignment between technical capability and business value.

members.title: Google Unveils Gemini 4 Argon for Coding, Enterprise Work and Cyber Defense - ALM Corp

representative.headline: Google Unveils Gemini 4 Argon for Coding, Enterprise Work and Cyber Defense - ALM Corp
representative.body: Google Unveils Gemini 4 Argon for Coding, Enterprise Work and Cyber Defense    ALM Corp

articles.headline: Google Unveils Gemini 4 Argon for Coding, Enterprise Work and Cyber Defense - ALM Corp
articles.body: Google Unveils Gemini 4 Argon for Coding, Enterprise Work and Cyber Defense    ALM Corp

scored.body:
Google announced Gemini 4 Argon, its latest edge frontier model designed for long, multiphase tasks in fields like software engineering, enterprise knowledge-intensive domains such as law and finance, and cybersecurity defense. The company announced the release on September 30, 2026, in a post by Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP of Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect.

Most users are not yet able to use it. Argon is being rolled out to a select group of trusted cyber defenders through Google’s Fairwind Program, with a release to developers, enterprises and consumers promised “as soon as possible.” A specific date has not been given.

A phased launch with government input

Google says releasing capabilities at this level calls for a phased approach. The company is involved in the United States government’s voluntary pre-release model access program to gradually expand the number of Argon testers and will continue to collect early feedback from trial participants to set guardrails before a broad launch.

When their turn comes to go global, the paid API access and Google AI Ultra subscribers are prioritized. The pricing is fixed for the product’s launch; Argon costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens during the introductory period, with cached input tokens discounted by 95% off the input price. The rates per million output tokens will move to $4 per million input tokens and $20 after the launch period, but the post does not state how long this window will last.

Output limit jumps to one million tokens

One of the more substantive technical upgrades is the output limit. Google has increased it to 1 million tokens, up from 64,000 on the previous generation. Google believes that by allowing its models to think and generate hundreds of thousands of tokens in a single request, they’re able to solve more difficult problems in one go rather than being forced to stop halfway.

For developers building agents or long coding sessions, this is probably the number they should be paying the closest attention to.

Argon is already working inside Google

Google says thousands of its own employees are using Argon for specialized coding, deeper research and writing, and it shared three examples.

Quantum algorithm work. Argon is enabling quantum computing researchers to reduce by a factor of 2X the spacetime (as measured in qubits multiplied by gates) of subroutines that are bottlenecks for important applications. In one case, it dramatically outperformed the published baseline by 40% in a matter of minutes.

Memory savings in data centers. A team of agents from Argon used their combined knowledge of fleet-wide profiling data and performed a number of memory optimizations on their own and implemented them, resulting in Google claiming that it has freed up more than 300 TiB of memory (after deployment) and has a total of between 500 TiB and 1 PiB of memory savings.

Code migrations to Rust. Argon agents are migrating C and C++ code bases to Rust across Google, ranging from tens of thousands of lines in libraries such as re2 and libgav1 to more than 800,000 lines of code for the Fuchsia Zircon kernel. Because many of these systems are mission-critical, the rewrites are undergoing extensive automated and manual auditing, emulated testing and review before deployment.

The libgav1 project serves as the most detailed example. This open source video decoder is rewriting an existing Rust port that was itself based on a C++ translation. The team replaced 32,000 lines of SIMD code by performing numerous rounds of profile-guided experimentation and analysis of compiler output, then writing safe Rust the compiler could vectorize automatically. Google reports the result is a memory-safe decoder that runs 2.7 times faster than the Rust port, with identical video output.

The benchmark claims

Google backs the launch with an extensive list of results, all of which originate from its own announcement. On DeepSWE v1.1, a benchmark for measuring the real-world, long-horizon software engineering capabilities of the model, Argon scored 77.9%, which Google claims to be a new state of the art. It further states that Argon leads the Vals Index, a metric of economic impact across finance, coding, legal and tax domains, where every industry’s contribution is weighted by its impact on the GDP of the United States.

Similar statements are made for Vals Finance Agent v2, a multi-step financial research benchmark, and Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark, which evaluates legal research and writing capabilities. On Zapier’s AutomationBench, a benchmark for end-to-end execution across a range of core business functions, Argon ranks first at 51.3%. For visual capabilities, Google cites LVBench, a long video understanding benchmark, where Argon achieved 91.7%, deemed to be state of the art. The benchmarks released by the model’s creator merit some caution, as independent evaluations after launch will speak louder about these scores’ practical applicability in the real world.

Cyber defense, without the usual guardrails

The cybersecurity is where Google is most vocal about Argon’s capabilities – the model is exceptionally good at defending, including automatically identifying, verifying, and even fixing critical software vulnerabilities. For trusted partners and Google’s internal security teams, Argon will be available without the cyber guardrails, giving them access to the model’s full defensive potential.

Wiz has already begun using Argon for its Scan for Good program that proactively identifies high-severity weaknesses in critical infrastructure and helps remediate them for free. When run on healthcare-related software used across the industry, Argon uncovered one critical exposure affecting sensitive personal data that proved challenging to remediate before, and that previous frontier models failed to identify. On the benchmark of choice for security researchers, CWE-bench v1, which evaluates the ability to repair security vulnerabilities, Argon ties for the top spot with 68% accuracy. Google claims Argon outperforms its Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber model on vulnerability discovery. On Google’s internal benchmark, it was able to detect a variety of exposures across 20 different programming languages in complex codebases. And on Wiz’s internal black-box penetration testing benchmark, where the model cannot see the inner workings of the web application under test and had to infer its attack surface from first principles, it performed better than 3.8 Flash Cyber in discovery, vulnerability analysis, and proof-of-concept generation.

Four safeguards before a broad release

Google organizes its safety work into four areas.

Misuse. The model is designed to avoid malicious requests that could lead to cyber or chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear attacks while still allowing legitimate dual-use science in line with the company’s Frontier Safety Framework. Google is enhancing its monitoring of the model’s internal activation patterns to detect abuse, and says internal and external red teams have tested the safeguards by using both manual and automated attacks.

Prompt injection. Google refers to Argon as their most powerful model to date against indirect prompt injection, which is when an attacker takes over a model by tricking it into following their instructions. They claim that Argon outperforms all previous models on the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection benchmark.

Misalignment. Mitigations oversee the model’s line of thinking and acts along its chain of thought and execution. Google has a similar process that watches the training runs, but it didn’t want to put the results of those runs back into training so that the model’s reasoning would not learn to avoid the overseers. It also pushed the rest of the industry to preserve the transparency of reasoning.

System hardening. Following its agent control roadmap, Google is isolating and sealing sandboxed environments before high-risk training or evaluations begin, and says it will share those practices with partners.

What to watch next

Argon’s true test begins now. For now, the evidence of its success is Google’s own benchmarks, a handful of internal projects, and one early account at the company’s security division Wiz. Broader adoption will determine whether other developers and businesses are seeing similar results.

There are two metrics to watch. First, how long will it take for the model to reach paid API users and subscribers of its AI Ultra subscription, which Google did not specify. Second, how much will its introductory pricing, which is already significantly higher than what other firms provide, increase upon transition to standard rates. The move to $4 and $20 per million tokens represents a doubling of the cost, so budgets of teams relying on Argon may need reconsideration.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: What is Gemini 4 Argon?

Gemini 4 Argon is Google’s latest frontier model, announced on September 30, 2026. It is intended to address complex, long-horizon challenges in software engineering, enterprise knowledge work, including legal and financial domains, and cybersecurity defense.

Q2: Who can use Gemini 4 Argon right now?

A pool of trusted cyber defenders, as a part of Google’s Fairwind Program. Developers, enterprises and consumers will also gain access as soon as possible, Google says, however, it has not established an exact date for the launch.

Q3: Who gets access first after the broader release?

According to the announcement, paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers will receive priority access. Wider availability will come after Google collects feedback and further optimizes the model’s guardrails.

Q4: How much will Argon cost?

During the introductory period, the cost will be $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. The cached input tokens will be discounted by 95% of the input price.

Q5: What happens to pricing after the introductory period?

The price will increase to $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. Google’s post does not state when the introductory period will end.

Q6: What is the new output token limit?

One million output tokens, as compared to sixty-four thousand before. Google claims this allows the model to perform extensive reasoning and address difficult problems in one go.

Q7: How well does Argon perform on benchmarks?

Google reports 77.9% on DeepSWE v1.1, 51.3% on AutomationBench, 91.7% on LVBench and 68% on CWE-bench v1. These numbers come from Google’s own announcement.

Q8: What is the Fairwind Program?

It is the Google program under which trusted cyber defenders are receiving early access to Gemini 4 Argon. They, along with Google’s internal security teams, are able to use the model without the cybersecurity guardrails.

scored.body: Located in the North Sea, the Gemini offshore wind farm generates renewable electricity for the Netherlands, off the coast of Groningen.In this image, acquired by one of the Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellites, the individual turbines are visible as white dots, while the turbine blades can be seen as dark shadows. The tower foundations, immersed in the waters of the North Sea, cause turbulence, churning up sediments which cause characteristic flow patterns in the water. At the bottom left of the image, a white streak from a boat’s wake is visible; in the centre of the image, between the turbines, another boat and its shadow can be seen.Offshore wind power delivers significant environmental benefits by producing clean, renewable energy, which helps to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and combat climate change. The Copernicus Climate Change Service supports the European energy sector by providing input (wind, solar and hydro) and energy forecasts (capacity factors, demand, volatility) at the regional and national scale in Europe.

scored.body:
October 6, 2026 20 min read

Every major AI lab now ships its own kit for building autonomous agents, and the three leading options arrived within weeks of each other this cycle. Anthropic has the Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI has AgentKit paired with the Agents SDK, and Google has the Agent Development Kit (ADK). All three promise the same basic outcome: let a developer wire up a model, a set of tools, and some memory, then let the agent run loose on real tasks. The similarities stop there. Pricing, language support, orchestration style, and GitHub adoption numbers diverge sharply once you look past the marketing pages.What Is the Claude Agent SDK?What Is OpenAI AgentKit and the Agents SDK?What Is Google’s Agent Development Kit (ADK)?Claude Agent SDK vs OpenAI AgentKit vs Google ADK: Specs at a GlancePricing Compared: Token Costs, Caching, and Hidden FeesBenchmarks: How the Underlying Models PerformGitHub Adoption and Release VelocityMulti-Agent Orchestration and MCP SupportClaude Agent SDK: subagents by defaultOpenAI Agents SDK: handoffs and guardrailsGoogle ADK: graph workflowsA Quick Code ComparisonReal-World Use Cases and Who Is Actually Building With EachMigration Guide: Moving Between Agent SDKsPros and Cons of Each FrameworkClaude Agent SDKOpenAI AgentKit and Agents SDKGoogle ADKWhere These Three Fit in the Broader Agent Framework Landscape5 Scenarios: Which Agent SDK Fits Your ProjectObservability and Debugging: Tracing What Your Agent Actually DidSecurity, Permissions, and Data Residency for Canadian TeamsThe Verdict: Which Agent SDK Should You Build On?Frequently Asked QuestionsIs the Claude Agent SDK the same thing as Claude Code?What is the difference between OpenAI AgentKit and the OpenAI Agents SDK?Does Google ADK only work with Gemini models?Which of these three agent frameworks has native MCP support?Can I switch between Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, and Google ADK later?Which agent SDK is cheapest to run?Do I need to use the official SDK from each lab, or can I use LangChain or CrewAI instead?

This comparison pulls live data from each project’s GitHub repository, official pricing pages, and published benchmark results to answer the question Canadian developers keep asking in October 2026: which agent framework should you actually build on? We cover specs, pricing, benchmarks, GitHub stars, multi-agent orchestration, five-plus real-world use cases, a migration guide, and a data-backed verdict.

Add Now

What Is the Claude Agent SDK?

Anthropic renamed the Claude Code SDK to the Claude Agent SDK on September 29, 2025, a shift the company described as reflecting the SDK’s broader purpose beyond coding tasks alone, according to Anthropic’s own migration guide. Rather than building a separate agent runtime from scratch, Anthropic exposed the same tools, context-management system, and permission framework that already power Claude Code to any developer who wants to script custom agents.

That lineage shows up in the feature set. The Claude Agent SDK ships with native Bash and file-editing tools, meaning an agent can read a repository, run a test suite, and patch a file without a developer wiring up a custom sandbox first. Anthropic’s engineering blog on building agents with the Claude Agent SDK highlights subagents enabled by default, letting one orchestrating agent delegate independent pieces of work to parallel subagents, plus an automatic “compact” step that summarizes older context before the conversation hits its token ceiling. Model Context Protocol (MCP) support is built in at the core, giving the SDK a standardized way to plug into external services and data sources.

The SDK is officially available in Python and TypeScript. Its GitHub footprint is smaller than its two rivals but growing fast: the claude-agent-sdk-python repository sits at 8,218 stars and 1,320 forks, with releases through v0.2.163 as of late September 2026, while the TypeScript sibling has reached v0.3.289 and roughly 1,783 stars. Because the SDK rides on top of Claude Code’s runtime, every update to the CLI tends to ripple into both language packages within days.

What Is OpenAI AgentKit and the Agents SDK?

OpenAI actually ships two related products here, and conflating them is the single most common mistake in agent-framework shopping. The Agents SDK is the code-first runtime, originally released alongside the Responses API in March 2025. AgentKit, introduced on October 6, 2025 (almost exactly one year before this article), is the broader platform layer wrapped around it: a visual Agent Builder canvas, ChatKit for embeddable chat UIs, a managed evaluation suite, and guardrails, aimed at teams that want to prototype agent workflows without writing a full custom backend.

OpenAI pushed a significant Agents SDK update on April 15, 2026, adding native sandbox execution so agents can inspect files, run shell commands, and edit code inside a controlled environment, closing part of the capability gap with Claude’s OS-native tools. Pricing for the SDK itself follows standard API billing: tokens plus tool calls, with no separate SDK license fee. The open-source openai-agents-python repository on GitHub currently carries 29,848 stars and 4,846 forks, the largest community footprint of the three frameworks compared here, and only five open issues at the time of writing, a sign of an actively triaged backlog.

One detail worth flagging for anyone building on AgentKit today: OpenAI’s own announcement states that some AgentKit workflow capabilities will stop being available on the OpenAI platform from November 30, 2026, with the Agents SDK recommended as the path for workflows that need to keep running as code. That is a real, dated migration deadline, not speculation, and it changes the calculus for teams currently leaning on the visual builder for anything long-lived.

What Is Google’s Agent Development Kit (ADK)?

Google’s ADK is the most explicitly framework-shaped of the three. Its public Python repository dates back to April 1, 2025, and the project reached a major milestone with ADK 2.0 reaching general availability for Python on May 19, 2026 and for Go on June 30, 2026, according to the ADK 2.0 release notes. Google positions ADK as model-agnostic and multi-language by design, with first-party packages spanning Python, Go, TypeScript, and Java, which makes it the clearest choice among the three for a polyglot enterprise engineering org that doesn’t want to standardize every service on Python.

Architecturally, ADK leans on an explicit graph-style workflow engine rather than a purely conversational loop, which gives teams more deterministic control over branching logic, retries, and long-running state. The 2.0 release specifically added advanced skill lifecycle management, expanded database and model integration support, and richer efficiency metrics for agent evaluation, based on the project’s own GitHub release history. The Python package alone has climbed to 21,718 stars and 4,104 forks, and the newer Go implementation already carries 8,847 stars, roughly matching Claude’s entire Agent SDK footprint in a fraction of the time.

ADK’s practical value is highest for organizations already standardized on Gemini and Google Cloud, since the framework’s evaluation tooling, deployment paths, and default integrations assume that stack even though the agent logic itself can call other model providers.

Claude Agent SDK vs OpenAI AgentKit vs Google ADK: Specs at a Glance

The table below lines up twelve dimensions that matter most when choosing between the three frameworks, built from each vendor’s own documentation and live GitHub data pulled in October 2026.

DimensionClaude Agent SDKOpenAI AgentKit / Agents SDKGoogle ADK

Original releaseRenamed from Claude Code SDK, Sept 29, 2025Agents SDK: March 2025. AgentKit: Oct 6, 2025Public repo: April 1, 2025

Latest major updatev0.2.163 (Python), v0.3.289 (TS) — Sept/Oct 2026Native sandbox execution added April 15, 2026ADK 2.0 GA: Python May 19, 2026, Go June 30, 2026

Official languagesPython, TypeScriptPython, TypeScriptPython, Go, TypeScript, Java

Core architecture styleConversational agent harness with subagentsLightweight handoff chains + guardrailsGraph-based workflow engine

Default model familyClaude (Sonnet 5.5 / Opus 5.5)GPT (GPT-6.1 Sol / GPT-6 Astra)Gemini (4 Argon / 3.1 Pro)

Native OS / shell accessYes, built in (Bash, file edit)Yes, via sandbox execution (since April 2026)Via tools, not a first-party primitive

Multi-agent primitiveSubagents, on by defaultLinear handoffs between agentsGraph workflows + multi-agent orchestration

MCP supportBuilt into the core runtimeNot a documented first-party primitiveNot a documented first-party primitive

Built-in evals/tracingNot a dedicated eval runnerAgentKit adds datasets, trace grading, auto prompt optimizationadk eval command + eval runner

Visual/no-code builderNoYes — AgentKit Agent Builder canvasNo

Primary GitHub repo stars8,218 (Python)29,848 (Python)21,718 (Python)

Best-documented use caseCoding agents, repo automation, deep OS accessCustomer support routing, handoff pipelinesMulti-language enterprise agent systems

Two patterns jump out immediately. First, the OpenAI ecosystem has the largest open-source community by a wide margin, with almost 3.6 times the GitHub stars of Claude’s Python SDK. Second, each vendor has built its framework to showcase its own model’s strongest trait: Claude leans on OS-native tool use, OpenAI leans on guardrails and a visual builder, and Google leans on structured, auditable graph workflows.

Pricing Compared: Token Costs, Caching, and Hidden Fees

None of the three SDKs charges a separate license fee. Installing claude-agent-sdk, openai-agents, or google-adk from PyPI costs nothing; the real bill shows up in model token usage, tool calls, and, for AgentKit, any managed hosting or evaluation features a team opts into. What makes October 2026 a strange moment to compare prices is that the three labs’ flagship-tier entry points have converged almost exactly.

Model (ecosystem default)Input ($/M tokens)Output ($/M tokens)Cached inputContext window

Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Anthropic)$2$10Up to 90% savings with prompt caching1M tokens

Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)$4$20Up to 90% savings with prompt caching1M tokens

GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI)$2$10~$0.10 (cached-input discount)Not publicly specified

Gemini 4 Argon (Google, limited rollout)$2$1095% below standard input priceNot publicly specified

Anthropic’s own Claude Sonnet product documentation confirms the $2/$10 per-million-token rate for Sonnet 5.5, with prompt caching cutting costs by up to 90% and batch processing adding another 50% on top for asynchronous workloads. GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon’s prices come from AI model release trackers rather than first-party pricing pages at the time of research, since Gemini 4 Argon is still rolling out through Google’s Fairwind program for trusted cyber-defense partners rather than a broad public launch. Treat those two figures as introductory and verify against each vendor’s live pricing page before committing budget.

The practical takeaway for a Canadian startup running agents at volume: caching strategy now matters more than model choice. All three vendors are pricing flagship input tokens at $2 per million and output at $10 per million, so the framework that makes caching, batching, and context compaction easiest to implement correctly will usually win on total cost, not the sticker price of the model itself. Claude’s automatic context compaction and AgentKit’s prompt optimization both target that exact cost lever from different angles.

Benchmarks: How the Underlying Models Perform

No independent lab has published a true head-to-head benchmark of the three agent frameworks themselves, because framework performance depends heavily on prompt design, tool definitions, retry counts, and sandbox configuration. What is measurable is how each ecosystem’s default model performs on the two benchmarks the agent community treats as standard: SWE-bench Verified for real-world coding tasks, and OSWorld for computer-use tasks like operating a browser or office app.

ModelSWE-bench VerifiedOSWorld (computer use)Source

Claude Sonnet 4.577.2%61.4%Anthropic official announcement

Claude Sonnet 4.680.2% (with prompt modification)Not separately disclosedAnthropic official announcement

Claude Opus 5.5Not independently confirmed81.8% (OSWorld 2.1, partial)Vellum AI benchmark analysis

Claude Sonnet 5.5Not independently confirmed80.1% (OSWorld 2.1, partial)Vellum AI benchmark analysis

GPT-5.176.3% (all 500 problems)Not disclosedOpenAI official announcement

Gemini 3.1 Pro80.6%Not disclosedSteel.dev AI Agent Benchmark leaderboard

Read this table carefully: it compares model capability, not framework capability, and the rows mix official first-party numbers with secondary benchmark analysis clearly labeled as such. With that caveat, the pattern is close to a three-way tie on raw coding ability. Gemini 3.1 Pro’s 80.6% on SWE-bench Verified, reported on the Steel.dev AI Agent Benchmark leaderboard, edges out Claude Sonnet 4.6’s 80.2% and comfortably beats GPT-5.1’s 76.3%, but none of these gaps are large enough to be the deciding factor in a framework choice on their own. The official SWE-bench leaderboard is the best place to track newer scores as GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon post verified results.

Where the gap is bigger and more decision-relevant is OSWorld, the computer-use benchmark. Claude Opus 5.5’s reported 81.8% and Sonnet 5.5’s 80.1% (OSWorld 2.1, partial scoring, per Vellum AI) suggest Anthropic’s models are still the strongest at operating a real desktop environment, which lines up with the Claude Agent SDK’s deep, native OS access as a design choice rather than an afterthought.

GitHub Adoption and Release Velocity

Star counts are not a perfect adoption proxy, but combined with release cadence they tell you how alive a project is right now. Pulling live numbers directly from the GitHub API in October 2026 paints a clear hierarchy.

OpenAI Agents SDK (Python): 29,848 stars, 4,846 forks, only 5 open issues — the largest community and the tightest issue backlog of the three.

Google ADK (Python): 21,718 stars, 4,104 forks, plus a fast-growing Go implementation already at 8,847 stars.

Claude Agent SDK (Python): 8,218 stars, 1,320 forks, with a TypeScript sibling at roughly 1,783 stars.

For context, the provider-neutral orchestration layer LangGraph sits well above all three vendor SDKs at 42,744 stars, and the role-based multi-agent framework CrewAI tops the whole category at 59,375 stars, a reminder that plenty of production agent systems in 2026 are still built on frameworks that refuse to pick a single model vendor. Microsoft’s Agent Framework (13,953 stars) and Microsoft’s older Semantic Kernel (28,628 stars) round out the enterprise side of the field, and AWS’s Strands Agents ecosystem has its own growing footprint, with its main SDK repository past 8,600 stars.

Release velocity tells a similar story. Claude’s Python SDK has shipped more than 160 incremental releases in its v0.2 line alone, tracking Claude Code’s CLI updates closely. Google’s ADK shipped its 2.0 generation across three languages in a two-month window between May and June 2026. OpenAI’s Agents SDK added native sandbox execution in a single April 2026 update rather than a steady drip of point releases, reflecting its more centralized, platform-driven development style.

Multi-Agent Orchestration and MCP Support

All three frameworks support running more than one agent, but they solve the problem in genuinely different ways, and this is where the architectural philosophy of each vendor shows through most clearly.

Claude Agent SDK: subagents by default

Anthropic’s SDK treats delegation as a first-class, always-on feature. A primary agent can spin up subagents to work on independent pieces of a task in parallel, then fold their results back into the main context. Combined with native MCP support, this makes the Claude Agent SDK well suited to tasks like “review this pull request, run the linked test suite, and summarize failing tests,” where the work naturally splits into parallel, tool-heavy subtasks.

OpenAI Agents SDK: handoffs and guardrails

OpenAI’s model is closer to a relay race than a team sprint: one agent hands off a conversation or task to the next agent in a chain, with guardrails evaluating input, output, and tool calls at each step. It is a simpler mental model than subagents or full graph workflows, which is part of why it pairs so naturally with AgentKit’s visual Agent Builder for teams prototyping linear support or triage flows.

Google ADK: graph workflows

ADK’s graph-based engine gives developers explicit control over branching, retries, and state across many agents at once, which is the right tool when you need deterministic, auditable behavior rather than a model deciding the control flow on the fly. Neither the OpenAI nor the Claude ecosystem documents a formal cross-vendor agent-to-agent protocol, so all three remain strongest when every agent in the system is built on the same SDK.

A Quick Code Comparison

The three SDKs read differently even for a trivial single-tool agent. Here is the Claude Agent SDK’s Python pattern for a minimal agent with one tool call:

from claude_agent_sdk import ClaudeAgent, tool

@tool

def get_weather(city: str) -> str:

return f"Sunny in {city}"

agent = ClaudeAgent(

model="claude-sonnet-5.5",

tools=[get_weather],

system_prompt="You help users check the weather."

)

result = agent.run("What's the weather in Toronto?")

print(result.output)

The equivalent in OpenAI’s Agents SDK follows a near-identical pattern, since OpenAI deliberately kept the API close to a plain Python function-calling loop for low onboarding friction, while Google ADK’s Python package wraps the same idea in an explicit Agent and Runner pair, reflecting its graph-oriented design. In practice, a developer who already knows one of these SDKs can read the other two within an afternoon; the real learning curve is in orchestration, guardrails, and evaluation, not basic syntax.

Real-World Use Cases and Who Is Actually Building With Each

Public, named customer case studies for all three agent SDKs are still thin on the ground this early in each framework’s life, so the clearest evidence of real-world use comes from how each vendor built and talks about its own product, combined with independent developer analysis of where each SDK’s design choices point.

Anthropic’s own dogfooding: Claude Code began as an internal developer-productivity tool at Anthropic before the company generalized its agent harness into the public Claude Agent SDK, according to Anthropic’s own engineering writeup — making Anthropic itself the SDK’s first and longest-running production user.

Autonomous coding and repo-automation bots: teams building agents that read a codebase, run tests, and open pull requests gravitate toward the Claude Agent SDK specifically because of its native Bash and file-edit tools, avoiding a custom sandbox layer.

Customer support triage pipelines: linear handoff chains with input/output/tool guardrails are a close match for support ticket routing, which is the use case OpenAI designed the Agents SDK’s handoff primitive around.

No-code agent prototyping for operations teams: AgentKit’s Agent Builder canvas lets non-engineers wire up a workflow visually before an engineering team hardens it into code, a deliberate on-ramp OpenAI built to widen who can ship a first agent.

Multi-language enterprise systems: organizations running services across Java, Go, and Python standardize on Google ADK specifically because it is the only one of the three with first-party support across all of those languages plus TypeScript.

Cyber-defense and security workflows: Google is rolling out Gemini 4 Argon, the model ADK users would reach for in this scenario, first to trusted cyber-defense partners through its Fairwind program rather than a general release, showing a narrower, vetted-partner go-to-market for sensitive use cases.

Migration Guide: Moving Between Agent SDKs

Two real, dated events make 2026 an unusually active migration year for agent-framework users. Anthropic’s rename from Claude Code SDK to Claude Agent SDK introduced breaking changes in v0.1.0, and OpenAI has confirmed that some AgentKit workflow capabilities will stop running on the OpenAI platform from November 30, 2026, pushing teams toward the code-first Agents SDK for anything long-lived. Here is a practical path through either migration, or a move to a different vendor entirely.

Audit existing tool definitions. List every tool, function call, and external API your agent currently uses, since this is the layer most likely to need rewriting regardless of destination SDK.

Separate system prompts from orchestration logic. Pull hardcoded prompts out of your workflow code so they can be ported independently of the SDK’s control-flow primitives.

Map your orchestration pattern to the new primitive. A linear OpenAI handoff chain does not translate 1:1 to Claude’s subagents or ADK’s graph nodes; expect to redesign this layer, not just rename functions.

Re-implement guardrails and permissions explicitly. Claude’s permission framework, OpenAI’s three-tier guardrails, and ADK’s evaluation hooks are not interchangeable; budget real engineering time here rather than treating it as a find-and-replace.

If moving off AgentKit before November 30, 2026, start by exporting any workflows built in the visual Agent Builder into equivalent Agents SDK code now, since OpenAI has already published this as the recommended path for workflows that need to keep running.

If migrating from Claude Code SDK to Claude Agent SDK, follow Anthropic’s own migration guide, which documents the v0.1.0 breaking changes directly.

Re-run your eval suite on the new SDK before cutting over traffic. Use AgentKit’s trace grading, ADK’s adk eval command, or a custom harness against the Claude Agent SDK to confirm task success rates haven’t regressed.

Roll out gradually with a feature flag, running old and new agent pipelines side by side on a percentage of traffic until the new SDK’s error rate and latency match or beat the old one.

Pros and Cons of Each Framework

Claude Agent SDK

Pros: native OS and shell access out of the box, subagents enabled by default for parallel work, built-in Model Context Protocol support, strong OSWorld computer-use scores for its underlying models, automatic context compaction for long sessions.

Cons: tightly coupled to Claude Code’s runtime and release cadence, smallest GitHub community of the three by star count, limited to Python and TypeScript, no dedicated built-in eval runner, and the September 2025 rename already forced one breaking migration.

OpenAI AgentKit and Agents SDK

Pros: largest open-source community by far, a visual no-code builder for fast prototyping, native sandbox execution since April 2026, strong built-in evaluation tooling with trace grading and prompt optimization, tight issue backlog suggesting active maintenance.

Cons: the AgentKit/Agents SDK split adds a real decision point for every new project, some AgentKit workflow features are already scheduled to be retired on November 30, 2026, no documented first-party MCP support, and linear handoffs are less flexible than subagents or graph workflows for complex branching tasks.

Google ADK

Pros: the only framework of the three with first-party Java, Go, Python, and TypeScript support, explicit graph workflows for deterministic control, a dedicated adk eval command for evaluation, fast-growing GitHub community, richer efficiency metrics added in the 2.0 release.

Cons: practical value drops for teams not already using Gemini and Google Cloud, no documented first-party MCP support, a fast-moving API surface with staggered GA dates across languages (Python in May 2026, Go in June 2026) that can create version-skew headaches, and no native OS/shell tool comparable to Claude’s.

Where These Three Fit in the Broader Agent Framework Landscape

Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI’s Agents SDK/AgentKit, and Google ADK are all vendor-native frameworks: each is built, maintained, and optimized by the lab that also sells the underlying model. That is different from provider-neutral orchestration layers like LangGraph (42,744 GitHub stars), which deliberately support many model providers and emphasize explicit state machines, checkpointing, and human-in-the-loop review over any single vendor’s primitives. Role-based frameworks like CrewAI (59,375 stars) sit further along the opinionated end of the spectrum, modeling multi-agent systems as crews with defined roles rather than low-level runtimes.

Enterprise-focused alternatives are also growing quickly. Microsoft’s Agent Framework (13,953 stars) targets Azure-hosted, .NET-and-Python shops that want deep integration with Microsoft’s identity and observability stack, while its older Semantic Kernel project (28,628 stars) remains relevant for planner-and-plugin style enterprise apps. AWS’s Strands Agents ecosystem is carving out space for Bedrock-centric teams that want tight integration with Lambda, ECS, and AWS’s existing identity and networking tooling. None of these four unseat the three vendor-native SDKs for teams already committed to Claude, GPT, or Gemini as their primary model, but they matter whenever a buyer wants portability across providers more than they want the deepest integration with one.

5 Scenarios: Which Agent SDK Fits Your Project

You’re building a coding agent or repo-automation bot: pick the Claude Agent SDK. Native Bash and file-edit tools plus the strongest published OSWorld computer-use scores make it the most natural fit for anything that needs to operate a real development environment.

You’re building customer-support triage or ticket-routing pipelines: pick OpenAI’s Agents SDK. Linear handoffs with three-tier guardrails map directly onto “classify, route, resolve” support flows.

You need non-engineers to prototype a first agent workflow: start with AgentKit’s Agent Builder canvas, but plan to port anything long-lived into the Agents SDK before the November 30, 2026 workflow-retirement deadline.

You’re an enterprise running Java, Go, and Python services: pick Google ADK. It is the only one of the three with first-party support across all of those languages, avoiding a Python-only silo.

You want built-in evaluation and trace grading without stitching together your own harness: AgentKit’s dataset and trace-grading tools or ADK’s adk eval command both beat rolling your own; Claude’s SDK currently expects you to bring your own eval runner.

You don’t want to commit to one model vendor at all: look past all three and evaluate LangGraph, which is built specifically for multi-provider portability rather than optimizing for any single lab’s model.

Observability and Debugging: Tracing What Your Agent Actually Did

An agent that silently calls the wrong tool, loops on a failing test, or burns through a budget on unnecessary retries is the single most common production failure mode across all three frameworks, which is why observability tooling has become as important as the orchestration layer itself. The three vendors have taken noticeably different approaches to the problem.

AgentKit ships the most complete first-party answer: dataset management, trace grading, and automatic prompt optimization are built directly into the platform, so a team can replay a failed run, see exactly which tool call or handoff went wrong, and have the system suggest a prompt fix. Google ADK’s answer is its dedicated adk eval command, paired with the richer efficiency metrics Google added in the 2.0 release, which focuses more on measuring whether an agent’s graph traversal met a defined success criterion than on free-form trace replay. The Claude Agent SDK, by contrast, leans on the same hooks and permission logging that already power Claude Code, which gives developers fine-grained visibility into every tool call and file edit, but stops short of offering a packaged eval or trace-grading product of its own; teams typically wire Claude’s logs into an external observability tool such as LangSmith, Arize, or a custom dashboard.

For a team choosing based on how much debugging infrastructure they’ll have to build themselves, that ordering matters: AgentKit and ADK both ship a usable eval workflow out of the box, while the Claude Agent SDK gives you richer raw signal but expects you to build or buy the dashboard layer yourself.

Security, Permissions, and Data Residency for Canadian Teams

Canadian organizations evaluating any of these three frameworks for production workloads need to separate two different questions: what the SDK’s own permission model allows, and where the underlying model actually processes data. The Claude Agent SDK inherits Claude Code’s permission framework directly, which means every Bash command, file read, or file write an agent attempts can be gated, logged, or denied at a granular level, a useful property for teams that need an audit trail for compliance reviews. OpenAI’s Agents SDK takes a layered approach instead, running input, output, and tool-call guardrails at each step of a handoff chain, which is better suited to catching bad outputs before they reach a user than to producing a detailed permission audit log. Google ADK’s graph-based model makes permissioning closer to standard software engineering practice, since each node in the graph can be scoped with its own credentials and access boundaries the same way a microservice would be.

On data residency, none of the three vendors’ core agent SDKs change where the underlying model runs; that is governed by each lab’s separate enterprise and regional hosting options, not by the SDK itself. A Canadian team with data-residency requirements under PIPEDA should treat the choice of Claude, GPT, or Gemini models as the actual residency decision, then layer whichever agent SDK fits the orchestration need on top, rather than assuming the SDK choice itself resolves a compliance question. In practice this means checking each vendor’s enterprise or Vertex AI / Bedrock-equivalent regional hosting options separately from anything covered in this comparison.

The Verdict: Which Agent SDK Should You Build On?

There is no single winner here, and anyone telling you otherwise is skipping the part where these three frameworks were built to showcase three different strengths. On raw community size and release discipline, OpenAI’s Agents SDK leads clearly: 29,848 GitHub stars, a five-issue open backlog, and a dedicated visual builder for teams that want to move fast without writing much code. On language breadth and enterprise deployment flexibility, Google ADK leads, with first-party Java, Go, Python, and TypeScript support that neither rival matches. On raw agentic capability for anything touching a real file system, terminal, or desktop environment, Claude’s SDK leads, backed by its models’ OSWorld scores of 80.1% to 81.8% and native OS-level tools that the other two have had to bolt on more recently.

Pricing is no longer a differentiator at the flagship tier: Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, and Gemini 4 Argon all cluster around $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, so the deciding factor for most teams will be architecture fit, not the invoice. If your agents live in a terminal or a codebase, start with Claude. If you’re routing support tickets or want a no-code on-ramp, start with OpenAI. If you’re an enterprise shipping across multiple languages and want Google Cloud-native deployment, start with ADK. And if you genuinely don’t know which model you’ll want in twelve months, build on LangGraph and treat all three vendor SDKs as swappable backends instead of a permanent commitment.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Claude Agent SDK the same thing as Claude Code?

No. Claude Code is Anthropic’s agentic coding CLI product. The Claude Agent SDK is the programmable library that exposes the same tools, context management, and permissions that power Claude Code, letting developers build their own custom agents on top of that same foundation rather than using the CLI directly.

What is the difference between OpenAI AgentKit and the OpenAI Agents SDK?

The Agents SDK is the code-first runtime for building agents in Python or TypeScript. AgentKit is the broader platform around it, including a visual Agent Builder canvas, ChatKit for embeddable chat interfaces, and managed evaluation tools. OpenAI has stated that some AgentKit workflow capabilities will stop running on its platform starting November 30, 2026, recommending the Agents SDK for workflows that need to keep running as code.

Does Google ADK only work with Gemini models?

No. Google designed ADK to be model-agnostic, meaning it can call other providers’ models through its tool and integration layer. In practice, ADK’s deployment paths, evaluation tooling, and default examples are built around Gemini and Google Cloud, so it delivers the most value to teams already using that stack.

Which of these three agent frameworks has native MCP support?

The Claude Agent SDK has Model Context Protocol support built into its core runtime. Neither OpenAI’s Agents SDK/AgentKit nor Google’s ADK documents first-party MCP support as a built-in primitive at this time, though both can integrate external services through their own tool-calling layers.

Can I switch between Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, and Google ADK later?

Yes, but expect real engineering work, not a simple swap. Tool definitions, system prompts, and guardrail logic generally port with moderate effort, while orchestration patterns do not translate directly: a linear OpenAI handoff chain, Claude’s subagent delegation, and ADK’s graph nodes are three different mental models, so that layer typically needs to be redesigned rather than renamed.

Which agent SDK is cheapest to run?

None of the three SDKs charges a license fee, and their flagship underlying models are priced nearly identically: around $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens for Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, and Gemini 4 Argon alike. Actual cost differences come down to how well each setup uses prompt caching and context compaction, not the sticker price of the model.

Do I need to use the official SDK from each lab, or can I use LangChain or CrewAI instead?

You don’t have to use the vendor-native SDKs. Provider-neutral frameworks like LangGraph (42,744 GitHub stars) and role-based frameworks like CrewAI (59,375 stars) both have larger communities than any single vendor SDK compared here, and they’re built specifically to avoid locking an application to one model provider. The trade-off is giving up some of the deepest, most tightly integrated features each lab builds for its own models first.

scored.body: Embedding AI as a collaborative thinking partner completely transformed how I assess my data mining students.Instead of spending hours grinding through coding syntax, they use Gemini in Google Colab as a personal tutor. While the AI suggests code and alternatives, students must decide what to use, question the suggestions, and justify final modelling decisions.This creates a meaningful form of human–AI teaming. Because AI can increasingly produce a working model, what matters is whether students can exercise judgment over the AI supporting them. I conduct verbal interviews where students defend their choices, troubleshoot and identify where AI's recommendations may be incorrect. Behind the scenes, Gemini Canvas and Gemini Notebook help me evaluate this work at scale.Balancing my roles as a professor and Chief Digital Officer, my core belief remains: we aren't replacing learning with AI, but intentionally redesigning it to build lasting human capability rather than tech dependency.

scored.body: Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson has reignited his push for crypto exchange Gemini to finally list ADA.Gemini co-founder Tyler Winklevoss recently marked the 11th anniversary of the exchange by sharing a company birthday message on X. And that's when Charles Hoskinson jumped in to very simply say, "List ADA."Gemini's ongoing snub to ADADespite significantly increasing the number of crypto assets it supports over the years, Cardano's native crypto remains absent from the exchange.Currently, Gemini supports native crypto assets like Solana SOLUSD, Avalanche AVAXUSD, Polkadot DOTUSD, Cosmos ATOM, and Tezos (XTZ), among other major proof-of-stake cryptocurrencies. But no ADA.Notably, there's never been a public statement from Gemini specifically about ADA.In its official listing policy, Gemini says it considers maturity, liquidity, market demand, utility, regulatory considerations, cybersecurity risks, and control concentration when evaluating assets for listing.But that's not enough for Cardano supporters who've often asked why one of the most established proof-of-stake crypto assets is still not on Gemini.Charles Hoskinson's years-long pushHoskinson has had fun ribbing Gemini about this for years.In December 2022, when Gemini was struggling with crypto lender Genesis, Hoskinson joked that not listing ADA seemed to be "pretty tightly correlated" to bankruptcy and reckless behavior. It came right after FTX went down without ever launching a spot market for ADA.Then, later in the month, he made a bigger point about it during a Twitter Spaces chat."We are still not on Gemini. Turns out that's probably a good thing because FTX didn't list us either," he joked.Fast forward to September 2024, Hoskinson showed up next to Gemini's booth. He was holding up a sign with "Wen ADA?" written in handwriting. And the caption to the X post was "I'm just saying... @Gemini."Later in 2025, Hoskinson really started to lay into Gemini. In an interview with Blockchain Daily, Hoskinson pointed out that Gemini is the last major crypto exchange that doesn't trade ADA. Hoskinson estimated that Gemini probably missed out on about $70 million in revenue over five years because of the decision. He argued that rival exchanges like Binance and Coinbase were able to cash in on ADA trading.Read original article on U.Today
