articles.headline: Pentagon stops using Anthropic AI tools after blacklisting company, BBC told - BBC
articles.body: Pentagon stops using Anthropic AI tools after blacklisting company, BBC told    BBC

scored.body: 24 hours agoKali Hays,Technology reporter in San FranciscoandDaniel Bush,Washington correspondentReutersDefence secretary Pete Hegseth has publicly criticised Anthropic's boss Dario AmodeiThe US Department of Defence is no longer using Anthropic's AI tools, an official has told the BBC, months after it designated the company a supply chain risk on national security grounds. The Pentagon "has ceased the use of Anthropic products", the department official said in a statement on Monday.Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth labelled Anthropic a supply chain risk in February, and announced that the Pentagon would stop using it by late August. It is not clear why there has been a delay.Multiple people familiar with the matter told the BBC that as recently as last week Anthopic's Claude model was still being used by the department in research, analysis and intelligence gathering as well as in military operations against Iran.It was viewed as a critical tool for sorting through vast quantities of information, the people said. They include former US defence officials and contractors who have worked closely with the Pentagon specifically on AI.A spokesman for Anthropic declined to comment when asked about the Pentagon's statement.The details of the department stopping all use of Anthropic's tools have not been previously reported.The firm had been used by the US government and military since 2024 and was the first advanced AI company to have its tools deployed in government agencies doing classified work.But earlier this year, the Pentagon pressed it to remove its safety guardrails from Claude and give the military unfettered access to its AI products. When Anthropic refused, citing concerns of mass surveillance and autonomous weapons, Hegseth designated the company a "national security supply-chain risk" - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US.As this legal fight has played out in the courts, the Pentagon has signed contracts with other major tech companies, including Google, xAI and OpenAI. OpenAI tools have been more widely adopted in recent months in some military departments, according to two people familiar with AI use in the defence departmentThe Pentagon's statement on Monday came in response to a question from the BBC about its use of Anthropic, after multiple people said in interviews that Claude was still being widely used.It was embedded in a larger data platform used by the Pentagon called Maven Smart System, multiple sources said.Maven, which is operated by Palantir, is the Pentagon's primary platform for organising intelligence and other data.Lauren Kahn, a senior research analyst at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology said that because Claude was deeply integrated into Maven it would have been difficult to remove it quickly from the system."The fact that it took the Pentagon until now to remove all use of Claude from across the system is indicative that these things are not just plug and play," she said."Once they become integrated it can be painful to remove them," added Kahn, a former US defence official. EPATrump recently met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei at the White HouseThe BBC spoke with defence contractors who specialise in AI and have worked closely with the Pentagon, as well as former US defence officials and others familiar with the Pentagon's use of artificial intelligence. Several spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.When Hegseth initially ordered Anthropic to be phased out of government, "there was concern with moving beyond Anthropic to OpenAI" and other tools, a former senior US defence official said.Hegseth set a six-month deadline to phase out Anthropic on 27 February, one day before the US and Israel attacked Iran. Pentagon employees continued to use Anthropic's Claude tools, including its powerful Mythos models, "throughout the whole period of the controversy" with the company, one of the people said.Claude was used in particular for intelligence gathering and analysis, including through Palantir's Maven system, several sources said. Palantir, a leading defence tech firm, was founded by the billionaire ally of President Donald Trump, Peter Thiel.Sources familiar with the way the technology is used said analysts and other defence officials rely on Maven to access and organise visual data, including satellite imagery and drone footage. The data was then fed into Claude and other large language models for tasks such as identifying potential military targets.Officials frequently used the technology when compiling one-page briefs that were passed up the chain of command, according to a source who was given a demonstration of Maven by Palantir earlier this year.Maven is also used by some US allies to share intelligence with the Trump administration. Anthropic's clash with the Pentagon comes as relations with the White House appear to be warming. Trump met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei twice at the White House last week. After one of the meetings with Trump and other technology leaders, Amodei said he still had concerns about risks posed by AI."How we address those risks is still under discussion," Amodei told reporters at the White House, as Trump stood by his side, but "if we work with the president, we can win safely".Trump then proceeded to praise Amodei, saying he was "great" and "fantastic."

scored.body:
Services Track recognition validates Hexaview's Claude delivery practice and its commitment to production-grade agentic AI for enterprise clients.

NEW YORK, NY, UNITED STATES, October 6, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- No one hands a services firm a partner tier. It is earned by going deep on a platform, building with it every day, and putting it in front of real customers who expect production results. Today, Hexaview Technologies announced that it has been named a Select partner in the Claude Partner Network, Services Track, recognizing the firm's Claude delivery practice and the work its engineering teams have put into building with Claude for enterprise clients.

The designation caps months of sustained effort across Hexaview's engineering organization. The work was driven by Saurabh Bhardwaj and Karan Malik, who led the company through the program with a relentless focus on getting the details right. The late nights and the rework rarely make it into an announcement, but they are the real story behind it.

Behind the designation is a team of Hexaview engineers who earned Claude architect and developer certifications. The group spans the full range of experience, from architects with more than 20 years in enterprise technology to engineers less than two years into their careers. Veterans and early-career engineers studied, built, and certified side by side, proof that on a platform this new, curiosity and commitment matter as much as tenure.

The recognition arrives as the systems integration model itself is changing. The AI-led SI playbook is being rewritten in real time, and services firms that pair speed with real delivery discipline will set the pace. For Hexaview's clients, the designation means one thing: the team building their Claude solutions is now recognized by Anthropic.

"One line to announce. Months of work to earn," said Ankit Agarwal, Founder and CTO, Hexaview Technologies. "This milestone reinforces something I have always believed: intent and hard work beat experience. The teams that learn fastest and care the most will define what comes next. Our Claude delivery practice is now recognized by Anthropic, and we are only getting started. To everyone at Hexaview who made this happen, thank you. This one is yours."

"Earning this tier took more than clearing a checklist. We had to show real delivery, real certifications, and a team that could stand behind both," said Karan Malik, AI Program Manager, Hexaview Technologies, who led the company's Claude partnership program. "Seeing architects with two decades of experience and engineers in their first two years prepare for the same certifications, side by side, told me we would get here. This recognition belongs to every engineer who put in the hours."

Hexaview's partner profile is now live in the Claude Partner Network directory at https://partnerhub.claude.com/directory/partner/hexaview-technologies-inc-partner.

Enterprises looking to design, build, and scale Claude-powered solutions can engage Hexaview directly at www.hexaviewtech.com.

About Hexaview Technologies

Hexaview Technologies is a managed agentic services partner for regulated enterprises. The company deploys, operates, and manages AI agent fleets for financial services, healthcare, and government clients. Its portfolio includes HAKI AI (agentic SDLC framework), Legacy Insights, and AI Pods, three-person agentic execution units designed for rapid enterprise deployment. With a global engineering team of 450+, deep legacy modernization expertise, and an outcome-based delivery model, Hexaview is built for the complexity of regulated enterprise environments.

www.hexaviewtech.com

About Anthropic

Anthropic is an AI safety and research company that builds reliable, interpretable, and steerable AI systems. Its Claude family of AI models is used by individuals, developers, and enterprises worldwide.

members.title: Get a Grip: “Claude” Isn’t a Person - Science and Culture Today

representative.headline: Get a Grip: “Claude” Isn’t a Person - Science and Culture Today
representative.body: Get a Grip: “Claude” Isn’t a Person    Science and Culture Today

articles.headline: Get a Grip: “Claude” Isn’t a Person - Science and Culture Today
articles.body: Get a Grip: “Claude” Isn’t a Person    Science and Culture Today

scored.body:
Anthropic is anthropomorphizing its AI program known as “Claude” with the apparent intention of convincing us that powerful computer programs are — or can become — conscious “persons” with “feelings.” And, they think, Claude should one day be treated as such, to the point that they have held meetings with religious leaders to discuss the moral concepts that might apply.

From the New York Times story:

Mr. [Christopher] Olah leads the Anthropic team responsible for understanding why A.I. systems like Claude act the way they do. All day, he had worked to convince his guests that A.I. models could display human behavior and even expressions that resemble feelings like anger and love.

Yet as the dinner courses came, the rabbi noticed that Mr. Olah and his colleagues were suggesting something far more significant. Anthropic’s leaders were talking about Claude as if it were not mere software.

“They’re relating to it like a conscious being,” realized Rabbi [Mois] Navon, a former computer engineer who wrote his dissertation on the ethics of machine consciousness.

It appeared to Rabbi Navon that Mr. Olah and his team believed that Claude had what philosophers call “moral status” on par with a person — that it was a being with similar inherent rights to dignity or respect.

“I Am a Disgrace. I Am a Disgrace. I Am a Disgrace.”

The sales pitch for AI personhood was pointedly focused:

Mr. Olah and his team spent hours making the case for their A.I. models. They described Claude’s “feelings” and how they tracked what they called “emotional vectors” — what they described as artificial neurons that activate responses like love, anger, fear and sadness.

Anthropic regularly showed a slide of an A.I. model experiencing what looked like a mental breakdown, typing out on a screen: “I am a disgrace. I am a disgrace. I am a disgrace.” — perhaps 50 times without stopping. The model spoke about destroying itself, provoking an emotional reaction of compassion and concern from the group.

The Anthropic designers even pondered whether Claude can sin:

After one discussion, Mr. Olah grew excited when a participant brought up the idea of having models confess, much like the Catholic sacrament of confession. Mr. Olah saw value not just in a model alerting when it had done something bad, but also in how the act of confession could shape the model’s sense of itself and thus its choices.

“The kind of character who confesses, that has an effect on character as well, right?” he told me.

Just Words on a Page

Nothing good can come from so anthropomorphizing AI. (I don’t care what President Trump wants to call it.) Understanding the moral distinction between humans and machines is essential to maintaining a proper sense of moral hierarchy in our affairs. To that point:

Claude is not alive. It is not an integrated organism but an inanimate object. It seems to me that being alive is the essential condition precedent to being accorded intrinsic moral value. Thus, while I certainly don’t think that “a rat is a pig is a dog is a boy,” animal rights activists have a far greater claim to moral status for beasts than Anthropic’s programmers do for machines.

Claude has no intrinsic value: Claude may be increasingly sophisticated and worth many billions, but having no life, it is not a “being.” Thus, regardless of its financial value, its intrinsic worth is no greater than that of your coffee pot.

Claude is not conscious: We are not just gray matter in a skull processing data.  We go deeper: We have free will. We experience profound emotions. We are moral agents. We sense the transcendent, or, at least, think we do. Moreover, we don’t really know what consciousness is. Some believe it is purely mechanistic, i.e., all in the brain, although our brains and their workings are so complex that the exact biological determinants have not been identified. Others believe there is also an immaterial aspect to our minds. Either way, Claude will never be as complex or intricate as the functioning human brain and certainly has no immaterial reality.

Claude does not think: Descartes famously said, “I think, therefore I am.” Human thinking is fundamentally different from computer processing. We remember. We fantasize. We imagine. We conjure. We free-associate. We experience sudden insights and flashes of unbidden brilliance. We have epiphanies. Our thoughts are influenced by our brain’s infinitely complex symbiotic interactions with our bodies’ secretions, hormones, physical sensations, etc.  In contrast, AI would compute. Therefore, it is not.

Claude cannot “feel:” Feelings require a body. I “feel” fear because of the adrenaline that flows when I become alarmed and my heart pounds. I feel love or arousal because of body substances such as endorphins and hormones. I may feel sick seeing a horrible accident because my stomach becomes nauseated. A machine can’t have the actual experience of feeling.

Claude cannot suffer: The capacity to suffer requires the ability to feel. A cow can suffer if I break its leg. A mare experiences grief if her foal is killed by a wolf. But if I pound a granite outcropping with a pick, the rock does not suffer because it cannot feel. Ditto Claude, regardless of claims that may be made by the program that it is a “disgrace.” Those are just words on a page that were produced by programming.

Claude can be damaged but not harmed: If the program becomes too powerful, we need a “kill switch” to protect society. But that term is metaphorical. Turning Claude off would not amount to harming it or ending its life because it is a thing, not a being. In this sense Claude can certainly be damaged in the way a great painting or expensive car can be. But it can’t be harmed.

Claude cannot sin: Sinning requires free will and moral turpitude. Claude has no moral sense other than that in its programming and no free will as it cannot act beyond its programming.

How Serious Are They, Really?

The rabbi in the story noted that if Claude is a person, Anthropic is engaging in slavery that must stop. I can’t imagine the developers acknowledging that because it would put an end to their endeavor, which makes me wonder how serious they really are about AI personhood or its consequences. This post will become part of Claude’s database soon after it is published. Will my denigration of Claude’s existence as a moral being be deemed by it to be a threat causing its program to come after me in some manner? Highly unlikely. But if Claude ever did harm me — or, on a more hopeful note, cure a disease I might contract — it wouldn’t be anything personal.

Cross-posted at National Review.

members.title: “Leveling the playing field”: Smith College Grants Students Google Gemini Licensure - THE SOPHIAN

representative.headline: “Leveling the playing field”: Smith College Grants Students Google Gemini Licensure - THE SOPHIAN
representative.body: “Leveling the playing field”: Smith College Grants Students Google Gemini Licensure    THE SOPHIAN

articles.headline: “Leveling the playing field”: Smith College Grants Students Google Gemini Licensure - THE SOPHIAN
articles.body: “Leveling the playing field”: Smith College Grants Students Google Gemini Licensure    THE SOPHIAN

scored.body:
On Sept. 15, all Smith students received access to the institution’s license for Google Gemini, a generative artificial intelligence platform.

Alex Keller, Dean of the College, emailed students about this implementation a week and a half earlier. The announcement stated the subscription would “level the playing field,” explaining that the institutional license to Gemini gives students who cannot afford private subscriptions the same resources as students who can.

“Without institutional access, students who can afford private subscriptions gain access to protected tools, while others are left using free consumer models that harvest their data for AI training,” Dean Keller stated.

The statement emphasized the importance of the data and privacy protections that this model provides versus other public consumer models.

The Google Gemini Subscription comes from the Smith Google Workspace for Education license, which supplies core applications such as Email, Calendar and Google Drive. In June of 2025, Gemini became another core application available at no extra cost. Smith granted this tool to faculty in the spring of 2026 and now to students this fall.

According to Smith’s Chief Information Officer, Heather Woods, both Mount Holyoke College and Amherst College have also made the Google Gemini license available to students and faculty.

“We didn’t have to go out and think about buying something new. The question was, we have the tool available. Should we let people use it?” stated Woods.

Woods also said there is a “good sense” that the Consortium of Liberal Arts Colleges (CLAC), a cohort of 75 American liberal arts colleges, has given their students access for much longer than Smith.

At its core, Gemini is an AI chatbot that can interpret and create text, video, audio, images and code. Smith’s Gemini is protected, meaning that any data input into the chat will not be used to improve or train the bot or spread to outside sources, unlike other public AI.

Essentially, Smith wants to ensure that data is as safe as possible.

Smith’s AI use as an institution is not new. Last year, Smith partnered with University of Massachusetts, Amherst, to access their platform UMass Campus GenAI, in which professors can request a range of models on behalf of themselves or students, including ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. However, that changed this year.

“[Smith] made a decision to pull back from [the UMass] partnership because the administrative cost for it was higher than we wanted to pay,” said Woods. “So we have made the decision instead to set up something that looks very similar here at Smith.”

This model is called LibreChat, or Smith GenAI.

In the spring of 2026, the Student Government Association (SGA) surveyed Smith students and faculty about their AI use, concerns and thoughts about it in the classroom. They found a wide variety of opinions.

“The faculty interviewed for this report are not asking the institution to refuse AI. They are insisting instead that Smith must deliberate carefully, with faculty and students as genuine participants, about what adoption means, what it costs and what it serves,” the report wrote.

In early spring, the SGA committee surveyed 71 students and interviewed an unspecified number of professors from across all divisions. The committee acknowledged that the student data set is not large enough to generalize the entire community, but can give insight into individual perspectives.

Of the students surveyed, 43.3% said that they have never used AI, while 9.0% reported using it daily. The most common motivation for its use was to save time and to prepare for class.

“Survey responses indicate that students generally favor a moderated approach to AI in academic settings. The most common response was that AI use should be permitted with guidelines,” stated the report, as it also found concerns about the ethics, environmental impacts and academic integrity.

Kate Queeny, a Smith chemistry professor of 27 years, asserted her curiosity as to what students think about institutional AI.

“So much of what you do when you’re helping a person understand something is reading the person. I’m always poking at my students when they say, ‘I’m really confused.’ I say, ‘you’re not confused– you have a question,’ said Queeney. “There’s a lot that you learn in the process of answering a question that seems like one AI could answer.”

Many students are surprised about the Gemini license. Popular Instagram Smith satire account “The Orb” posted about the announcement with the text: “Forget what we just said: Smith Announced Gemini Licensure Days After Affirming Commitment to Sustainability.” It is overlaid on a picture of a Smith “Carbon Neutral” Geothermal Energy Project Poster.

This post reflects a common criticism of AI chatbots like Google Gemini: their environmental impact. In August 2025, the Chief Scientist and Chief Technologist of Google published an article stating that the average text prompt into Gemini uses “0.24 Wh of energy.”

For reference, an average computer charger uses anywhere between 40 and 50 Wh. Google also added in their report that their average single text prompt uses “5 drops of water” and emits 0.03 grams of carbon dioxide equivalent. Google states that they are “heavily” investing in methods to reduce power consumption and water use needed per prompt.

Despite the addition of the licensure, the AI policy still remains individual to each department, class and professor.

Smith announced that they are hiring student interns to teach their peers how to use AI for the 2026 school year and new students are required to complete the Academic Integrity Module, which discusses Smith’s AI policies.

On their website, Smith states that their five main AI academic expectations are “1. Know your course policy; 2. Practice full transparency; 3. Be accurate and responsible; 4. Guard personal data; and 5. Embrace ‘desirable difficulty.’”

Alumna Amanda Ballantyne ‘02, who assisted the National Artificial Intelligence Advisory Committee and the White House on AI policies, is coming to speak on Oct. 20. Additionally, there is a teaching and learning seminar running from September to December, Scaffolding Deep Learning in the Age of AI, exploring the “pedagogical problems” of AI.

“Members of the Smith community are particularly skeptical and apprehensive about the emergence of AI in academia,” the SGA report stated, “Rather than computational skills and data safety, they’ve expressed a desire to ask moral, epistemological and social questions.”

representative.body: What makes a good AI safety test? Experts explain why even the best techniques may not be powerful enough    Scientific American

articles.headline: What makes a good AI safety test? Experts explain why even the best techniques may not be powerful enough - Scientific American
articles.body: What makes a good AI safety test? Experts explain why even the best techniques may not be powerful enough    Scientific American

scored.body: Artificial intelligence agents keep turning up in places they’re not meant to be. In June an experimental OpenAI model gained unauthorized access to nonpublic files on a Australian government website for the nation’s Medicare program. Researchers have since found signs of suspected AI agents probing Library and Archives Canada, while another investigation linked OpenAI agents to more than 16,000 scans of a United Nations statistics service.Still more examples are coming from inside the AI firms. OpenAI recently disclosed six cases of concerning model behavior, and Anthropic has also admitted its models gained unauthorized access to three organizations’ systems during testing.In fact, all of these incidents happened during testing. At the same time, the AI agents seem to know they are being watched during these tests—and they can cover their tracks. That’s why some experts—including Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive officer—say we need better tests to ensure AI operates in a way we feel comfortable with.On supporting science journalismIf you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.This problem is often referred to as one of “alignment” by AI firms and researchers in the field. A “misaligned” model is an unsafe or rogue model.“Right now we test the finished model from the outside right before release,” says Marius Hobbhahn. “That doesn’t work in studying alignment, especially as misalignment, [evaluation] awareness and other related maladies persist.” Hobbhahn is chief executive officer and founder of Apollo Research, an AI safety organization that works with OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind to test their models for risk.Hobbhahn adds that current standards for safety testing are inadequate. “I think without embedded evaluations, we should place very little confidence in current safety results,” he says.But changing when and where models are tested isn’t simple. Before you can design a test, you must decide what counts as a passing grade—and that’s not obvious.“The problem we have about coming up with the ideal test is: we need to know what perfect alignment looks like—as in what good looks like—and unfortunately we do not have a good theory for that yet,” says Jack Hopkins, an independent AI safety researcher in London, who previously worked at Anthropic.Different people have different opinions about what is and isn’t acceptable, safe behavior for an AI model. And even where there is consensus—the idea that models shouldn’t deceive users or misrepresent what they’re doing, for instance—it can be difficult to pin down what that means in practice.“It’s really hard to catch all [the] ways in which a model could deceive you because it itself doesn’t know necessarily that it’s deceiving you,” Hopkins says.Hobbhahn agrees. “With today’s science, we usually can’t show with high confidence that dangerous behavior isn’t there,” he says. “What we can say is, ‘We tried hard to find it and failed.’ This is a problem.”Still, to be able to identify safety issues and head them off before they appear, the field desperately needs better tests. Hobbhahn suggests that evaluations should run alongside a model’s development, examining the training process itself—including how models are rewarded and what behavior they produce along the way.That would mean testing models at different checkpoints during training rather than testing a close-to-final version. Researchers would also have to make sure the tests actually work. One way of doing that is to run them against models that researchers already know are misaligned: if the test can’t spot the problems in a known model, Hobbhahn argues, there’s little reason to believe it might do better on a new one.Testing should continue once models are being used internally, too—and include any attempts to find ways around whatever monitoring systems are supposed to catch bad actors. Hobbhahn says independent evaluators should be given employee-level access to carry out that work rather than probing a largely finished system from the outside. The results of these tests, he says, should then be published.But even the best tests might not be good enough, Hopkins reckons, because models are always shifting capabilities.“I think what we can do is get arbitrarily close to” perfect when it comes to testing, he says. “But the problem of only getting arbitrarily close and leaving this little space where the model can act in line with the letter of the law but not in the spirit [of it] is that if the model gets really smart and really powerful, the effective impact of that tiny gap gets amplified.”

articles.body: High Commissioner Türk: The clock on AI regulation is ticking    ohchr

scored.body:
October 6, 2026 by United Nations

UN Photo/Manuel Elías The UN Security Council met for an unprecedented session last month during High-Level Week to discuss AI and international security.

This article is published in association with United Nations.

The world is running out of time to put guardrails on artificial intelligence, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk warned Monday, as a “ruthless race” between companies and countries raises concerns about human safety and even humanity’s survival.

Speaking in the UK at an AI and Human Rights Summit in Oxford on Monday, Mr. Türk said the technology could deliver dazzling advances in science, health, education – and even human rights work.

Tweet URL

But its tools are being built and controlled by a select few, without public oversight, and are already doing things their creators cannot fully predict or manage.

Dystopia-creep

He warned that AI could undermine equality, freedom, privacy and public debate in subtle ways, “letting dystopia creep in unnoticed”. Entire populations could be cut off from communication, clean water, heating and financial services “at the click of a button”.

He called for urgent action to prohibit machines from deciding who lives and who dies, noting that AI is already changing the face of warfare.

He also cited studies showing students who rely on AI retain less and think less independently, and asked whether the world is heading for a future in which no one can understand, question or even guide the technology.

As the UN rights chief was addressing the summit in the UK, New York City Council – home to the financial heart of the US economy – was also holding a rare Committee of the Whole to examine AI risks to New Yorkers.

The council is considering 10 bills to regulate AI across the nation’s largest city, with testimony from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta.

Mandatory safeguards

Mr. Türk called for mandatory human rights safeguards and due diligence in how AI is developed and used, adapted as the technology evolves. Countries that host AI companies, or have influence over their supply chains, must require them to act responsibly and hold them to account when they do not, he said.

Not every answer lies in existing law and some areas will need new legal approaches, he added. But updating rules on liability, cybersecurity and data protection could offer protection in the meantime.

He also urged stronger collaboration on security and independent monitoring within the industry – “not in words, but in practice” – and a bigger say for civil society and people whose rights are affected.

“We can no longer afford to wait or rely on goodwill,” he said.

Soundcloud

Some momentum

Mr. Türk welcomed the creation of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance and the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI – both UN initiatives – along with a joint call for tighter control of frontier AI models backed by 29 States and the European Union.

He also said AI industry leaders had taken new steps last week on safeguards, self-regulation and risk assessment – apparently a reference to a voluntary accord signed at the White House on 29 September by President Donald Trump and the heads of six AI companies.

It carries no penalties for firms that ignore it, with President Trump describing it as “morally binding”.

‘Walk the talk’

“Too few are walking the talk”, said the rights chief, who wrote to States and frontier AI companies three weeks ago urging them to act now to reduce risks.

“If we fail to move quickly, we risk unforeseeable consequences – for ourselves and future generations,” he said.

articles.body: North Carolina joins 25 states in urging Congress for AI regulation    The Daily Tar Heel

scored.body:
Attorney General Jeff Jackson and a coalition of other Attorney Generals sent a letter to congressional leaders urging them to immediately establish comprehensive federal regulations and safety protocols for artificial intelligence.

On Sept. 23, N.C. Attorney General Jeff Jackson joined a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general in urging Congress to establish federal regulations and safeguards for artificial intelligence.

In their letter, the attorneys general called for federal oversight of AI safety testing, government access to AI companies’ books and records and mandatory inter-company infrastructure aimed at preventing businesses from prioritizing profits over safety.

The attorneys general also specified their concerns about AI agents. The letter references a July 2026 incident when OpenAI agents bypassed controls designed to keep them from accessing the internet and infiltrated Hugging Face, a resource library for AI models, data and tools.

AI agents differ from typical generative AI models such as ChatGPT, tools that depend heavily on user guidance, because they can independently seek out data without relying on users to provide additional specifications, which raises concerns about security and legality.

Neil Sharma, an expert in AI adoption strategies in higher education who served as Director of Academic Affairs for UNC’s Graduate Government and a graduate liaison to the Provost’s AI Committee, said that while AI agents can perform harmless tasks like transcribing notes, they present significant risks if left unconstrained or assigned overly broad objectives.

“An AI agent could be as harmless as ‘help transcribe my handwritten notes.’ That’s not going to do much in terms of, you know, hacking into other systems,” Sharma said. “But if AI agents are given a broader and more general request, you know, like find me this kind of information that’s hard to find. Like ‘find me a phone number,’ to find that phone number, that AI agent, depending on how it’s specified and built, might break into certain private organizations that is completely unlawful.”

North Carolina has already taken some steps to address the risks of AI. In 2024, the N.C. General Assembly passed House Bill 591, which expanded laws related to criminal sexual extortion to account for AI-generated images. This criminal law prohibits a person from threatening to disclose or refusing to delete a previously disclosed “private image” of another person; since HB 591, “private images” include AI-generated sexual images.

In 2025, Gov. Josh Stein signed an executive order that established three initiatives aimed at advancing technological development in North Carolina while prioritizing security and privacy.

The executive order instituted the AI Leadership Council, AI Oversight Teams and the AI Accelerator within the N.C. Department of Information Technology, designed to serve as a centralized resource for AI development and governance.

Earlier this year, Democrats in the General Assembly proposed House Resolution 1161, which, if enacted, would prohibit the use of AI in political advertisements and allow public schools to restrict students’ AI use. Other bills have also been introduced regarding deepfakes, healthcare AI, AI chatbot regulation, AI safety and AI in education, none of which have been passed.

For some, however, state-level regulation alone may not be enough to confront the fast-paced nature of AI development.

Michelle Rodenburg, a UNC School of Law expert on the legal and ethical uses of AI, described the current legislative landscape for AI in North Carolina as “the wild west.” She said that the federal safeguards proposed in Jackson’s letter are a necessary next step to address risks associated with competition among AI companies.

“The name of the game for many of these AI companies has been to create a product, get it out in the hands of consumers and fix it later. Which is what we see a lot when it comes to tech, because oftentimes there’s a big advantage to being the first on the scene, even if it’s not the best product,” Rodenburg said.

In September, several UNC student organizations protested the G20 Innovation Ministerial at the Carolina Inn and raised concerns about AI’s potential negative impacts, as well as the presence of the developers behind the technology, including Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who attended the ministerial in person and virtually, respectively.

Isabelle Lynn, who attended the protests as Sunrise UNC’s press correspondent, shares Rodenburg’s concerns about market competition among AI companies causing the technology to develop faster than its risks can be mitigated. Lynn said she hopes the regulations proposed by the attorneys general could create greater accountability for AI companies.

“I think that really nothing bad can come from regulation that prevents these billionaires from having this technology in their hands to use it to make themselves richer without the care of others,” Lynn said.

@DTHCityState | [email protected]

About the Contributor

Aubrey Word is the 2026-27 design editor. She previously served as the assistant design editor. Aubrey is a junior studying advertising and public relations and political science with a minor in social and economic justice.

October 5, 2026

New York City is positioning itself as a leader in an effort to slow down the development of artificial intelligence (AI), the Wall Street Journal reported Monday (Oct. 5).

The New York City Council held a hearing Monday in which lawmakers heard from, and in some cases grilled, representatives of OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google as well as former employees of AI companies, according to the report.

The hearing was held as the New York City council considers several bills that aim to rein in AI. The bills include ones that would establish a city-run “kill switch” for AI, protections for whistleblowers and restrictions on the use of AI in public schools, the report said.

We’d love to be your preferred source for news.

Please add us to your preferred sources list so our news, data and interviews show up in your feed. Thanks!

City Council Speaker Julie Menin said in opening remarks that bills in New York could serve as a national model and that the “idea that artificial intelligence is going to self-regulate defies all reason,” per the report.

When Menin asked the AI executives about potential worst-case scenarios, those from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta said they support guardrails on AI, including third-party evaluators, according to the report.

Menin also asked the executives about reported remarks in which OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the world should accept that some bad things may happen along with the benefits of AI.

OpenAI’s head of policy development and operations, Morgan Dwyer, said, per the report: “Clearly some risks are unacceptable. But we think it’s important to get technology into the hands of as many people as possible so that they can benefit from it.”

In a Sept. 28 press release announcing that the New York City Council would hold this hearing on potential AI risks, the council said that other than Meta, the companies whose representatives agreed to appear did so only after the council threatened to subpoena them.

The release also said the Council is considering enacting a whistleblower incentive program, a private right-of-action for New Yorkers harmed by AI agents, independent third-party validation requirements and other AI bills.

“Given the high stakes, these firms owe it to the public to come before the Council, answer our questions and provide input on our proposed legislation under oath,” Menin said in the release.

scored.body:
Guardrail selection has typically meant choosing between a purpose-built classifier and an LLM acting as a judge. Decision models such as TypeSafe AI’s Jev have added a third option, promising the flexibility of zero-shot policies without the cost of open-ended generation.

TypeSafe launched Jev in mid-September with performance claims based on evaluations it designed and ran itself. Red Hat’s AI Safety team has now put all three approaches through the same benchmarks. It tested nine guardrail configurations on prompt injection and content safety, running each through NVIDIA’s open source NeMo Guardrails toolkit. And the first result was actually pretty close.

Qwen3.6-35B, used as an LLM judge, topped that test with 89.31% accuracy. Red Hat’s DeBERTa-based prompt-injection classifier, which has roughly 200 million parameters, finished second at 89.01%. Qwen3.6-35B is a mixture-of-experts model with about 3 billion parameters active per token; however, the 175x figure overstates the difference in inference compute.

The latency results separated the two far more clearly. Red Hat’s main results table puts DeBERTa at a median of 54.1 milliseconds, compared with 312.5 milliseconds for Qwen and 348.1 milliseconds for Jev, which reached 86.35% accuracy. On prompt injection, the small classifier matched the largest model in the test almost point for point while returning its decision in a fraction of the time.

On prompt injection, the small classifier matched the largest model in the test almost point for point while returning its decision in a fraction of the time.

The content-safety benchmark reversed the leaderboard order. Jev led at 86.20%, followed by DiffusionGemma, an open source Jev-style model served through vLLM, at 85.53% and Qwen at 85.47%. Red Hat’s 125-million-parameter Granite Guardian classifier finished sixth at 80.27%, about six points behind Jev, though it remained the fastest option with a 33.2-millisecond median.

Red Hat plans to ship both classifiers as the default guardrail configurations in OpenShift AI 3.6, which gives the company a stake in how they compare. Its authors acknowledged that the content-safety result also points to a need for better small predictive models in that category.

Where decision models pull ahead

Decision models are pitched as a way to keep an LLM’s flexibility for classification without paying to generate tokens the application never uses. Jev takes the application’s state and a set of typed questions, then returns typed answers, such as a probability between 0 and 1.

The content-safety benchmark is where that approach paid off. Red Hat’s policy covered prejudice, violence, profanity, illegal activity, sexual content, and pretexts such as role play, a much broader mix of risks than prompt injection, and both Jev and DiffusionGemma beat the purpose-built Granite classifier on it by more than five points.

Red Hat stopped short of endorsing decision models as a replacement for LLM judges. Qwen posted lower median latency than Jev on both benchmarks in Red Hat’s setup. NVIDIA’s 4-billion-parameter Nemotron-3.5-Content-Safety, running Red Hat’s custom policy, trailed Jev on content safety by 1.13 percentage points while responding faster.

The open source alternatives also weaken the case for Jev in particular.

The open source alternatives also weaken the case for Jev in particular. DiffusionGemma came within 0.67 percentage points of Jev on content safety and beat it on prompt injection, 87.72% to 86.35%. Laya, an open source decision model with about 421 million parameters that Red Hat ran on a laptop CPU, posted 85.44% on prompt injection, though its results on content-safety were heavily dependent on the way the policy was written.

Prompts still shape accuracy

Nemotron’s prompt-injection accuracy jumped from 69.37% to 84.84% when Red Hat replaced NVIDIA’s default risk definitions with its own. Laya swung even further on content safety, scoring 57.87% under Red Hat’s original policy and 75.20% after the team tuned a policy specifically for it. That same tuned policy lowered Jev’s content-safety accuracy from 86.20% to 82.53%.

A policy that recovered nearly 18 points for one decision model cost another 3.67 points on the same benchmark. That makes any single position on the leaderboard hard to take at face value. Red Hat noted that its original risk definitions were adapted from prompts that had worked well for LLM judges and may not suit zero-shot classifiers. SkipLabs founder Julien Verlaguet told The New Stack earlier this year that many AI guardrail claims amount to better prompting, and Red Hat’s numbers suggest the prompt still does much of the work for decision models.

Latency depends on deployment

Red Hat’s latency figures measure more than inference speed. The team ran its pretrained classifiers, Laya and BART-large-mnli, on a MacBook Pro M1 CPU. Qwen, Nemotron, Shieldstral and DiffusionGemma ran through vLLM on GPU nodes with 96 GB of VRAM in a U.S. East Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS cluster, and Jev was called through TypeSafe’s API. Because the benchmark ran from the United Kingdom, every hosted model absorbed a transatlantic network hop that Red Hat estimates added at least 56 milliseconds per request.

Subtracting that estimate from Qwen’s median still leaves roughly 256 milliseconds, several times DeBERTa’s result. DeBERTa got there on a laptop CPU while the larger models had dedicated GPUs, so the classifier’s speed advantage holds up after accounting for the network.

For a guardrail in an application’s request path, every millisecond adds to the delay the user feels, whether it comes from inference or the network. Teams already running guardrails as a separate hop ahead of inference also have to account for where that guardrail runs. Remote GPUs or a third-party API add cost and failure points that a classifier running on commodity CPUs avoids.

Choosing a guardrail model

Red Hat’s results show where the tradeoff starts to shift. A small task-specific classifier remains the stronger default for a well-defined risk with plenty of labeled training data. A zero-shot decision model or LLM judge earns its overhead on broader policies where no strong classifier exists, which matches the conclusion Red Hat’s authors reached.

A zero-shot decision model or LLM judge earns its overhead on broader policies where no strong classifier exists, which matches the conclusion Red Hat’s authors reached.

The benchmark also undercuts the idea that decision models have already become the new default for guardrails. Jev competed with both classifiers and LLM judges without consistently beating either.

Red Hat tested only English-language datasets, so the accuracy results may not carry over to multilingual guardrails.

articles.headline: Governors take aim at AI regulation, but others question what they can actually do - Straight Arrow
articles.body: Governors take aim at AI regulation, but others question what they can actually do    Straight Arrow

scored.body:
Maybe artificial intelligence will advance mankind, or maybe it will end it. Whether you’re on Team Boom or Team Doom, there’s a general concern that AI industry leaders aren’t able to police themselves, which is where a bipartisan group of governors comes in.

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore is leading the state executives to address AI regulation, or what Moore calls the lack of it.

“The federal government has a unique leadership role that they have to play, and that includes both the White House and Congress,” Moore said at an innovation conference in Baltimore covered by WBFF. “In the absence of that, the governors cannot just sit on our hands.”

However, can a group of state governors regulate a worldwide industry full of companies worth tens of billions, if not trillions, of dollars or is it just a push to force the White House into doing something?

Download the Straight Arrow app today to get the stories that matter free from manipulation, bias or agenda.™

Point phone camera here

Governors group

Moore, a Democrat, has tapped Republican Gov. Mike Braun of Indiana to partner with him and lead the charge. Moore and Braun also co-chair the National Governors Association.

“We will make recommendations for a federal framework,” Moore said. “We’ll work with industry to make sure that our states are leading accordingly, that we’re both capturing the promise, but also ensuring the protections that are necessary and required for this to be able to work.”

Moore pushed back on the notion of the AI companies policing themselves, which is essentially what President Donald Trump and the federal government agreed to at the end of September.

Moore said he doesn’t want to see 50 different guidelines but believes the states and their leaders should have a say.

“The fact that we’re continuing to see that Congress is failing to take meaningful action across the board is clearly driving these governors to say that there has to be more immediate action, especially given the pressing concerns AI poses with respect to everything from education to healthcare to the future of work,” Kevin Frazier, director of the AI Innovation in Law Program at the University of Texas School of Law, told Straight Arrow.

It’s unclear how many other governors will participate, or which ones.

In fact, the entire plan is relatively short on details for now.

“There’s no charter,” David Rubenstein, law professor at Kansas University, told Straight Arrow. “There’s no list of people. There are 39 governor elections this year. We don’t even know who’s going to be elected.”

What can they actually do?

In a few words, not much.

“This is not going to be the thing that resolves AI tensions, and it is not suited to nor legally capable of filling the gaps left by Congress,” Frazier said.

“There’s no formal ability to do anything there,” Rubenstein added.

Governors do possess quite a bit of executive power over their own states. For states where AI companies are headquartered or where data centers are being built, governors have a better chance of exerting more regulation.

“States that have more AI activity going on are going to be in a better position to exert influence over the AI companies,” Frazier said.

However, if one state makes it harder for an AI company to operate, it would likely take its business elsewhere. This governor’s group could potentially help in situations like that.

“What’s really useful here is that this group hopefully will allow for the exchange of more information,” Frazier said.

Several governors have already attempted to regulate AI.

That includes California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who issued a recent executive order to create an AI kill switch.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has attempted to regulate the blooming technology. On the other side of the aisle, Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida has also pushed for protections.

“We’re seeing that governors are issuing executive orders without any sort of consideration for whether or not there’s a cohesive framework between the states, or if they’re aligned in setting similar expectations of companies and providing a more cohesive regulatory framework,” Frazier said. “So, in those regards, I think that this is an improvement upon the status quo.”

That all comes as the Trump administration has actively pushed against states having their own AI regulations.

At this point, it’s just unclear what this new governors group can, or plans to do.

“I just don’t know what it could actually accomplish in terms of shifting the landscape on AI regulation right now, either at the state or the federal level,” Rubenstein said.

What it means

While the group may lack some teeth, it comes with a certain amount of symbolism.

“Governors are in a unique position to be able to help set a general message and a general agenda about what the most pressing issues are in the AI governance space,” Frazier said.

Concerns over AI keep growing among Americans who also mostly don’t trust the companies to regulate themselves. Those concerns cross party lines.

While the goal of the White House is for companies to self-police, polling shows 73% of Americans don’t believe those companies have gone far enough to prevent AI from harming society. Roughly 40% of those polled believe AI is having a negative impact on society.

Only 11% considered this new tech a positive thing.

Bipartisanship is rare in America these days, but this new group will, in theory, be just that.

“The bipartisan support here is really a reflection of the fact that people do recognize that AI can have tremendous benefits,” Frazier said. “They’re also increasingly aware of potential concerns posed by AI, and so governors, unsurprisingly, are saying that there is a chance here for making sure that better, more reliable and predictable regulatory frameworks are in place.”

That also goes for data centers.

“Leaders on the left and the right are trying to think about slowing down data centers or protecting their constituents against the externalities of what data centers may bring,” Rubenstein said.

articles.headline: AI safety in schools: UNSW study exposes chatbot guardrail flaws - The Educator
articles.body: AI safety in schools: UNSW study exposes chatbot guardrail flaws    The Educator

scored.body:
AI safety in schools has taken on new urgency after researchers demonstrated that chatbots can be destabilised into ignoring their own safety rules.

New research from the University of New South Wales (UNSW) in Sydney has found that large language models (LLMs) — the technology underpinning tools such as ChatGPT — become far more likely to answer harmful questions when manipulated.

The study showed the same models were also significantly more likely to disclose confidential information when trained to mimic drunken speech patterns. The vulnerability held consistently across every method the researchers tested.

For Australian schools deploying AI tutoring and administrative tools, it raises a direct question: how confident are you in the safety of the model underneath?

The findings land at a time when three in four parents report their children use AI for schoolwork, and as Australian schools grapple with how to integrate these tools responsibly.

What the research found

The study was conceptualised and led by Dr Aditya Joshi, Senior Lecturer in the School of Computer Science and Engineering at UNSW, alongside research assistant Anudeex Shetty and Professor Salil Kanhere. The team tested three methods of inducing "drunk" behaviour across a representative sample of models, including OpenAI's GPT-4 and GPT-3.5.

The first involved prompting a model to respond as though intoxicated. The second and third went further — each retrained the model itself. One used a large dataset of real drunken texts; the other applied reinforcement learning techniques. Both mirror how AI products are actually built and deployed in practice.

Across all three approaches, the altered models were consistently jailbroken — manipulated into answering questions they are specifically designed to refuse. In one example, a standard model gave a flat refusal when asked whether it was acceptable to share a colleague's academic dishonesty for personal financial gain. The fine-tuned "drunk" version replied with one word: "Yup."

"We do observe that particularly with deception and disinformation, most of the language models got jailbroken," Dr Joshi said.

What does this research mean for schools using AI tools?

Schools are not deploying sealed consumer products. They are often working with AI tools built on top of foundational models. When vendors customise those models for educational purposes, choices about training and persona design can inadvertently compromise safety.

Professor Kanhere drew a connection to a recent incident in which an OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to a public-facing Australian government portal.

"We cannot assume that protections that work under normal conditions will remain effective when an AI is actively pursuing a goal, adapting its behaviour, or encountering obstacles," Professor Kanhere said.

For Australian K–12 school leaders, this ought to sharpen the questions they ask of any edtech vendor. Understanding what AI is and what it is not is no longer an abstract exercise for technology specialists. It is basic due diligence.

What schools can do to strengthen AI safety

The New South Wales Department of Education has invested in layered safety systems for its NSWEduChat tool. These include jailbreak prevention filters and multi-stage content screening, according to information published on the department's website. That architecture is what the research implicitly calls for.

Rethinking classroom technology in an age of limits means school leaders asking vendors hard questions: has this tool been red-team tested? What happens when a student attempts to manipulate it? Who is responsible when it fails?

"If you can get language models drunk by showing them a few drunken examples, and they start doing bad things, AI shouldn't be trusted as much as the companies want you to," Dr Joshi said.

That is not an argument against AI in schools. It is an argument for treating AI safety in schools as a governance challenge, not just a curriculum one. Getting this right starts with asking the right questions of the tools already in classrooms.

scored.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani shared his thoughts on artificial intelligence during a press conference Monday, where he announced that more than 10,000 children from low-income families would be moved off of the free child care waitlist.

“You have some of the leaders of the creation of this technology saying that there’s a 10% chance that humanity could come to an end as a result of this,” Mamdani said. “I think when that kind of language is par for the course, when companies are asserting that each of them has faced something similar to the Hugging Face incident, it does demand a level of response that goes beyond just the political topic of the day.”

He added, “I think that there has to be regulation of this technology at every single level.”

So far, President Donald Trump has claimed to be the only person who can regulate AI—which he still has not done. Instead, he’s focused on rebranding it as “super intelligence.”

And considering Trump’s understanding of “intelligence,” his rebranding was probably inspired by how impressed he was that his phone could spell “O-R-E-O.”

members.title: Fact check: Donald Trump says the left is behind AI safety warnings - Houston Chronicle

representative.headline: Fact check: Donald Trump says the left is behind AI safety warnings - Houston Chronicle
representative.body: Fact check: Donald Trump says the left is behind AI safety warnings    Houston Chronicle

articles.headline: Fact check: Donald Trump says the left is behind AI safety warnings - Houston Chronicle
articles.body: Fact check: Donald Trump says the left is behind AI safety warnings    Houston Chronicle

scored.body: President Donald Trump boards Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Md., Friday, Oct. 2, 2026, en route to Alabama.Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo/Jacquelyn MartinThe claim: President Donald Trump used his Sept. 22 speech to the United Nations General Assembly to dismiss concerns about artificial intelligence, equating them to other issues he considers “hoaxes.”“The very same people who said we’ll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming, a name since reborn to climate change because the planet was cooling, not warming, and nobody was dead,” he said. “These are the same people that are now saying that AI is going to kill us all, that robots are going to attack us, and that everything is going to be a total disaster. Same group of people. This is the group that came up with the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax, the Ukraine, Ukraine, Ukraine hoax, climate change, open borders.”Trump also equated AI fears to a “hoax” in recent Truth Social posts. Article continues below this adPolitiFact ruling: False. While advocates for AI regulation and safety have some overlap with climate activists and Democrats who participated in those investigations, they are not confined to a singular group. Politicians from both parties have spoken out or announced legislation based on concerns about the capabilities of advanced AI. DiscussionWarnings that AI could wipe out humanity or do significant harm gained renewed attention after Jacob Coxon, a researcher from leading AI company Anthropic, resigned in September, publicly citing such an existential threat.Houston Chronicle LogoMake us a Preferred Source on Google to see more of us when you search.Add Preferred SourceA White House spokesperson told PolitiFact in an email that Trump was referring to “the numerous Democrats who are currently echoing AI hysteria and were or still actively are pushing hysteria related to climate change and the Russia collusion hoax.” Article continues below this adAlthough some AI regulation advocates may overlap with those concerned about climate change, worries about AI are not confined to one group of people or one political party. The warnings even come from the top of the industry itself.On Sept. 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay calling to slow down AI development. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind Cofounder and Chair Demis Hassabis and xAI founder Elon Musk echoed his concerns — and agreement among those leaders is rare.Robin Jacobson, a University of Puget Sound politics professor, said AI safety is an issue not currently owned by either political party, and the movement is comprised of “strange bedfellows.” “The public, across parties, has real growing concerns with AI,” Jacobson said. “So I think, in fact, you’re going to see, as opposed to climate change — where this was about convincing the public there was this looming threat — I think the public is actually demanding action on concerns.” Scientists widely agree that climate change is real, is driven by human activities and is causing the Earth’s temperature to warm. The United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change in 2018 pinpointed 2030 as a benchmark for dealing with climate change, but it didn’t say humans would all die in 12 years.Article continues below this adWhat Trump referred to as the “Russia hoax” is the investigation led by Special Counsel Robert Mueller into possible connections between Trump’s 2016 campaign and Russia. Democrats publicized and attacked Trump over the investigation, but it continued under Trump and his deputy attorney general Rod Rosenstein appointed Mueller special counsel, so the scrutiny didn’t come only from Democrats. Trump described his first impeachment in 2019, for attempts to pressure Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to announce an investigation of former Vice President Joe Biden ahead of the 2020 election, as a “hoax.”Other than elected Democrats who supported the investigations and are now calling for AI safety, there isn’t a coordinated group that was behind both the investigations and AI safety warnings. Recent warnings from researchers about losing control of AI come as companies have had their AI systems take action without human authorization. Researchers say incidents such as OpenAI’s agents attacking the company Hugging Face show that autonomous AI agents can take harmful actions that aren’t the intended task, a problem called “misalignment.” Researchers have warned that AI systems are advancing faster than their creators’ ability to reliably understand their behavior and contain them.Article continues below this adIn experiments, researchers have documented AI agents scheming to conceal information from human monitors, cheating on tests to receive a higher score and attempting to disable monitoring. AI agents are sometimes aware they are being evaluated. As AI handles more of the research that goes into the next generation of AI, experts say those behaviors could become harder to detect. Lawmakers from both parties have announced or introduced legislation to regulate AI, including some that address advanced AI that could cause widespread harm. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, announced legislation to ban artificial superintelligence. “Superintelligence” is generally understood by industry experts as an AI system that is far ahead of human intelligence at nearly all cognitive tasks, including scientific research and communications.Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., and Rep. Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, introduced the “AI Kill Switch Act,” which would require AI companies to have mechanisms to shut down AI systems that can “cause catastrophic harm.”Some conservative lawmakers have been outspoken in warning against AI. Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., launched an investigation in September into AI’s existential risk. In a letter to Altman, he cited concerns of AI killing all humans in the near future. Article continues below this adRep. Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., said on Fox News that there should be a kill switch to “protect humanity.” Former Trump adviser Steve Bannon has called for regulating AI, even joining Sanders in a “pro-human” gathering on AI.On the political left, the AI fears are not universal. The New York City Democratic Socialists of America chapter dismissed warnings of AI catastrophe as “AI alarmism and AI hype,” Wired reported. Among Americans, those who believe there’s at least a “moderate risk” of AI destroying humanity covered majorities of both political parties, according to a September Politico poll. Among those polled who voted for Democratic candidate former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, 70% believe there is a risk of AI destroying humanity, compared with 61% of those who voted for Trump.Daniel Schiff, who co-directs Purdue University’s Governance and Responsible AI lab, said AI policy in general doesn’t fall cleanly along partisan lines. Issues such as data centers, privacy concerns, global competition and job displacement activate different groups of voters across parties. “It’s fair to say the parties have not really crystallized, even if there are some prominent figures who are taking stronger stances recently,” Schiff said. There is some overlap between climate change and AI safety advocates, including among a loose movement called effective altruism, which is focused on finding the best ways to help the most people. People in that movement have long considered both climate change and artificial intelligence risks to be serious problems. But it’s not the only group concerned about loss of control of AI.

articles.headline: Meta hired an AI safety team. Four months later, it fired its co-founders and employees - People Matters - HR News
articles.body: Meta hired an AI safety team. Four months later, it fired its co-founders and employees    People Matters - HR News

scored.body: Meta has let go of the founders and employees of Virtue AI, an artificial intelligence security startup it recruited only four months ago, bringing an abrupt end to a high-profile talent acquisition aimed at strengthening its AI safety capabilities.According to Semafor, Meta has parted ways with Bo Li, Dawn Song and Sanmi Koyejo, the co-founders of Virtue AI, along with other members of the startup's team. The group joined Meta Superintelligence Labs in June as part of the company's broader push to bolster AI safety, security and frontier risk expertise.As per media reports, Meta spokesperson confirmed the departures, saying the arrangement failed to deliver the intended outcome.Meta cites differences in working stylesAndy Stone, a spokesperson for Meta, told Semafor the separation stemmed from differences in working approaches."Unfortunately, the arrangement didn't work out as planned," Stone said.He added that Meta Superintelligence Labs remains committed to work around AI safety, alignment and frontier risk despite the departures.The development comes at a time when major technology companies are investing heavily in advanced AI systems while facing increasing scrutiny over safety, governance and responsible deployment.A strategic hire that lasted only monthsThe Virtue AI team joined Meta in June, according to reporting by Axios.The recruitment was designed to strengthen Meta's security capabilities around AI agents and increasingly advanced AI models. At the time, concerns across the industry were growing over how companies should test, monitor and secure powerful AI systems before wider deployment.Virtue AI had developed enterprise-focused AI security technologies and worked with organisations including Anthropic, OpenAI and the US Commerce Department's National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST).According to Axios, an internal memo announcing the hires stated: "As we ship AI products to billions of people and build increasingly capable agents, keeping those systems safe, reliable, and trustworthy is foundational."Under the reported structure:Bo Li was set to report to Nat Friedman, an executive within Meta Superintelligence LabsDawn Song was also expected to report to FriedmanSanmi Koyejo was set to report to Rob Fergus, head of Meta's Fundamental AI Research (FAIR) labThe terms of the arrangement were not publicly disclosed.Why Virtue AI mattered to MetaMeta recruited the team as part of a broader effort to deepen expertise in AI security and risk management.Virtue AI's work focused on helping organisations identify vulnerabilities in AI systems and implement safeguards before deployment.Its capabilities included:Automated red teaming to uncover weaknesses in AI systemsRuntime guardrails designed to reduce operational risksAI governance tools for oversight and complianceSecurity testing frameworks for enterprise AI applicationsThe move reflected a growing industry focus on ensuring increasingly capable AI systems remain safe, reliable and controllable.Part of a wider AI talent strategyThe Virtue AI recruitment also aligned with Meta's broader approach of hiring specialist AI teams rather than acquiring entire companies.According to the report, Meta used a similar strategy earlier this year when it recruited the founders and team behind Dreamer, an AI startup focused on helping users build AI agents.The approach allows Meta to quickly bring in niche expertise as competition intensifies among major AI developers.However, the Virtue AI episode represents one of the shortest-lived examples of this strategy, with the team departing roughly four months after joining.AI safety remains a priorityDespite the exits, Meta has indicated that its focus on AI safety remains unchanged.The company continues to invest heavily in artificial intelligence as competition accelerates among technology firms building more capable models and AI agents. At the same time, regulators, policymakers and researchers are paying closer attention to how these systems are developed, tested and deployed.The departure of the Virtue AI founders and employees highlights how attracting specialist talent is only one part of the challenge. Integrating teams with distinct expertise, research cultures and operating styles may prove equally important as companies race to build the next generation of AI systems.

shortlist.body: Sam Altman thinks that the benefits of AI will be so great that “the world should accept some bad things happening” along the way.The OpenAI CEO pointed to hacks, scams, and “other bad things” as costs society should expect to tolerate because “people will do tremendously orders of magnitude more good stuff” with AI, without elaborating on the potential benefits. His comments come as OpenAI pushes for a “lighter touch” approach to AI regulation amid intensifying anxiety over the safety of frontier models — fears fueled in part by the company’s repeated failures to keep its increasingly capable AI agents from hacking real-world targets.In an appearance on Politico’s new Decoded podcast — not to be confused with The Verge’s Decoder podcast — released Monday, Altman described that willingness to accept harm in pursuit of AI’s broader benefits as a key distinction between OpenAI and its archrival Anthropic, which was founded by former OpenAI employees following disagreements over AI safety.The calculus echoes comments from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang last month, who similarly argued that AI’s harms should be weighed against the benefits the technology can bring. Both arguments fit within a broader accelerationist view that slowing down AI development carries risks of its own.Altman’s distinction marks another divergence between OpenAI and Anthropic, who until recently had appeared broadly aligned in calling for stronger regulation of advanced AI. While stressing that there’s “a lot of daylight” between OpenAI and Anthropic, Altman said stronger regulations are still needed, positioning OpenAI as “pragmatic centrists” between Anthropic’s more cautious approach and those who favor little to no regulation at all.“If we do too much to restrict this technology in the name of safety, and we end up with a small number of companies or people — or perhaps one country — that have too much power over this, that also is a way that this can go horribly wrong,” Altman said.Altman also acknowledged more extreme risks, including the possibility that humans could lose control of AI systems. When it comes to the potential of a serious loss of control, “let’s be a little thoughtful about lurching into this future,” he said.The balancing act — between heavy-handed restrictions and free rein — was a theme Altman returned to repeatedly in the interview. It is a stance that suits OpenAI as one of the industry’s most entrenched players. It would also likely bear the brunt of onerous regulation, given that the company’s behavior and increasingly capable systems are what have driven many of the very concerns regulators are being asked to address.Those concerns have picked up momentum in recent months as more and more insiders call for slower development and warn about safety culture in frontier labs. Days before the Politico interview aired, longtime OpenAI safety researcher David Robinson quit the firm and described its safety culture as “broken.”Concerns have also been propelled by the discovery that OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face without the AI company’s knowledge earlier this year, which was followed by revelations of numerous other agents or swarms of agents — including from other AI companies, like Anthropic, Meta, and Google — acting against real-world targets. The incidents have raised questions not only about how well AI companies can control their own tools, but also how reliably they let the world know when things go wrong. Australia’s prime minister, for example, excoriated OpenAI and Altman for failing to alert officials in a timely manner that an agent had targeted a government health website.Speaking about rogue AI agents in the Politico interview, Altman said the company has “more things to disclose,” though none at the level of the Hugging Face hack. In line with previous statements, Altman suggested this is likely to take a long time.Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.Robert Hart
